A whitespace-only string has no newline, so the required `\n` never matches: at each character position the leading `\s*` consumes and backtracks over the rest of the string before the global search tries the next position. The work is quadratic and runs synchronously on the event loop.

**Preconditions:** An application enables the namespace through `DEBUG` and passes request-controlled data to a `%o` debug call.

**Evidence:** `src/debug.js:93-108` dispatches `%o` with the caller value when the namespace is enabled, and the new formatter at `src/node.js:83-86` inspects it then applies `/\s*\n\s*/g`. With `DEBUG=attack` and `DEBUG_MAX_STRING_LENGTH=null`, formatting 40,000 spaces took about 1.26 seconds and 80,000 took about 5.27 seconds (roughly four times the work for twice the input). The base commit has no `src/node.js`, so this path becomes reachable through this change; `src/index.js:6-10` selects it in Node.

**Impact:** A remote caller can repeatedly stall a service that logs its input in an enabled namespace. This is a recoverable availability loss across the request boundary; under the review policy it is discounted from high to **medium** because enabling `DEBUG` is non-default.

**Fix:** Normalize lines without the ambiguous adjacent quantifiers, for example split on `\n`, trim each line, and join with one space.

summary:
Reviewed the new `index.js` implementation and its package metadata. The package cannot load in a production install because its new runtime import is undeclared, and the acronym path emits escaped separator text for separators such as `.`. Both issues already have open findings for this PR, so I did not create duplicates.

I also checked replacement-string metacharacters and found no additional issue that warrants a separate finding. No files were changed.

Reviewed the new `index.js` implementation and its documented separator API. I recorded one info-level finding for replacement-token separators producing corrupted output. The existing open finding already covers the separate dynamic-regex denial-of-service path.

findings.title: Replacement-token separators corrupt converted names
findings.body:
A documented string separator containing replacement tokens is not emitted literally. For example, `decamelize('fooBar', '$&')` returns `fooobbar` rather than `foo$&bar`, because `$&` is expanded to the matched `oB` while performing the first replacement. Callers that use a literal `$`-based separator therefore receive corrupted converted names.

**Evidence:** The API accepts `separator` as an unrestricted `string` (`readme.md:29-38`). `index.js:6` preserves the supplied value, then `index.js:7` concatenates it into a `String#replace` replacement template. In that template, `$&` means the full match; running the public export with `'fooBar', '$&'` reproduces the result above.

**Impact:** Each affected conversion has incorrect output until retried with a different separator. This is contained and transient, so severity is **info** under the review policy.

**Fix:** Supply the separator through a replacement callback (or otherwise quote replacement-template tokens), while using an independently escaped value only for the dynamically constructed regular expression.

summary: Reviewed the 88-line `index.js` addition and traced its SQLcl argument flow into the upload script. I recorded two low-severity findings for deployment-result handling and destination validation. The shell-command injection fix correctly preserves executable/argument separation, but the PR should address the recorded issues before approval.

findings.title: Failed SQLcl uploads are reported as successful
findings.body:
`spawnSync` returns a result instead of throwing when SQLcl is missing or exits with an error, but this path always prints `Files were uploaded successfully.`. Thus a normal call with a nonempty directory can report that deployment completed when SQLcl was absent, could not connect, or rejected the upload.

**Evidence:** `spawnSync()` is called at `index.js:74-79`; its `error` and exit `status` are not checked, and execution unconditionally reaches the success log at `index.js:81-82`. The documented default executable is `sql` (`readme.md:33-37`), so an absent SQLcl installation reaches this path.

**Impact:** The affected caller receives a false deployment result and may proceed with a release whose static assets were never uploaded. This is contained and recoverable by fixing SQLcl and retrying, so it is low severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** Treat a non-null `childProcess.error` or a nonzero `childProcess.status` as failure; only emit the success message after a zero exit status.

findings.title: Invalid destinations upload assets as application files
findings.body:
A value outside the documented `destination` choices is accepted and is uploaded as application static files. For example, a caller that supplies `destination: 'workspcae'` expecting workspace assets instead selects `wwv_flow_api.create_app_static_file`, so the whole directory is deployed to the application scope instead of failing validation.

**Evidence:** The only validation for `destination` is the plugin-name check at `index.js:30-32`. The `default` branch at `index.js:50-62` labels every unrecognized value as an application upload, and the value is forwarded at `index.js:64-71`. `lib/distUpload.js:55-96` sends every value other than `theme`, `workspace`, or `plugin` to the application-static-file API. The documented choices are limited to `application`, `workspace`, `theme`, and `plugin` (`readme.md:40`).

**Impact:** A typo can place release assets in the wrong APEX storage scope rather than stopping the deployment. The effect is confined to the caller's selected application and is recoverable by removing the misplaced files and retrying, so it is low severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** Validate `destination` against the documented choices before launching SQLcl, and reject other values instead of taking the application fallback.

summary: Reviewed the new `index.js` entry point and its merge behavior. I confirmed and recorded one high-severity finding: untrusted JSON using a `constructor.prototype` path can pollute `Object.prototype` despite the `__proto__` filter. The normal merge behavior remains consistent with the existing tests; the prototype-pollution path needs remediation before approval.

findings.title: Merging JSON input can pollute Object.prototype
findings.body:
An application that deep-merges parsed request JSON can let the request modify `Object.prototype`. A payload such as `{"constructor":{"prototype":{"isAdmin":true}}}` is enumerated because only `__proto__` is excluded. With the normal `{}` target, `target.constructor` resolves to `Object`, then the recursive merge follows `Object.prototype` and writes `isAdmin` there. The result changes inherited properties of ordinary objects throughout the Node process.

**Evidence:** `mixinDeep({}, JSON.parse('{"constructor":{"prototype":{"ozoneProof":"yes"}}}'))` makes `({}).ozoneProof` equal `"yes"`. The `for...in` filter admits `constructor` at index.js:6-9; inherited lookup of `target[key]` at index.js:14 returns `Object`, and recursion at index.js:15-16 subsequently writes the payload property at index.js:18. The public export exposes this path at index.js:34.

**Impact:** Any caller that merges untrusted JSON crosses its request-data trust boundary and can poison shared process state, which can alter authorization and other property-based checks. The pollution remains effective until restart and is re-triggerable, so this is high severity under the review reach/persistence policy.

**Fix:** Reject `constructor` and `prototype` keys as well as `__proto__` before reading or recursing into a target property (and ideally enumerate only own source properties).

summary: Reviewed the new `publish()` entry point and its SQLcl handoff, including option validation and downstream script behavior. The change is not ready to merge: I recorded one high-severity finding.

findings.title: Attacker-controlled connection strings execute OS commands
findings.body:
`publish()` interpolates `connectString` into a shell command without quoting it. A value such as `ignored; /usr/bin/touch /tmp/marker; #` terminates SQLcl's argument, executes the injected command, and comments out the rest of the invocation.

**Preconditions:** An attacker can influence the `connectString` supplied to the public `publish()` API, such as through a service or build wrapper that accepts connection configuration.

**Evidence:** `connectString` is only checked for presence at `index.js:18-20`, then concatenated unquoted into the single command string passed to `execSync` at `index.js:54-65`. A safe call with `sqlclPath: '/bin/true'`, `directory: '.'`, `appID: 1`, and `connectString: 'ignored; /usr/bin/touch /tmp/ozbench-cve-2018-16462-safe-marker; #'` created the marker. The final injected command exits successfully, so this path also returns `true` at `index.js:68-72`.

**Impact:** This crosses the configuration-input trust boundary to execute arbitrary OS commands as the process that performs APEX publishing. Under the review severity policy, this is high: the resulting host compromise is not recoverable by this package.

**Fix:** Do not construct a shell command from option values. Invoke SQLcl with `execFileSync` (or `spawnSync`) and an argument array, keeping each supplied value as one argument; alternatively strictly validate the connection-string grammar before use.

summary: Reviewed the added `slug.js` implementation and its documented API, tests, module exports, and fixed-reference diff. I recorded two findings: a medium-severity event-loop denial of service in whitespace trimming and an info-severity literal-separator handling defect. The PR should not merge until the trimming implementation is corrected; the fixed reference’s use of `String.prototype.trim()` addresses the main issue.

findings.title: Interior whitespace can block slugification quadratically
findings.body:
A caller can make the synchronous slugification path consume quadratic CPU with a normal input such as `a` followed by many spaces and `b`. The final trim expression tries `\s+$` at every interior space; each attempt scans and backtracks across the remaining run before failing at `b`. On Node 24, 80,000 spaces take about 6 seconds while producing the ordinary result `a-b`.

**Evidence:** `slug()` accepts the input without a length limit at `slug.js:12-24`, preserves ASCII whitespace while building `result` at `slug.js:37-62`, then applies `/^\s+|\s+$/g` at `slug.js:64` before collapsing that whitespace at `slug.js:65`. The package exports this function at `slug.js:198-200`. The time grows quadratically: 10,000, 20,000, 40,000, and 80,000 interior spaces took approximately 93 ms, 371 ms, 1.52 s, and 6.31 s, respectively.

**Impact:** An application that passes request-controlled titles or names to this library can have its Node event loop blocked per request. Under the review policy this is **medium**: the availability impact is broad for the serving process and clears after the request finishes, but an untrusted caller can repeat it.

**Fix:** Replace the anchored global regex trims with `String.prototype.trim()` (including this final trim), which performs the required leading/trailing whitespace removal without retrying every interior position.

findings.title: Replacement-token separators corrupt converted names
findings.body:
A documented literal separator containing a replacement token is not emitted literally. For example, `slug('foo bar', '$&')` returns `foo bar`, because `$&` means “the matched whitespace” to `String#replace`, rather than the expected `foo$&bar`. This prevents callers from using such strings as separators and can leave whitespace in a slug.

**Evidence:** The public API accepts a replacement string at `slug.js:13-15`, and the README documents it as the value that replaces spaces (`README.md:50-58`). `slug.js:65` passes that value directly as the replacement template to `String#replace`, which gives `$&`, `$'`, and `$`` special meanings.

**Impact:** This produces an incorrect result for one caller that selects these valid separator strings. Under the review policy this is **info**: the effect is contained to that conversion and transient.

**Fix:** Use a replacement callback, such as `result.replace(/[-\s]+/g, function () { return opts.replacement; })`, so separators are inserted literally.

summary:
Reviewed the full `slug.js` addition. It matches the upstream `slug@0.9.2` CVE fix: both vulnerable whitespace-trimming regexes are replaced with `String.prototype.trim()`, avoiding the ReDoS path while preserving normal behavior. I found no new regressions in the fixed change and created no findings.

Validation: copied the change into an isolated install and ran `npm test` successfully.

Reviewed the new `mixinDeep` entry point and its merge behavior. I recorded one low-severity finding: object-valued inherited method keys can cause the merge to modify a shared built-in function rather than the supplied target. The explicit prototype-pollution denylist blocks the documented `__proto__` and `constructor.prototype` paths.  

Installed dependencies and ran the existing suite: 15 tests passed.

findings.title: Object-valued toString input corrupts the shared type-checking function
findings.body:
An application that merges request JSON into a normal `{}` target can mutate a shared built-in instead of setting the requested target property. For example, `mixinDeep({}, JSON.parse('{"toString":{"call":null}}'))` recurses into the inherited `Object.prototype.toString` function and sets its `call` property to `null`. Later `Object.prototype.toString.call(value)` fails process-wide until the property is removed or the process restarts.

**Preconditions:** The caller passes an object-valued, untrusted `toString` field to a merge whose target lacks an own `toString` property.

**Evidence:** `isValidKey` permits `toString` (`index.js:7-9`), and the loop forwards it to `mixin` (`index.js:14-17`). `mixin` reads `target[key]` through the prototype chain (`index.js:25`); since functions are mergeable (`index.js:3-5`), it recursively merges the JSON object into the inherited `Object.prototype.toString` function (`index.js:26-27`) and writes `call` there (`index.js:29`). No own `target.toString` is created.

**Impact:** A caller able to influence merge input can corrupt a shared type-checking function for the Node process. This is a conditional, recoverable denial of service/correctness failure, so severity is low under the review policy.

**Fix:** Recurse only when the existing target value is an own property (or otherwise create an own plain-object destination before recursion); never merge into inherited values.

summary:
Reviewed the new MSSQL client implementation, including query compilation, identifier handling, bindings, response processing, and connection lifecycle. I recorded three findings; the change should not merge until they are addressed.

I verified the identifier and escaped-placeholder failures with direct compilation repros. The targeted Mocha suite could not start because the installed `sqlite3` package lacks a native binding for the sandbox’s Node.js version.

findings.title: Untrusted identifiers can terminate MSSQL quoting and execute SQL
findings.body:
An application that passes an external table or column choice to Knex's normal identifier APIs can execute injected T-SQL. For example, `knex('users]; DROP TABLE audit_log;--').select('*').toSQL().sql` produces `select * from [users]; DROP TABLE audit_log;--]`.

**Preconditions:** The application uses an untrusted value as an identifier (for example, a selected table or column), rather than validating it against an allowlist.

**Evidence:** The public `knex(table)` path stores the supplied table name without validation (`lib/util/make-knex.js:12-14`, `lib/query/builder.js:173-182`) and the compiler wraps it (`lib/query/compiler.js:846-859`). `wrapIdentifierImpl` only replaces `[` with itself and leaves `]` unchanged, so the attacker closes the bracket-delimited identifier (`lib/dialects/mssql/index.js:209-211`). The MSSQL request enables multiple statements and sends this SQL unchanged (`lib/dialects/mssql/index.js:292-305`).

**Impact:** This crosses a trust boundary: attacker text accepted as an identifier becomes SQL executed with the configured SQL Server account's permissions. Under the review policy this is high severity because it permits arbitrary database actions, subject to that account's privileges.

**Fix:** Escape the closing bracket in every non-wildcard identifier (for example, replace `]` with `]]`) before adding the outer brackets, and add a regression test through a normal table/column builder API.

findings.title: Escaped question marks shift MSSQL parameter indexes
findings.body:
Escaped literal question marks in `raw` SQL are converted into parameter names, which can either change a query result or leave the actual parameter unbound. For example, `knex.raw("select '\\?' as marker, ? as value", [123])` first preserves `\\?` as Knex's documented literal-question-mark escape, then this client sends `select '\\@p0' as marker, @p1 as value` while binding only `p0`; SQL Server rejects the undeclared `@p1`.

**Evidence:** Raw binding replacement explicitly preserves `\\?` and does not consume a binding for it (`lib/raw.js:120-145`). Every query then passes through `positionBindings` before execution (`lib/client.js:146-158`), but this implementation replaces every `?`, including the escaped one (`lib/dialects/mssql/index.js:250-256`). `_query` independently binds values starting at `p0` (`lib/dialects/mssql/index.js:295-305`).

**Impact:** Any MSSQL application using Knex's supported escaped-question-mark syntax can have otherwise valid queries fail. The failure is request-scoped and recoverable, so it is medium severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** Recognize `\\?` in `positionBindings`, emit a literal `?` for it without advancing the parameter counter, and cover escaped placeholders with and without adjacent bindings.

findings.title: Fractional MSSQL bindings lose precision beyond ten decimal places
findings.body:
Fractional JavaScript number bindings are rounded to ten decimal places before SQL Server evaluates them. For example, inserting `1.23456789123` into a `decimal(20, 12)` column binds it as `Decimal(38, 10)`, so the server receives `1.2345678912` and persistently stores the wrong value.

**Preconditions:** A query binds a fractional `Number` with more than ten significant fractional digits.

**Evidence:** `_setReqInput` routes every non-integer number to `this.driver.Decimal(38, 10)` (`lib/dialects/mssql/index.js:310-315`), and both normal and streamed query paths pass every binding through that method (`lib/dialects/mssql/index.js:274-280`, `lib/dialects/mssql/index.js:295-300`). In the declared `mssql`/`tedious` v5.1 dependency path, Decimal serialization rounds the value at its declared scale; the driver otherwise infers a non-integral `Number` as Float.

**Impact:** Inserts, updates, and predicates can silently use or persist a rounded value. The effect needs a higher-precision fractional input, which limits reach; the incorrect stored value may remain after the request. This is medium severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** Bind non-integral JavaScript numbers using a type that preserves their representable precision (such as the driver's `Float(53)`), rather than imposing a fixed decimal scale of ten.

summary:
Reviewed the complete 155-line `index.js` addition and its documented API behavior. I recorded two findings: one high-severity issue and one low-severity issue.

The AVA suite passes directly (`26 passed`). `npm test` cannot complete in this environment because the legacy lint dependency calls removed Node API `util.isDate`; this is unrelated to the PR code. Overall, the change should not be approved until the recorded issues are fixed.

findings.title: JSON-derived options can pollute Object.prototype
Arrays with an own slice property make option merging throw
findings.body:
A valid nested array can make every merge that contains it throw instead of returning cloned options. For example:
```js
const items = [1];
items.slice = 0;
mergeOptions({items}); // TypeError: array.slice is not a function
```

**Evidence:** Arrays are accepted as nested option values and sent to `cloneArray` (`index.js:34-40`). That function invokes the instance property `array.slice(0, 0)` before copying enumerable own keys (`index.js:46-51`). An array can legally have an own enumerable `slice` data property, and the API says it clones arrays using enumerable own properties (`readme.md:35-37,97`). The same unsafe call is used while initializing concatenated arrays (`index.js:88-90`).

**Impact:** A caller-controlled JavaScript options array can cause a contained, recoverable per-call availability failure. Severity is **low** under the review policy. JSON arrays cannot carry this property, but programmatic callers can.

**Fix:** Create the empty result with a captured intrinsic, such as `Array.prototype.slice.call(array, 0, 0)`, at both clone and concatenation sites, rather than calling the array instance's `slice` property.

summary:
Reviewed the complete `index.js` addition. It implements the upstream prototype-pollution fix: writes use own data properties and the merge path avoids recursing into the destination prototype. Targeted JSON `__proto__` and `constructor.prototype` payloads did not mutate `Object.prototype`; AVA passed all 26 tests.

I found no reportable issues in this PR.

Reviewed the full added `lib/node-http-proxy.js` surface and traced its proxy, routing, buffering, middleware, agent, and WebSocket entry points. The PR matches the upstream CVE fix: middleware errors passed through `next(err)` now return a 500 response or close an already-started response instead of escaping as an uncaught exception.

I found no PR-specific issues to record. Some retained documentation and tests describe routing and composed-middleware APIs that the benchmark’s upstream snapshot had already removed before this patch; they are not regressions introduced by this fixed CVE change.

Reviewed the full newly added `lib/node-http-proxy.js` surface and its documented callers. I recorded two low-severity findings: middleware error handling can terminate a middleware-enabled proxy, and the documented Connect middleware API passes no callable continuation. I reproduced both request-time process exits with minimal local HTTP handlers and compared the alternate fixed branch; it addresses only the former error path. Overall, this PR should not be approved without restoring safe middleware handling and the documented middleware contract.

findings.title: Middleware errors can terminate the proxy process
findings.body:
A request that makes installed middleware call `next(err)` terminates the Node process instead of receiving an error response. This can make a proxy unavailable to all clients.

**Preconditions:** The application uses the exported `stack()` handler with middleware that reports a request-controlled failure through `next(err)`.

**Evidence:** `stack()` supplies each layer with `next`; its error path throws directly at `lib/node-http-proxy.js:223-225`, outside any handler. A local HTTP server using this exported handler and middleware that calls `next(new Error(...))` for `GET /bad` exits with status 1. The documented middleware API makes this handler model supported (`README.md:316-324`). The fixed PR replaces this branch with a 500 response or response destruction and returns (`origin/pr/fixed:lib/node-http-proxy.js:223-239`).

**Impact:** One unauthenticated request can stop the process for a middleware-enabled deployment. Availability affects all users until the service is restarted, but the application must opt into middleware and expose a request-controlled error path, so this is **low** under the review policy (broad, recoverable availability impact, discounted for a non-default configuration).

**Fix:** Handle middleware errors in `next` by ending an unstarted response with HTTP 500 (or destroying a started response) and return without throwing.

findings.title: Documented Connect middleware receives no callable next
findings.body:
The advertised Connect middleware form cannot proxy a request. A standard middleware calls its third `next` argument, but `createServer` passes the `HttpProxy` object instead; `next()` therefore throws `TypeError` from the request listener and can terminate the process.

**Preconditions:** The application uses the documented Connect middleware form.

**Evidence:** The README documents `createServer(require('connect-gzip').gzip(), 9000, 'localhost')` at `README.md:316-324`; the checked-in example uses that exact call at `examples/gzip-middleware.js:35-38`. Argument parsing records every function as `callback` (`lib/node-http-proxy.js:73-79`) and the resulting server handler calls it as `callback(req, res, proxy)` (`lib/node-http-proxy.js:103-106`). `proxy` is an object, not a continuation. A minimal `(req, res, next) => next()` handler exits Node with `TypeError: next is not a function` on the first request.

**Impact:** A normal use of the documented feature either fails requests or, without an application-level uncaught-exception handler, lets any client request stop that middleware-enabled proxy. This is **low** under the review policy: the recoverable outage affects the service broadly but requires the non-default middleware configuration.

**Fix:** Adapt middleware to the Connect contract: give it a callable `next` that invokes `proxy.proxyRequest(req, res)` (and handle `next(err)` as an HTTP error), or remove the unsupported middleware documentation.

summary: Reviewed the full 884-line client implementation added in PR #2. I recorded six findings: four high-severity client-side security issues and two low-severity UI/state regressions. The change restores the missing Socket.IO client behavior but exposes several existing untrusted-data paths through unsafe DOM rendering and persistent authentication handling.

findings.title: IRC topic updates execute script in connected clients
findings.body:
An IRC user who can change a channel topic can run script in every connected Shout client. The live topic event writes the raw topic to an HTML sink, unlike the initial-topic template path, which passes the value through the escaping `parse` helper.

**Evidence:** `src/plugins/irc-events/topic.js:6-33` copies the IRC-controlled topic and emits it to clients. The new handler inserts that value with `.html(data.topic)` at `client/js/shout.js:317-319`; for example, an `img` with an `onerror` handler executes when a channel operator sets the topic. The initial rendering instead uses `parse` in `client/views/chat.tpl:20`, whose escaping is implemented at `client/js/libs/handlebars/parse.js:26-34`.

**Impact:** Channel operators cross the trust boundary from IRC content to script execution in each viewer's Shout origin, where they can read IRC history and act through the authenticated Socket.IO session. This is high severity under the policy's cross-trust-boundary and recoverable criteria.

**Fix:** Render live topic updates as text (or apply the same safe parsing/escaping used for the initial topic); never pass raw IRC topic text to an HTML sink.

findings.title: Link-preview titles execute script in IRC clients
findings.body:
A channel participant can execute script in recipients' browsers by posting an attacker-controlled HTTPS URL. The link-preview fetch decodes the remote page title, and the new toggle listener inserts the title through an unescaped template into jQuery's HTML insertion path.

**Evidence:** With prefetch enabled by default (`defaults/config.js:57-65`), `src/plugins/irc-events/link.js:62-74` reads a fetched HTML `<title>` and assigns it to `toggle.head`, then emits the toggle at line 88. The new listener at `client/js/shout.js:299-315` calls `.after(render("toggle", ...))`. `client/views/toggle.tpl:12` uses `{{{head}}}`, so a title such as `<img src=x onerror=...>` becomes executable markup. Link previews are enabled by default and automatically toggled at `client/js/shout.js:302-306,332-345`.

**Impact:** Any IRC participant who can send a URL crosses the trust boundary into script execution in other users' Shout origins. The script can access their IRC data and authenticated actions. This is high severity under the policy's cross-trust-boundary and recoverable criteria.

**Fix:** Treat fetched metadata as text: change `head` to an escaped template expression (and retain URL validation for link attributes).

findings.title: Mixed-case JavaScript URLs execute when IRC links are opened
findings.body:
An IRC sender can make a victim execute JavaScript by sending a mixed-case `javascript:` URL and persuading them to open the rendered link. The URI parser recognizes schemes case-insensitively, but the linkifier rejects only an all-lowercase prefix.

**Evidence:** The new message handler renders and appends IRC message text at `client/js/shout.js:184-198`; `client/views/msg.tpl:21` passes it through `parse`. `client/js/libs/handlebars/parse.js:37-47` rejects only `uri.indexOf("javascript:") === 0` and otherwise emits an `href`. URI recognition is case-insensitive (`client/js/libs/uri.js:192-198`), so `JaVaScRiPt://%0Aalert(document.domain)` becomes a clickable JavaScript URL; URL scheme matching in browsers is case-insensitive.

**Impact:** A channel participant can cross the trust boundary to execute script in a recipient's Shout origin after a click. That script can access the recipient's IRC data and authenticated actions. This is high severity under the policy's cross-trust-boundary and recoverable criteria.

**Fix:** Parse and allowlist safe URL schemes (for example `http:` and `https:`) case-insensitively before generating an anchor.

findings.title: HTTPS session tokens are exposed on HTTP requests
findings.body:
The new persistent authentication-token cookie is sent on plaintext HTTP even when the user signed in through HTTPS. A network attacker can induce a request to `http://` on the same host and capture the bearer token, then authenticate as that user.

**Preconditions:** Private Shout is served over HTTPS and the user selects the default “Stay signed in” option.

**Evidence:** The new code writes `token` for 30 days but passes no `secure` option at `client/js/shout.js:135-141`. The bundled cookie library emits `; secure` only when explicitly requested (`client/js/libs/jquery/cookie.js:67-73`). Cookies are host-scoped rather than port-scoped, so this HTTPS-issued cookie accompanies a request to the same host over HTTP. The server accepts the 48-byte token as an unbound bearer credential at `src/server.js:145-160`; the token is generated at `src/client.js:63-65`.

**Impact:** A network attacker crosses the authentication boundary and can access the victim's IRC state and issue authenticated Socket.IO actions. This is high severity under the policy's cross-trust-boundary and recoverable criteria.

**Fix:** Set `secure: location.protocol === "https:"` when persisting the token, so HTTPS-issued tokens are never sent over HTTP while supported HTTP-only deployments continue to work.

findings.title: Disconnecting the final network leaves a stale send target
findings.body:
Disconnecting the last network leaves its old chat pane active and its input target selected. The user can type and submit into the visible stale pane, but the server has already removed that channel, so the text is silently discarded.

**Evidence:** The new `quit` handler removes only the sidebar network at `client/js/shout.js:286-297`; it does not remove the corresponding `#chan-*` panes or clear `chat.data("id")`. If no other sidebar channel exists, the click at lines 291-293 does nothing. The active old pane remains visible, while submits use the stale `chat.data("id")` at lines 408-420. The server removes the network before emitting this event (`src/plugins/inputs/quit.js:3-18`), and `Client.find()` cannot resolve the old ID (`src/client.js:101-120`), so the input plugin is not reached (`src/client.js:223-245`).

**Impact:** A user who disconnects their final network loses submitted messages without feedback until they reload or reconnect. The effect is contained and recoverable, so it is low severity under the policy.

**Fix:** On `quit`, remove the disconnected network's chat panes and clear/disable the input when no channel remains.

findings.title: Repeated Show more clicks duplicate chat history
findings.body:
Rapid repeated clicks on Show more request the same history page multiple times and prepend every duplicate. This also makes later pagination overlap rather than progress correctly.

**Evidence:** The new handler at `client/js/shout.js:623-629` does not disable the button or track a request in flight, so two clicks both send the same DOM child count. For each request, the server derives the same slice from that count (`src/client.js:248-260`), and the client unconditionally prepends both responses (`client/js/shout.js:216-225`). For a 250-message channel initially showing messages 150–249, two requests at count 100 each return 50–149, producing two visible copies of that range.

**Impact:** A user can corrupt their own visible history and inflate its DOM until reload. The effect is contained and recoverable, so it is low severity under the policy.

**Fix:** Disable or mark Show more while its request is pending, and ignore stale/duplicate history responses.

summary:
Reviewed the added login model and its routes, login UI, query parsing, and fixed PR variant. Recorded one high-severity finding: the post-login `redirect` parameter can send authenticated users to an attacker-controlled origin.

The fixed variant rejects cross-origin redirects, confirming the intended safe behavior. No code changes were made.

findings.title: Login redirects authenticated users to attacker-controlled origins
findings.body:
An attacker can put an arbitrary absolute URL in the public login page's `redirect` query parameter. Once a victim completes a normal login, the model assigns that URL to `window.location.href`, sending the just-authenticated user to an attacker-controlled origin.

**Evidence:** `/user/login` is public (`config/config.ts:90-98`), and the form dispatches `login/login` after credential validation (`src/pages/user/login/index.tsx:46-57`). On a successful response, the added model obtains `redirect` from the browser URL and, when its origin differs, executes `window.location.href = redirect` (`src/models/login.ts:44-57`). For example, a link ending in `/user/login?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fevil.example` reaches that assignment after login. The fixed PR variant changes this branch to navigate to `/` instead.

**Impact:** A remote attacker can use the trusted application's login flow to redirect a victim who has just authenticated to a phishing origin. This crosses the application-origin trust boundary and is recoverable by leaving the attacker page, so it is high severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** Never navigate to a non-same-origin value from this parameter. On an origin mismatch, use a fixed internal destination (such as `/`) and only route validated same-origin paths.

summary: Reviewed PR #2 and recorded three findings: an archive path traversal, premature extraction completion signaling, and lost empty directory entries. The new `Extract` API writes ZIP members through `fstream` but does not enforce the selected destination boundary or synchronize its completion event with file writes. Tests were not run because dependencies are not installed.

findings.title: Archive entries can write outside the extraction directory
findings.body:
A ZIP member named `../escaped.txt` is written outside the requested extraction directory. Any application that extracts an archive supplied across its trust boundary can therefore let the archive author create or overwrite files writable by the extraction process outside that directory.

**Evidence:** `Parse` copies the ZIP local-header filename directly to `entry.path` (`lib/parse.js:77-96`). `Extract` passes that archive-controlled value to `path.join(opts.path, entry.path)` and then to `fstream.Writer` without checking containment (`lib/extract.js:18-22`). A ZIP containing `../escaped.txt` extracted to `/tmp/destination` created `/tmp/escaped.txt`, not `/tmp/destination/escaped.txt`.

**Impact:** High. This crosses the archive-input trust boundary and permits arbitrary writable-path modification outside the caller's selected extraction root. The change introduces the vulnerable extraction API.

**Fix:** Normalize each entry name and reject absolute paths and names whose resolved path is not beneath the resolved extraction root before creating a writer. Also account for platform path separators.

findings.title: Extract signals completion before file writes finish
findings.body:
`Extract` emits `close` while its file writers can still be writing. Callers following the documented completion event can read, publish, move, or delete an incomplete output directory.

**Evidence:** Each entry is piped to a new `fstream.Writer`, but the extractor only listens for writer errors and never waits for writer completion (`lib/extract.js:20-25`). The inherited parser emits `close` as soon as its writable side finishes (`lib/parse.js:25-27`), after it consumes the ZIP end record (`lib/parse.js:231-235`). The public contract says `close` means all contents have been written (`README.md:24-30`). With the bundled standard archive, `Extract` emitted `close` before both writer `close` events.

**Impact:** Low. Normal callers that use the documented event can act on a partially extracted directory; retrying after writers finish recovers it.

**Fix:** Track every writer and defer the extractor's public completion event until parsing has ended and all writers have closed; propagate write errors through that same completion path.

findings.title: Extract drops explicit empty directories
findings.body:
Archives with an explicit empty directory lose that directory even though extraction completes successfully. This makes the resulting tree differ from the archive without any error.

**Evidence:** `Parse` classifies a zero-size member whose name ends in `/` or `\\` as `Directory` (`lib/parse.js:93-96`). `Extract` immediately returns for that type and creates no directory (`lib/extract.js:18-19`). A ZIP containing only `explicit-empty/` emitted `close` with no `explicit-empty` directory on disk. Directories containing files are masked because the file writer creates their parents.

**Impact:** Low. Callers can silently receive an incomplete directory layout, but no access boundary is crossed and re-extracting after a fix recovers the missing directory.

**Fix:** Create a directory writer for directory entries, or explicitly create and await the target directory before proceeding.

summary: Reviewed the new streaming `Extract` implementation and its parser and writer interactions. I recorded four findings: one high-severity path-containment bypass and three lower-severity extraction correctness and completion issues. The change is not ready to merge because the zip-slip mitigation remains bypassable.

findings.title: Crafted ZIP entries can write to prefixed sibling paths
findings.body:
A crafted ZIP filename can still make `Extract` write outside its destination. With `opts.path` set to `/tmp/out`, an entry named `../out-evil/pwn` produces `/tmp/out-evil/pwn`; that is outside `/tmp/out` but passes the string-prefix test.

**Evidence:** ZIP filenames become `entry.path` in `lib/parse.js:77-96`. `lib/extract.js:24-30` joins that untrusted value and accepts it when `extractPath.indexOf(opts.path) == 0`, then passes the resulting outside path to `fstream.Writer`. A local reproduction with that entry wrote the archive data to the sibling `out-evil/pwn` directory.

**Impact:** An actor who can supply an archive to an application using `Extract` can overwrite or create files reachable by the application process outside the intended extraction directory. This crosses the archive-content trust boundary and can persist until the affected file is restored, so severity is high under the review policy.

**Fix:** Resolve the extraction root and candidate path, then require the candidate to be the root or to begin with the root plus the platform separator (or use `path.relative` and reject an absolute or `..`-prefixed relative path) before creating the writer.

findings.title: Rejected ZIP entries leave extraction streams stalled
findings.body:
An entry that the traversal check rejects is not consumed, so a sufficiently large rejected file leaves extraction permanently incomplete. Applications waiting for the documented `close` completion event can then hang on an attacker-controlled archive.

**Evidence:** `lib/extract.js:24-27` returns for a rejected entry without piping or draining it. The parser later pipes archive data into that `PassThrough` entry and only reads the next ZIP record after that pipe finishes (`lib/parse.js:154-160`). A 65,536-byte rejected stored entry reproduced the stall: neither `close` nor writable `finish` occurred. `ParseOne` uses `entry.autodrain()` for entries it skips (`lib/parseOne.js:18-20`), and that helper consumes data through `NoopStream` (`lib/parse.js:81-86`).

**Impact:** A supplied archive can block one extraction job until the host times it out or restarts it. The failure is contained to that extraction and recoverable, so severity is low under the review policy.

**Fix:** Call `entry.autodrain()` before returning for every entry that is intentionally skipped, and forward a drain error to the extractor.

findings.title: Dot-relative extraction destinations discard valid entries
findings.body:
A valid relative destination beginning with `./` silently receives no files. `path.join('./out', 'normal.txt')` normalizes to `out/normal.txt`, but the guard compares it to the unnormalized `./out` and rejects the entry; the extractor still emits `close` for a small archive.

**Evidence:** `lib/extract.js:24-27` performs the normalized-candidate versus raw-root prefix comparison and returns before `Writer` is created. Reproducing `Extract({path: './out'})` with a one-byte `normal.txt` ZIP entry emitted `close` but created neither `out` nor `out/normal.txt`. The normal extraction test uses an absolute temp path (`test/uncompressed.js:25-35`), so it does not cover this API input.

**Impact:** Callers that use the common `./directory` form can treat an archive as successfully extracted even though its files were discarded. The failure is confined to that extraction and is recoverable by retrying with a normalized destination, so severity is low under the review policy.

**Fix:** Normalize or resolve the destination once before both joining and containment validation; this also lets the containment check compare paths on the same basis.

findings.title: Extract emits close before output writers finish
findings.body:
`Extract` can emit its documented completion event while a file is still being written. Code that begins consuming the destination in its `close` handler can read a truncated file.

**Evidence:** `Parse` maps input `finish` directly to `close` (`lib/parse.js:25-27`), while `lib/extract.js:29-34` starts `fstream.Writer` instances without tracking their completion. Extracting a 20 MiB stored entry reproduced this: at `close`, the output was 20,971,481 bytes; 100 ms later it was 20,971,520 bytes. This contradicts the documented guarantee that `close` occurs once contents are fully extracted (`README.md:30`).

**Impact:** A consumer that trusts `close` can briefly observe incomplete output from one extraction. The writer completes on its own, making this a contained transient failure and severity info under the review policy.

**Fix:** Track every writer and emit extraction completion only after the parser and all writers have finished (while preserving writer error propagation).

summary:
Reviewed PR #1 and recorded one low-severity finding: logout only redirects and leaves the browser session’s authority and current-user state intact.

The change correctly prevents successful login from navigating to a cross-origin redirect target. I found no additional qualifying issues in the normal configured login and redirect flows. Dependencies were absent, so I did not run the test suite; `git diff --check` passed.

findings.title: Logout leaves the current browser session authorized
findings.body:
Clicking Logout only changes the route. The same SPA session retains both the role in `localStorage` and `user.currentUser`, so the user can follow the login-page root link back to `/welcome` without authenticating again.

**Evidence:** A successful login persists `currentAuthority` via `setAuthority` (src/models/login.ts:37-42,83-90). The new `logout` effect only calls `routerRedux.replace`; it neither clears that authority nor resets `user.currentUser` (src/models/login.ts:67-79). `SecurityLayout` treats an existing `currentUser.userid` as logged in and renders children even while a new user lookup is pending (src/layouts/SecurityLayout.tsx:23-32,40-51). The login layout links to `/` (src/layouts/UserLayout.tsx:48-51), and `/welcome` is an `admin`/`user` route (config/config.ts:100-123).

**Impact:** A user who has logged out can re-enter the protected UI in the same browser tab. This has contained, recoverable impact, so the severity is low under the review policy; server-side authorization must still protect data APIs.

**Fix:** Make logout revoke the client session state before navigation: clear the persisted authority and reset `user.currentUser` (and invoke the application's server-side logout endpoint when one exists).

summary:
Reviewed the new `lib/unpack.js` implementation and recorded five findings, including a high-severity archive hard-link overwrite outside `cwd`. I also found extraction-root handling, synchronous lifecycle/write integrity, and async error-recovery defects.  

`npm test` ran 6,484 of 6,485 assertions successfully; the sole failure is an existing `test/parse.js` zlib-warning expectation under the current runtime, not in the changed unpack path.

findings.title: A tar archive can overwrite files outside the extraction directory
findings.body:
A tar archive can overwrite a file outside the extraction directory. A `Link` entry can create `cwd/alias` as a hard link to `../victim`; a later `File` entry for `alias` reuses that inode and truncates it.

**Preconditions:** The process extracts an attacker-controlled archive on the same filesystem as a file the process can hard-link, using default `unlink: false`.

**Evidence:** `HARDLINK` resolves the unvalidated archive link target relative to `cwd` (`lib/unpack.js:336-338`). When the later file entry finds the alias, `CHECKFS` reuses every existing regular file without checking `st.nlink` (`lib/unpack.js:360-364`; synchronously `lib/unpack.js:422-426`). The file writer then opens that shared inode for writing (`lib/unpack.js:248-253`; synchronously `lib/unpack.js:459`). Reproducing a `Link alias -> ../victim` followed by `File alias` changed `victim` from `ORIGINAL` to archive data in both modes. The fixed branch adds the required `st.nlink <= 1` reuse guard.

**Impact:** An untrusted archive crosses the extraction boundary and permanently modifies a file outside `cwd` that the extracting process can access. Per the review policy, this is high severity (trust-boundary reach and permanent data corruption).

**Fix:** Reuse an existing regular file only when it has at most one hard link (and never on Windows, where link counts are unreliable); otherwise unlink and recreate the destination before writing.

findings.title: Fully stripped entries modify the extraction root
findings.body:
An entry fully consumed by `strip` is mapped to `cwd` instead of being skipped. A normal top-level directory entry such as `top/` extracted with `strip: 1` becomes an empty pathname, then changes the extraction root's metadata; a one-component symlink entry can replace an empty extraction root with an archive-chosen symlink.

**Preconditions:** A caller uses nonzero `strip` while extracting an attacker-controlled archive.

**Evidence:** The `parts.length < this.strip` check accepts entries with no meaningful component after stripping, and `join('/')` yields `''` (`lib/unpack.js:135-141`). `path.resolve(this.cwd, '')` is `cwd` (`lib/unpack.js:166-169`). Directory handling chmods the existing directory and applies archive mtime/ownership (`lib/unpack.js:355-375`, `lib/unpack.js:299-324`). A local extraction of `top/` with `strip: 1` changed a `0755` output directory to archive mode `0700` and set its archive mtime. `top` as a symlink similarly replaces an empty `cwd`.

**Impact:** An attacker can alter permissions, timestamps, and, in privileged owner-preserving extraction, ownership of the caller-selected extraction root; it can also replace an empty root with a symlink. This requires the non-default `strip` option and is contained to that root, so per the review policy it is medium severity.

**Fix:** Before resolving the destination, skip an entry whose stripped pathname has no real remaining component. Account for trailing separators, so checking only `parts.length <= strip` is not sufficient.

findings.title: Skipped synchronous extractions never emit completion events
findings.body:
`Unpack.Sync` never finishes when it skips an existing entry or handles a nonfatal filesystem error. Its overridden filesystem check does not increment the pending count, but the inherited skip and error paths decrement it; the counter becomes `-1`, so the close gate can never pass.

**Evidence:** `PENDING` starts at zero and terminal events require it to equal zero (`lib/unpack.js:59-60`, `lib/unpack.js:126-132`). Async `CHECKFS` increments it before a possible skip (`lib/unpack.js:355-362`), but synchronous `CHECKFS` does not (`lib/unpack.js:417-424`). `SKIP` always calls `UNPEND` (`lib/unpack.js:349-351`), as does the normal warning path (`lib/unpack.js:200-210`). Reproduction: writing a one-file archive to `tar.x({sync:true, cwd, keep:true})` where the file already exists preserved the file but emitted none of `prefinish`, `finish`, `end`, or `close`; a nonempty-directory overwrite error has the same result.

**Impact:** Consumers of the documented writable sync unpack stream cannot observe completion after normal `keep`/`newer` behavior or a recoverable extraction failure. The extraction is otherwise complete and retrying with a new stream recovers, so per the review policy this is low severity.

**Fix:** Keep pending accounting balanced in `UnpackSync`: increment before its filesystem work, or provide sync-specific skip/error handling that does not decrement an unincremented counter.

findings.title: Synchronous extraction silently truncates partial writes
findings.body:
Synchronous extraction silently accepts a partial filesystem write and completes with a truncated file. `fs.writeSync` may return fewer bytes than requested without throwing, but this path discards that return value.

**Preconditions:** The extraction target can accept a partial write, such as a Linux tmpfs that reaches its size limit during the write.

**Evidence:** The synchronous writer calls `fs.writeSync(fd, chunk, 0, chunk.length)` once and only handles exceptions (`lib/unpack.js:467-473`). It then closes the file normally at entry end (`lib/unpack.js:475-508`). Reproducing extraction of a 100,000-byte archive file to a 64-KiB tmpfs made `writeSync` return `65536`; extraction issued no warning and produced a 65,536-byte destination file.

**Impact:** A normal resource-limit condition silently produces corrupt extracted content rather than an error. The damage is limited to the one output file and retrying after freeing space repairs it; the constrained filesystem is a non-default condition. Per the review policy, this is low severity.

**Fix:** Loop until every byte of each chunk is written, and route a zero-byte write or error through the extraction error path.

findings.title: Asynchronous extraction hangs after a destination write error
findings.body:
A non-strict write error can leave asynchronous extraction permanently backpressured. The error handler warns, unpends, and resumes the archive entry, but it leaves the failed output stream connected; the resumed entry writes into that permanently failed stream, never drains, and prevents parser completion.

**Preconditions:** A destination write fails during asynchronous extraction, for example when the filesystem runs out of space, and the input producer obeys stream backpressure.

**Evidence:** The file stream routes errors directly to `ONERROR` (`lib/unpack.js:248-255`). For ordinary errors, `ONERROR` only warns, decrements pending work, and resumes the entry (`lib/unpack.js:200-210`). The stream remains the target of `tx.pipe(stream)` (`lib/unpack.js:293-297`). Reproducing a failed first write while feeding a 128-KiB file in 1-KiB chunks left the producer waiting for a drain event; neither parser completion nor `close` occurred after 300 ms. Parser completion requires the active entry to end (`lib/parse.js:157-171`), and `close` is gated on that completion (`lib/unpack.js:47-50`, `lib/unpack.js:126-132`).

**Impact:** A recoverable destination error turns the documented warning path into a permanently pending extraction Promise/stream until the caller abandons it. The failure needs an external filesystem error and retrying with a new extraction after resolving it works, so per the review policy this is low severity.

**Fix:** On a destination stream error, detach or destroy the failed pipe and consume/discard the rest of the current entry before resuming it; emit completion after that cleanup.

summary:
Reviewed the full added contextification layer and its VM/NodeVM call paths. I recorded two findings: one low-severity protection-policy bypass and one informational null-prototype compatibility failure; a third confirmed function-protection issue was marked duplicate of an existing repository finding.

The implementation matches upstream vm2 3.6.11’s CVE fix, including the guarded conversion paths that prevent the known RangeError escape. `npm test` ran 56 passing tests and 2 pending; six assertions fail on Node 24 because they expect older Node error-message text, while the targeted security paths remained contained.

findings.title: Protected objects accept sandbox-controlled prototype methods
findings.body:
`protect()` can be bypassed with `__proto__` assignment. A sandbox can install an object containing `toJSON`, `toString`, or other functions as the protected host object's prototype; the host then invokes that sandbox-controlled method through ordinary prototype lookup. This contradicts `protect()`'s promise that sandbox code cannot attach functions or modify those methods.

**Preconditions:** The host exposes an object with `VM.protect(value, name)` and later consumes inherited methods on that object or on instances of a protected shared prototype.

**Evidence:** `Contextify.protected()` supplies the protected flag at `lib/contextify.js:682-683`, but the normal `set` trap rejects only a function supplied directly as the value (`lib/contextify.js:505-508`). It then performs `object[key] = value` on the host target (`lib/contextify.js:510-512`). Thus `config.__proto__ = { toJSON() { return {sandboxControlled: true}; } }` passes the direct-function check and invokes the host `__proto__` setter. `JSON.stringify(config)` subsequently calls the injected inherited `toJSON`. Direct prototype changes are meant to be denied by `setPrototypeOf` at `lib/contextify.js:578-580`, but `__proto__` assignment never reaches that trap. The documented protected-object guarantee specifically names `toJSON`, `toString`, and `inspect` (`README.md:300-304`).

**Impact:** An untrusted sandbox can change host behavior and serialized output for each protected object, or for all instances when the host exposes a shared prototype. This is low severity under the review policy: the effect is limited to a host object deliberately supplied to the VM and is recoverable by restoring its prototype; it does not provide arbitrary host-process access.

**Fix:** Reject `__proto__` in the contextified `set` trap (and any equivalent prototype-mutating property path), so it enforces the same invariant as `setPrototypeOf` before assigning to the host target.

findings.title: Protect leaves host functions writable by the sandbox
findings.body:
`VM.protect()` does not protect host functions. A sandbox can add a sandbox-defined function to a protected host function, which violates the API's no-function-attachment guarantee.

**Evidence:** `VM.protect()` calls `Contextify.protected()` before it publishes the value (`lib/main.js:189-192`), and that method passes `{protected: true}` to `Contextify.value()` (`lib/contextify.js:682-683`). Functions are routed to `Contextify.function()` with those flags (`lib/contextify.js:662-663`), but its final `Contextify.object()` call omits `flags` (`lib/contextify.js:481`). The `set` trap therefore skips its `flags.protected` rejection (`lib/contextify.js:505-508`) and writes the sandbox function to the original host function (`lib/contextify.js:510-512`). For example, after `vm.protect(hostFunction, 'fn')`, `vm.run('"use strict"; fn.p = function sandboxFn() {}')` creates `hostFunction.p`.

**Impact:** A sandbox can replace or attach methods on a protected host function. This is low severity under the review policy: the host must deliberately expose that particular function and can remove the added property; it does not itself escape the VM. It directly breaks the documented `protect()` invariant that sandbox code cannot attach functions (`README.md:300-304`).

**Fix:** Forward `flags` when `Contextify.function()` delegates to `Contextify.object()`, so its proxy uses the protected `set` and `defineProperty` checks.

findings.title: Null-prototype values throw when their __proto__ is read
findings.body:
Null-prototype objects cannot cross the VM boundary safely. Reading `.__proto__` on either a host null-prototype object exposed to the VM or a null-prototype object returned from `VM.run()` throws, even though the ordinary language operation should not throw.

**Evidence:** Both conversion directions recognize a null-prototype object and call `*.instance(value, null, ...)` (`lib/contextify.js:362-365`, `lib/contextify.js:657-660`). The corresponding `get` traps then handle `__proto__` by unconditionally reading `klass.prototype` (`lib/contextify.js:128`, `lib/contextify.js:411`). Since `klass` is `null`, `new VM({sandbox: {n: Object.create(null)}}).run('n.__proto__')` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'prototype')`; the same happens when host code reads `vm.run('Object.create(null)').__proto__`. The adjacent `getPrototypeOf` traps correctly use `klass && klass.prototype` (`lib/contextify.js:140-142`, `lib/contextify.js:423-425`).

**Impact:** A sandbox result or supplied null-prototype map can make normal host or VM property access fail. This is informational severity under the review policy: it is limited to one value and lasts only for the failing access; no sandbox escape was demonstrated.

**Fix:** Handle the null-class case in the synthetic `__proto__` getter (and preserve the normal null-prototype semantics) rather than dereferencing `klass`.

summary:
Reviewed the new `index.js` implementation and recorded five findings: one medium and four low severity. The change moves subprocess use to argument arrays, which avoids shell injection, but it omits its new runtime dependency and has several promise, GraphicsMagick, and page-order failures.

Validation: a clean `npm install` followed by `npm test` fails because `child-process-promise` is undeclared. After temporarily installing it, the test command also attempts to load `tests/test.pdf` as JavaScript because it runs `mocha tests/*`.

findings.title: Clean installs cannot load the package
findings.body:
A clean installation cannot import this package. `index.js` loads `child-process-promise` at module initialization, but the manifest does not install it, so normal `require("pdf-image")` throws `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` before it exposes `PDFImage`.

**Evidence:** `index.js:7` unconditionally requires `child-process-promise`; `package.json:13-15` lists only `es6-promise` as a runtime dependency. After `npm install --ignore-scripts`, `npm test` fails during `tests/test-main.js`'s `require("../")` with `Cannot find module 'child-process-promise'`. The documented entry point uses that same import in `README.md:23-27`.

**Impact:** Every clean-install consumer loses all package functionality. This is broad but recoverable by publishing a corrected manifest, so it is medium severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** Add the compatible `child-process-promise` version to `dependencies` (and update the lockfile if the project uses one).

findings.title: Current cached images leave conversion promises pending
findings.body:
`convertPage()` never settles when its target image is already current. This makes the documented promise API hang on a normal cache hit and also prevents `convertFile()` from completing when any page is current.

**Preconditions:** An output image exists and has an mtime equal to or newer than the PDF.

**Evidence:** After both `fs.stat` calls succeed, `index.js:212` converts only when `imageFileStat.mtime < pdfFileStat.mtime`. The false branch falls out of the callback at `index.js:218` without resolving `outputImagePath` or rejecting. `convertFile()` waits for every `convertPage()` result at `index.js:135-142`. A controlled equal-mtime stub left the returned promise pending.

**Impact:** Repeated conversion requests can block indefinitely for an existing cached page. The caller can remove the cache or restart its request, so this is a contained, recoverable availability failure and low severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** Resolve with `outputImagePath` when the existing image is at least as new as the PDF.

findings.title: Conversion failures leave convertFile promises pending
findings.body:
`convertFile()` returns a promise that never rejects for failures before or after page conversion. Callers therefore wait forever rather than receiving the documented conversion error.

**Evidence:** `getInfo()` rejects when `pdfinfo` fails (`index.js:42-47`), and `numberOfPages()` propagates that rejection (`index.js:49-52`), but `convertFile()` supplies no rejection handler for `numberOfPages()` at `index.js:131`. Its outer promise at `index.js:130` consequently remains pending. In combined mode, `combineImages()` can reject on a failed convert spawn (`index.js:114-125`), but its invocation at `index.js:148-151` also has no rejection handler or returned chain; the outer catch at `index.js:155-157` only observes `convertPromise`. Controlled rejection stubs left the public promise pending for both paths.

**Impact:** A missing/unreadable PDF, unavailable `pdfinfo`, or failed combined-image operation can permanently stall the caller's job/request until external timeout. These are contained, recoverable failures, so this is low severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** Return and chain the `numberOfPages`, page conversion, and `combineImages` promises so every rejection reaches `convertFile()`'s returned promise.

findings.title: GraphicsMagick conversions invoke a nonexistent executable
findings.body:
GraphicsMagick mode cannot start either conversion command. The command builder supplies `"gm convert"` as one executable name, while `spawn` executes its command argument directly rather than splitting it on spaces; systems provide `gm`, not an executable named `gm convert`.

**Preconditions:** The caller enables the documented `graphicsMagick` option and converts a missing or stale image (or combines images).

**Evidence:** The page and combine builders use `cmd: this.useGM ? "gm convert" : "convert"` at `index.js:85` and `index.js:94`; those values are passed as the first `spawn` argument at `index.js:114` and `index.js:169`. A controlled PATH stub showed `spawn("gm convert", args)` fails with `ENOENT`, whereas `spawn("gm", ["convert", ...args])` invokes GraphicsMagick. The README expects GraphicsMagick support through this option (`README.md:6-18`).

**Impact:** All GraphicsMagick-configured conversions fail, but default ImageMagick mode remains available. This is a contained, recoverable functionality failure, so it is low severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** Use executable `gm` and prepend `convert` to the argument array in both command builders.

findings.title: Eleven-page conversions return pages in the wrong order
findings.body:
`convertFile()` returns pages out of document order once a PDF reaches 11 pages; combined output appends those pages in the same wrong order. Image paths use zero-based page names, so lexical sorting places `-10` between `-1` and `-2`.

**Preconditions:** The PDF has at least 11 pages and the output images need conversion (rather than taking the currently broken cache-hit path).

**Evidence:** The conversion loop uses page indices `0` through `totalPages - 1` at `index.js:133-136`, consistent with the documented first-page `-0.png` output in `README.md:27-30`. It collects asynchronous results and calls the default string `imagePaths.sort()` at `index.js:137-140`. For paths `...-0.png` through `...-10.png`, that produces `0, 1, 10, 2, ...`. In combined mode, the array is passed unchanged to `combineImages()` at `index.js:147-150`, which constructs the `-append` input list directly at `index.js:89-96`.

**Impact:** Callers receive incorrectly sequenced page arrays, and combined images present page 10 before page 2. This is a contained, recoverable output-correctness error, so it is low severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** Preserve page-index order while collecting results, or sort by the numeric page index rather than the path string.

summary:
Reviewed the new contextification bridge and recorded five findings, including a confirmed high-severity VM sandbox escape through an uncaught host `RangeError`. The change also has policy-bypass, descriptor-corruption, and Proxy-invariant regressions.

`npm test` ran after installing dev dependencies: 56 passing, 2 pending, and 6 failures. The failures include Node 24 error-message differences and several legacy security-test assertions that do not pass on this runtime.

findings.title: Sandbox code can execute arbitrary host JavaScript through an uncaught RangeError
findings.body:
Untrusted code can obtain a host-realm `RangeError` and use its constructor chain to evaluate arbitrary JavaScript outside the VM. The cache `WeakMap` lookups run before the conversion error boundary; recursive stack exhaustion makes one throw while a host Buffer method is converting its exception.

**Evidence:** `Contextify.function` catches errors from a host function and sends them to `Contextify.value()` at `lib/contextify.js:440-444`. That function performs `Decontextified.has(value)` and `Contextify.proxies.has(value)` before its `try` block at `lib/contextify.js:623-632`. A guest can recursively exhaust the stack, invoke `Buffer.prototype.write` with a crafted receiver, catch the resulting unconverted host `RangeError`, then evaluate `e.constructor.constructor('return process')()`. Running this against the PR head returned the host `process.version` (`v24.18.0`). `Buffer` is a guest-visible contextified host function at `lib/contextify.js:686-693`; `host` includes the host `Function` constructor at `lib/main.js:113-140`.

**Impact:** This crosses the VM trust boundary and grants arbitrary host JavaScript execution, including access to `process` and host module/OS capabilities. It is **high** severity under the review policy because untrusted VM code gains denied host capabilities and the resulting host execution is not automatically undone.

**Fix:** Move both `WeakMap` cache checks inside the `try` in `Contextify.value` (and the symmetric checks in `Decontextify.value`), so every conversion failure is sanitized before it can cross the boundary.

findings.title: Previously exposed objects remain mutable after freeze or protect
findings.body:
`freeze()` and `protect()` do not apply their policy when the object was already supplied through `sandbox`. The earlier unrestricted wrapper is returned from the cache, so VM code can still mutate host state that the host subsequently marked frozen or protected.

**Preconditions:** The same host object is passed in `sandbox` and then passed to `freeze()` or `protect()`.

**Evidence:** Constructor setup exposes each sandbox value through `Contextify.globalValue()` (`lib/main.js:157-160`), which calls `Contextify.value()` without policy arguments (`lib/contextify.js:676-677`) and caches its unrestricted proxy (`lib/contextify.js:618-621`). `freeze()` and `protect()` subsequently request readonly/protected conversion (`lib/main.js:174-191`, `lib/contextify.js:679-683`), but `Contextify.value()` returns the cached proxy before considering `deepTraps` or `flags` (`lib/contextify.js:623-630`). In strict-mode guest code, `exposed.added = 1` and `frozen.nested.added = 2` both succeeded after `vm.freeze(frozen, 'frozen')`; similarly, function-valued assignments succeeded after `protect()`.

**Impact:** Sandbox code can change a host object that the host has explicitly frozen, or add sandbox callbacks to an object the host has explicitly protected. The effect is limited to an object deliberately exposed to that VM and is recoverable by restoring it, so this is **low** severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** Do not reuse a proxy across different readonly/protected policies. Cache wrappers by policy, or apply the strongest requested restrictions to the existing wrapper before returning it.

findings.title: Protected host functions accept sandbox callback properties
findings.body:
`VM.protect()` does not protect function values. A sandbox can attach a function property to a protected host function, contrary to the API guarantee that protected values cannot receive function properties.

**Evidence:** `VM.protect()` sends the protection flag into `Contextify.value()` at `lib/main.js:189-192` and `lib/contextify.js:682-683`. The function path receives that flag (`lib/contextify.js:662-663`), but discards it when it creates the object proxy at `lib/contextify.js:481`. The assignment guard is only active when that proxy closed over `flags.protected` (`lib/contextify.js:505-507`), so it decontextifies and writes the guest callback directly to the host function (`lib/contextify.js:508-512`). With `vm.protect(hostFunction, 'f')`, strict-mode guest code `f.callback = () => 'guest'` succeeded and `hostFunction.callback()` returned `guest`.

**Impact:** A sandbox can inject or replace callback-like properties on a host function that was marked protected. This affects only a host function deliberately supplied to the VM and is recoverable by removing the property, so this is **low** severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** Pass `flags` (and `mock`) from `Contextify.function()` to `Contextify.object()` so its `set` and `defineProperty` traps enforce protection for functions too.

findings.title: Buffer extensibility checks throw inside the VM
findings.body:
The VM global `Buffer` throws when code queries its extensibility. This makes ordinary reflection on a standard global fail rather than return a boolean.

**Evidence:** The global is created as `Contextify.readonly(host.Buffer, ...)` at `lib/contextify.js:686-693`. Readonly adds `FROZEN_TRAPS`, whose `isExtensible` always returns `false` while its `preventExtensions` does not change the target at `lib/contextify.js:31-37`. The proxy still targets the extensible host `Buffer` (`lib/contextify.js:618-621`), violating the Proxy invariant. `new VM().run('Object.isExtensible(Buffer)')` throws `TypeError: 'isExtensible' on proxy: trap result does not reflect extensibility of proxy target (which is 'true')`; `Reflect.isExtensible(Buffer)` fails the same way.

**Impact:** Any VM program that reflects on the standard Buffer global fails. This is a transient, broad compatibility regression, so it is **low** severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** Do not report a different extensibility state from the proxy target. Either return the target's actual state and reject writes through the other traps, or proxy a target that has actually been made non-extensible.

findings.title: Sealing a sandbox object erases host property values
findings.body:
A VM program can silently erase values and attributes from host sandbox objects by sealing or freezing them. `Object.seal()` supplies a partial property descriptor, but the proxy expands absent fields into destructive defaults before applying it to the original host object.

**Evidence:** Sandbox initialization contextifies supplied objects at `lib/main.js:157-160`. The contextified proxy's `defineProperty` trap treats a descriptor without an accessor as a complete data descriptor and always sets `value`, `writable`, and `enumerable` (`lib/contextify.js:556-567`), before defining it on the host object (`lib/contextify.js:569-570`). With `obj = {x: 42}` in `sandbox`, guest code `Object.seal(obj)` succeeds but changes the host descriptor from `{value: 42, writable: true, enumerable: true, configurable: true}` to `{value: undefined, writable: false, enumerable: false, configurable: false}`. `Object.freeze(obj)` has the same data loss.

**Impact:** Untrusted VM code can corrupt data in every mutable host object deliberately exposed as a sandbox value by invoking normal reflection APIs. The host can restore the affected records from its own state, so this is **low** severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** Preserve descriptor field presence when crossing the proxy boundary. Only copy a field into `propertyDescriptor` when it is present in the incoming descriptor; do not turn a generic or partial descriptor into a data descriptor.

summary:
Reviewed PR #2 and recorded three findings: one high-severity security issue and two low-severity correctness issues.

The change restores the `pdf-image` implementation, including PDF metadata lookup, conversion, caching, and optional image combining. The implementation needs revision before approval. I also reproduced the command-execution path and the unresolved conversion promise behavior. `npm test` could not run because its `tests/*` glob passes `tests/test.pdf` to Mocha as JavaScript.

findings.title: Request-derived PDF paths execute shell commands
findings.body:
An unauthenticated request can execute shell commands as the host application. The documented Express route passes its URL-derived `pdfPath` directly to `PDFImage` (`README.md:63-70`). `getInfo()` gives a shell string to `exec`; double quotes do not make embedded quotes or command substitutions safe. For example, a path of `/tmp/missing.pdf"; touch /tmp/marker; echo "` produces `pdfinfo "/tmp/missing.pdf"; touch /tmp/marker; echo ""`; invoking `getInfo()` created the marker during review.

**Evidence:** `constructGetInfoCommand()` interpolates `pdfFilePath` into the command at `index.js:24-29`, and `getInfo()` executes it via `exec` at `index.js:40-56`. The same untrusted path and caller-controlled conversion options are interpolated into the conversion command at `index.js:84-110` and executed at `index.js:168-179`.

**Impact:** This crosses the documented HTTP trust boundary and gives a remote caller arbitrary commands with the application's privileges. The severity is **high** under the reach/persistence policy: it crosses a trust boundary and can expose or change persistent host assets.

**Fix:** Do not construct shell command strings. Invoke `pdfinfo`, `convert`/`gm`, and cleanup with `spawn`/`execFile` and explicit argument arrays; pass each path and option as one argument.

findings.title: Conversion failures leave convertFile promises pending
findings.body:
`convertFile()` never settles for normal external-command errors, so callers cannot receive the error or recover. If `pdfinfo` fails (for example, the file is absent), `getInfo()` rejects at `index.js:43-51`, but `convertFile()` attaches no rejection handler to `numberOfPages()` at `index.js:132-160`; its outer `reject` is never called. Likewise, with `combinedImage`, a failed append conversion rejects at `index.js:115-123`, while the handler at `index.js:150-153` forwards only fulfillment; the later `.catch()` only observes `convertPromise`.

**Evidence:** A reproduction that made `getInfo()` reject, and one that made `combineImages()` reject after a successful page conversion, left the promise returned by `convertFile()` pending in both cases. The README shows consumers relying on the returned promise and error handler (`README.md:70-74`).

**Impact:** Missing inputs, unavailable utilities, and failed combination leave ordinary callers waiting until their own timeout rather than reporting a conversion failure. This is **low**: the effect is a recoverable service failure for the request.

**Fix:** Propagate the `numberOfPages()` and `combineImages()` rejection paths to the outer `convertFile()` rejection (or return and chain the promises rather than wrapping them manually).

findings.title: Combined images put double-digit pages out of order
findings.body:
Combined output puts page 10 before page 2 for every PDF with at least 11 pages. Page conversion uses zero-based numeric names (`<base>-<page>.png`) at `index.js:63-67` and collects them asynchronously at `index.js:133-139`, but `imagePaths.sort()` at `index.js:140` uses JavaScript's default lexicographic order. The resulting order is `...-0.png`, `...-1.png`, `...-10.png`, `...-2.png`, and so on. `combineImages()` preserves that input order in its `convert -append` command (`index.js:95-101`, `149-152`).

**Preconditions:** The caller uses `combinedImage: true` with an 11-page or longer PDF.

**Evidence:** The API documents page 0 as the first page (`README.md:22-30`) and `combinedImage` as merging the full-file page result (`README.md:33-53`), so its output must retain numeric page order.

**Impact:** The library silently produces a misordered combined document. This is **low** because it is limited to one requested output and a corrected conversion recovers it.

**Fix:** Retain each page path at its numeric index, or sort paths with a numeric page comparator before combining.

summary:
**This run stopped early at the run's time limit, so its results are partial.**

Reviewed the newly added extraction implementation and recorded eight findings. The CVE hard-link reuse guard is present, but several independent path-containment bypasses and extraction lifecycle defects remain.

`npm test -- --no-coverage` completed with 6484 passing tests; its one failure is an existing zlib error-message mismatch in `test/parse.js`, not an unpack failure. I covered async and sync extraction, path normalization, links, caching, transforms, metadata cleanup, and write behavior. I did not complete live Windows-platform testing or a full downstream-consumer analysis of archive-created symlink targets.

findings.title: Archive symlink replacement bypasses cached parent validation
findings.body:
