A crafted archive can replace a cached directory with a symlink and make a later member write outside `cwd`, with default options.

**Evidence:** A `Directory a` is created and cached by `mkdir` (`lib/unpack.js:300-325`; `lib/mkdir.js:54-69`). A following `SymbolicLink a -> ../outside` removes that directory, creates the symlink, but does not invalidate the cache (`lib/unpack.js:367-387`, `lib/unpack.js:333-335`, `lib/unpack.js:413-420`). For a later `File a/pwn`, `CHECKFS` asks `mkdir` for parent `a`; its cache hit returns before `lstat` can reject the symlink (`lib/unpack.js:367-372`; `lib/mkdir.js:68-69`). The pathname writer then follows `a` and writes `outside/pwn` (`lib/unpack.js:249-254`). I reproduced this sequence in both `Unpack` and `Unpack.Sync`: `outside/pwn` contained the archive body.

**Impact:** An untrusted archive crosses the extraction boundary and permanently writes a file that the process can access outside the selected destination. Per the review policy, this is high severity (trust-boundary reach and permanent data corruption).

**Fix:** Invalidate cached directory paths whenever extraction removes or replaces them, or revalidate cache hits before accepting them. The invariant is that every parent used for an extracted member must be a real directory, not an archive-created symlink.

findings.title: Hard-link members can expose files outside the extraction root
findings.body:
A hard-link member can name an existing file outside `cwd` as its source, so extraction places an alias to that file inside the output tree even when path preservation is disabled.

**Preconditions:** The outside source is on the same filesystem and the extracting process may create a hard link to it.

**Evidence:** `CHECKPATH` validates only `entry.path` (`lib/unpack.js:136-172`). For a `Link`, `HARDLINK` directly resolves unchecked `entry.linkpath` against `cwd` (`lib/unpack.js:337-339`) and `LINK` passes it to `fs.link` (`lib/unpack.js:413-420`). I reproduced a default synchronous extraction with `path: 'leak'`, `linkpath: '../outside'`: `cwd/leak` and the sibling `outside` had the same inode and reading `leak` returned `outside`'s contents. The new `nlink <= 1` guard prevents a subsequent ordinary file member from overwriting that inode, but does not prevent creation of the outside-file alias (`lib/unpack.js:358-386`).

**Impact:** An untrusted archive crosses the extraction boundary by exposing an accessible outside file through the extracted namespace. The alias persists until removed; per the review policy this is high severity (trust-boundary reach and recoverable persistence).

**Fix:** Apply the same containment validation to hard-link sources as destinations. Reject or sanitize a `linkpath` that resolves outside `cwd` when `preservePaths` is false.

findings.title: Fully stripped entries replace the extraction root
findings.body:
An entry with every path component stripped is extracted to `cwd` rather than skipped. A file can therefore remove an empty extraction directory and replace it with archive content.

**Preconditions:** The caller uses a positive `strip` value while extracting an untrusted archive into an empty root.

**Evidence:** `CHECKPATH` accepts a path with exactly `strip` components and assigns it `''` (`lib/unpack.js:136-142`); resolving that empty path produces `cwd` (`lib/unpack.js:167-170`). The resulting file entry goes through the normal clobber path, which removes a directory for a non-directory entry and then writes the file (`lib/unpack.js:367-400`, `lib/unpack.js:249-254`). With public `tar.extract({ file, cwd: root, strip: 1, sync: true })` and an archive containing only `top`, I observed the empty `root` directory become a regular file containing `top`'s body. The async API has the same behavior.

**Impact:** An attacker can delete and replace the caller-selected extraction root. This needs the non-default `strip` option and is contained to that root, so per the review policy it is medium severity.

**Fix:** Skip an entry whose path has no meaningful component after stripping, before resolving the destination. Handle trailing separators rather than relying only on a component-count comparison.

findings.title: Synchronous skipped entries never emit completion events
findings.body:
`Unpack.Sync` never signals completion after it skips an existing entry or handles a nonfatal filesystem error. Its filesystem check does not increment the pending counter, but inherited skip and error paths decrement it, leaving the counter negative.

**Evidence:** Pending starts at zero and terminal events require it to be exactly zero (`lib/unpack.js:60`, `lib/unpack.js:127-133`). Async `CHECKFS` increments it before possible skips (`lib/unpack.js:367-374`), whereas the synchronous override does not (`lib/unpack.js:429-457`). `SKIP` and the normal `ONERROR` branch both call `UNPEND` (`lib/unpack.js:201-211`, `lib/unpack.js:345-353`). I extracted a valid one-file archive through `tar.x({ sync: true, cwd, keep: true })` with a pre-existing destination: content was preserved but none of `prefinish`, `finish`, `end`, or `close` fired. A nonempty-directory overwrite error behaved the same way.

**Impact:** Consumers of the documented synchronous writable extraction stream can wait indefinitely after normal `keep`/`newer` behavior or a recoverable extraction error. The operation can be retried with a fresh stream, so per the review policy this is low severity.

**Fix:** Balance pending accounting in `UnpackSync`, either by incrementing before synchronous filesystem work or by using sync-specific skip/error handling that does not decrement an unincremented counter.

findings.title: Transform stream errors crash or stall async extraction
findings.body:
A transform stream returned by the documented `transform` option can emit an error that is neither reported by `Unpack` nor allowed to complete extraction. This can crash the process or leave the public async extraction Promise pending.

**Evidence:** For a distinct transform stream, the implementation wires `entry -> tx -> stream` but attaches an error listener only to the destination writer; `tx` has no error listener (`lib/unpack.js:251-255`, `lib/unpack.js:294-297`). The pending unit added for the entry (`lib/unpack.js:367-369`) is released only once the destination finishes and closes (`lib/unpack.js:257-264`), while terminal events require pending to reach zero (`lib/unpack.js:127-133`). I extracted a one-file archive with `tar.x({ file, cwd, transform: () => new Transform({ transform: (c, e, cb) => cb(new Error('boom')) }) })`; it raised an uncaught `boom` and the returned Promise was still unsettled after 500 ms.

**Impact:** A normal failure in application-supplied transform code can terminate the Node process or indefinitely stall its extraction workflow. The caller supplies the transform and can correct it, so per the review policy this is low severity.

**Fix:** Listen for transform errors, tear down the pipeline, close the writer, and route the error through a single completion path that balances pending state and emits `error`.

findings.title: Metadata failures close extraction before file cleanup completes
findings.body:
If both optional file metadata operations fail, extraction emits `close` before all metadata work has completed, decrements the pending count twice for one file, and leaves its descriptor open.

**Preconditions:** Both timestamp fallback and ownership fallback fail for an extracted file; ownership processing is enabled.

**Evidence:** On writer finish, timestamp and ownership actions run concurrently and each increments `actions` (`lib/unpack.js:266-289`). A failure calls `done(er)`, which immediately invokes `ONERROR` instead of decrementing `actions` or closing the descriptor (`lib/unpack.js:257-264`). `ONERROR` calls `UNPEND` for each failure (`lib/unpack.js:201-211`), although `CHECKFS` added one pending unit (`lib/unpack.js:367-369`). In a reproduction where both fallback pairs failed and ownership fallback was delayed, the timestamp failure emitted `close` with pending zero and no `fs.close` call; the later ownership failure reduced pending to -1. The second metadata operation was still active after the completion signal.

**Impact:** On this uncommon filesystem/ownership-error path, callers can act on a premature completion signal and the process leaks a file descriptor. The operation already failed and the trigger needs special metadata failures, so per the review policy this is info severity.

**Fix:** Make metadata completion single-shot: wait for all started actions, record the first error, close the descriptor, then decrement pending exactly once and report the error.

findings.title: Synchronous extraction silently accepts short writes
findings.body:
Synchronous extraction silently accepts a partial `fs.writeSync` result and leaves a truncated file while reporting success.

**Preconditions:** The filesystem permits a short regular-file write, such as an OS file-size limit.

**Evidence:** The sync writer invokes `fs.writeSync` once per chunk and ignores its returned byte count (`lib/unpack.js:479-485`), then closes successfully at entry end without checking size (`lib/unpack.js:487-521`). With `ulimit -f 2`, extracting a 4096-byte one-file archive made the actual call return 2048; the extractor emitted no error and produced a 2048-byte file. Node's `writeSync` API permits this return value.

**Impact:** Under a bounded-resource condition, consumers can treat incomplete extracted data as complete. Retrying after correcting the resource limit restores the file, so per the review policy this is low severity.

**Fix:** Loop until each chunk is fully written, or treat a short write as an extraction error.

findings.title: Mixed-separator absolute paths escape the extraction root
findings.body:
A mixed Windows/POSIX absolute member name can be rewritten into a POSIX absolute destination and escape `cwd` on POSIX hosts.

**Evidence:** Path validation treats `C:\\ /tmp/victim`-style mixed-separator names as Windows absolute and removes the Windows root (`lib/unpack.js:144-157`). For `C:\\/tmp/victim` specifically, `path.win32.parse()` removes `C:\\` and leaves `/tmp/victim`; the later platform-specific `path.isAbsolute()` accepts that remainder and assigns it directly to `entry.absolute` (`lib/unpack.js:167-170`). `CHECKFS` and the file writer then operate on that absolute path (`lib/unpack.js:367-400`, `lib/unpack.js:249-254`). This bypasses the intended absolute-name relativization without `preservePaths`.

**Impact:** An untrusted archive can permanently write a process-accessible file outside the selected extraction directory. Per the review policy, this is high severity (trust-boundary reach and permanent data corruption).

**Fix:** After removing a Windows root, ensure the remaining pathname is relative under the host platform; reject it if it is absolute under either path implementation. A containment check on the final resolved path would enforce the invariant directly.

summary:
No findings recorded.

The PR restores Fastify’s validation module and sets the default Ajv `allErrors` option to `false` in `lib/validation.js:170-178`, limiting validation work on malformed requests while preserving an explicit application-level override. The added file matches the upstream CVE-2020-8192 fix. Linting passed, as did the validation internals and input-validation suites; the unchanged validation-error suite still expects the prior aggregate-error default and fails accordingly.

**This run stopped early at the run's time limit, so its results are partial.**

Reviewed the added browser client across Socket.IO events, rendering, authentication, connection setup, history, and network lifecycle. The topic-handler removal fixes the direct topic HTML sink, but the added client still introduces several confirmed security and correctness issues, including client-side script execution and public-server availability impact; findings were recorded in Ozone.

I did not complete an end-to-end browser run with the legacy dependency stack, so browser-specific behavior under the project’s original runtime remains untested.

findings.title: Mixed-case JavaScript URLs execute when IRC links are opened
findings.body:
An IRC participant can make a victim execute JavaScript in the Shout origin by sending a mixed-case `javascript:` URL and having the victim follow the rendered link.

**Evidence:** Message text reaches the client unchanged through `src/plugins/irc-events/message.js:31-63` and is rendered by `client/js/shout.js:184-198` with the raw `parse` helper (`client/views/msg.tpl:20-22`). `client/js/libs/handlebars/parse.js:37-47` recognizes URL schemes case-insensitively but rejects only the lowercase string `javascript:` before placing the original URL in `href`. Thus `JaVaScRiPt://%0Aalert%281%29` produces a link that browsers treat as JavaScript when clicked; the newline ends the comment.

**Impact:** A channel participant crosses a trust boundary and can run script in each connected user's authenticated Shout origin after a click. This is **high** under the review policy (cross-trust-boundary, recoverable compromise).

**Fix:** Parse the URL and reject dangerous schemes after case-normalizing the scheme (ideally allow only an explicit `http:`/`https:` allowlist) before generating an anchor.

findings.title: Footer windows retain the previous channel as the hidden send target
findings.body:
Opening Settings or Connect clears the visible channel but preserves the previous send target. A user can therefore type while the settings/connect window is displayed and send text to a channel they cannot see.

**Evidence:** Footer controls have `data-target` but no `data-id` (`client/index.html:35-39`), yet they use the shared navigation handler because `sidebar` includes `#footer` (`client/js/shout.js:31,442-456`). In this jQuery version `.data("id", undefined)` is a getter, so it retains the ID from the last channel selection. The global composer remains available (`client/index.html:271-281`) and always emits that cached `chat.data("id")` (`client/js/shout.js:404-415`). The server resolves that ID and sends plain text to its IRC channel (`src/client.js:223-240`; `src/plugins/inputs/msg.js:3-22`).

**Impact:** A normal user can accidentally disclose a message to the previously selected IRC channel. The message is sent externally but the user must submit it, so this is **low** under the review policy (contained, recoverable).

**Fix:** Clear the composer target and disable/hide the composer when opening a non-channel window, or retain a visible active-channel indication and deliberately preserve that target.

findings.title: Concurrent WHOIS results fail to open later query tabs
findings.body:
Two quick user lookups can leave the later query tab unopened. The client uses one global Boolean for all outstanding lookups, so the first `join` event consumes it and the next query is filtered out.

**Evidence:** A user click sets `whois = true` and emits `/whois` (`client/js/shout.js:540-551`). Each lookup result creates a query and emits a `join` (`src/plugins/irc-events/whois.js:11-21`). The first join clears the shared flag; on the second join, `client/js/shout.js:174-181` filters the newly created `.query` tab with `:not(.query)`, then clicks an empty set. The later result exists but the user remains on the first query.

**Impact:** Rapid normal lookups fail to navigate to the later result; no data is lost and the tab can be selected manually. This is **low** under the review policy (contained, recoverable).

**Fix:** Mark the join event created by the WHOIS plugin and select based on that event property, rather than tracking an unrelated global Boolean.

findings.title: Transient socket failures erase remembered login tokens
findings.body:
A transient socket failure makes a remembered user lose the persistent login because the client deletes the token before knowing that authentication succeeded.

**Evidence:** On `auth`, the browser removes the token cookie before emitting it (`client/js/shout.js:84-87`). The cookie is restored only in `init` (`client/js/shout.js:135-142`), while either a disconnect or connection error reloads the page (`client/js/shout.js:70-74`). If the connection drops between those operations, the next load has no token. The server does not consume or rotate successful tokens (`src/server.js:146-160`), so deletion has no authentication benefit.

**Impact:** A normal transient connection loss requires the user to enter credentials again. This is **low** under the review policy (contained, recoverable).

**Fix:** Keep the existing token until `init` confirms authentication (then replace it if a new token is returned); remove it only after an explicit authentication failure or sign-out.

findings.title: Invalid Connect ports let public users terminate the server
findings.body:
An unauthenticated visitor can terminate a default public Shout server by submitting an invalid IRC port through Connect.

**Preconditions:** The default public configuration is reachable.

**Evidence:** New configurations default to `public: true` and listen on all interfaces (`defaults/config.js:11,19`; `src/command-line/index.js:24-30`). Public Socket.IO clients are initialized without credentials and receive the `conn` handler (`src/server.js:50-56,107-110,133-143`). The added client serializes the arbitrary port field unchanged and emits `conn` (`client/index.html:107-109`; `client/js/shout.js:666-692`). `Client.connect` passes it straight to `net.connect`/`tls.connect` before attaching an error listener (`src/client.js:122-152`). Node synchronously throws `RangeError` for values such as `70000`; no caller catches it, so the process exits.

**Impact:** An unauthenticated Internet user can stop the default service with one request. This is **high** under the review policy (broad, recoverable availability loss).

**Fix:** Validate and coerce the port on the server before connecting, reject values outside 1–65535 through a socket error response, and catch synchronous connection-construction errors.

findings.title: Disconnecting a background network changes the active conversation
findings.body:
Disconnecting a background network unexpectedly changes the active conversation to the first remaining channel.

**Evidence:** The `quit` handler always activates `sidebar.find(".chan").eq(0)` after removing the network (`client/js/shout.js:286-294`). It does not check whether the removed network contained the active channel. Thus disconnecting any non-active network moves the user away from the conversation they were reading or composing in.

**Impact:** A normal user loses their current conversation context and can subsequently type into the newly selected channel. This is **low** under the review policy (contained, recoverable).

**Fix:** Select a replacement only when the removed network owned the active pane; otherwise preserve the current active channel and its send target.

summary:
Reviewed the full generated parser addition, its grammar source, parser integration, build scripts, and distribution paths. I recorded one medium-severity finding: the checked-in fix is overwritten by the supported parser-generation workflow, which restores formula-controlled `eval`.

The new generated artifact itself no longer executes array contents. No other evidence-backed regressions were found in the changed parser surface.

findings.title: Regenerating the parser restores formula-controlled eval
findings.body:
The generated fix is not durable: the supported generator restores formula-controlled JavaScript execution. `npm run generate-parser` uses `grammar-parser.jison`, whose ARRAY action still executes `eval("[" + yytext + "]")` at `src/grammar-parser/grammar-parser.jison:189-197`, while this new generated action replaces it with `split(',')`.

**Preconditions:** A maintainer runs the documented `npm run generate-parser` command before building or publishing.

**Evidence:** With Jison 0.4.18, regenerating that grammar and parsing `X([globalThis.proof=73])` with `X` returning its arguments yields `[[73]]` and sets `globalThis.proof` to `73`. The checked-in parser instead returns `['globalThis.proof=73']` and leaves `proof` unchanged. The generation command is defined at `package.json:20`; the generated parser is loaded by `src/parser.js:3,15`.

**Impact:** A later supported regeneration silently turns a security fix back into arbitrary JavaScript execution when an application parses an untrusted formula. This requires a maintainer regeneration step, so the demonstrated cross-boundary impact is discounted one tier to medium.

**Fix:** Make the `ARRAY` action in `grammar-parser.jison` use the same non-evaluating parsing rule, regenerate `grammar-parser.js`, and add a regression test that regenerates or otherwise verifies formula text cannot execute JavaScript.

summary:
Reviewed the full new `lib/validation.js` surface and traced its schema compiler through route setup, request parsing, validation, and error responses. I recorded one high-severity finding: the default AJV configuration permits public requests to cause excessive validation-error allocation and formatting.

The remaining implementation matches the stated Fastify baseline and its callers. The fixed PR sibling changes the identified unsafe default.

findings.title: Schema validation lets public requests exhaust server resources
findings.body:
A public schema-validated endpoint can be made to allocate and format millions of validation errors before it returns a 400. An unauthenticated client can send a default-limit (1 MiB) JSON array of empty objects to a route whose item schema has required fields. With ten required fields, roughly 350,000 items produce about 3.5 million errors; the request body limit does not bound this error count.

**Preconditions:** A reachable route validates a repeated request structure (for example, an array of objects with required fields). This is a normal use of route schemas.

**Evidence:** The default compiler sets Ajv `allErrors: true` at `lib/validation.js:170-177`. Every schema route builds with that compiler (`lib/route.js:261-272`), request validation runs before the handler (`lib/handleRequest.js:83-87`), and a failed AJV validator returns its complete `.errors` array (`lib/validation.js:88-94`). Fastify both retains that array and concatenates each entry into the error message (`lib/validation.js:116-123,157-164`). Thus each attacker-controlled invalid item can multiply retained and formatted errors by the number of failed constraints. The body parser accepts bodies up to the default 1 MiB limit (`lib/contentTypeParser.js:127-130,144-153`; `lib/configValidator.js:635`).

**Impact:** An unauthenticated client can consume heap and event-loop time and send a very large 400 response repeatedly, denying service. This crosses the public-request trust boundary and persists until the process recovers or traffic stops, so this is **high** under the review policy.

**Fix:** Set the framework default to `allErrors: false` (while allowing an explicit application opt-in if needed), so validation stops at the first failure rather than accumulating attacker-controlled error sets.

summary: Reviewed the new `server.js` HTTP and WebSocket demo server. I confirmed the path traversal is reachable and that the existing PR #2 high-severity finding already covers it, so I did not create a duplicate. No other independently reportable regression was found.

Reviewed the new NodeBB blog-comments plugin implementation and recorded three findings: missing CSRF protection on both mutation routes, broken Load-more pagination, and a crash when the optional default category is unset.

The primary security issue is confirmed against the NodeBB middleware behavior and the repository’s fixed branch. I also checked the apparent linkback injection path; it is not reachable through this plugin’s supported NodeBB hook contract. `npm test` cannot run because the project defines no test suite.

findings.title: Cross-site requests can post replies and publish articles as victims
findings.body:
Both state-changing endpoints accept a cross-site POST without a CSRF token. An attacker can submit a reply as any logged-in victim, or make a logged-in administrator/publisher create an attacker-controlled topic.

**Evidence:** `init` applies `middleware.applyCSRF` to the data GET but registers `/comments/reply` and `/comments/publish` without it at `library.js:250-252`. The reply handler passes `req.user.uid` to `topics.reply` (`library.js:118-129`). The publish handler authorizes that same session user and calls `topics.post` with that UID (`library.js:166-185`). The normal widget obtains a token from the GET response (`library.js:105`) and submits `_csrf` in both forms (`public/templates/comments/comments.tpl:15,64,89`), so adding this middleware preserves valid requests.

**Impact:** This crosses the session-authentication trust boundary and persists content under a victim account. The victim can delete the unwanted content, so severity is high under the review policy's cross-boundary, recoverable category.

**Fix:** Register `middleware.applyCSRF` before each POST handler, as for the GET route, so both mutations require the session-bound token.

findings.title: Load-more pagination skips existing comments
findings.body:
The server returns fewer comments than the client expects on every Load more request after the first, leaving some replies permanently absent from the widget.

**Evidence:** The client increments `pagination` for Load more and appends the returned posts (`public/lib/general.js:109-119,177-180`). The route requests `start = pagination * 10` but `stop = 9 + pagination * 9` (`library.js:40`). NodeBB treats `stop` as inclusive, so page 1 is positions 10--18 and page 2 starts at 20: position 19 is never returned. Each later page is shorter still. The local zero default at `library.js:29` is also unused; an allowed request with no pagination segment produces `NaN` bounds at line 40 and an empty list.

**Impact:** Visitors cannot see some existing comments in topics with more than one page. This is contained, recoverable display corruption, so severity is low under the review policy.

**Fix:** Use the normalized `pagination` variable and compute the inclusive end as `start + 9`.

findings.title: Unset default category crashes article publishing
findings.body:
Publishing a new article crashes instead of using the documented default category when an administrator has not saved the optional default-CID setting.

**Preconditions:** The article has no page-specific category, so the shipped client submits `cid = -1`, and `blog-comments:cid` has not been saved.

**Evidence:** All shipped clients use `-1` for that fallback path (`public/lib/general.js:151-168`, `public/lib/ghost.js:151-154`, `public/lib/wordpress.js:168-171`). The handler enters it at `library.js:147`, then dereferences `meta.config['blog-comments:cid']` with `.toString()` at line 162. The ACP field only supplies placeholder `1`, not an initial value (`public/templates/comments/admin.tpl:11-12`), so an unset setting is `undefined` and throws before the following `|| 1` fallback on line 163 can run.

**Impact:** A normal first-time configuration prevents an authorized publisher from creating an article until the setting is manually saved. The failure is contained and recoverable, so severity is low under the review policy.

**Fix:** Default the configuration value before converting or splitting it, then retain category 1 as the fallback.

summary: Reviewed the complete new `library.js` implementation and its NodeBB 1.12 integration paths. The PR correctly adds CSRF middleware to both state-changing routes, but I recorded three low-severity issues involving embedded-comment pagination, malformed publish tags crashing a worker, and a nonfunctional source-linkback hook. I also checked the suspected stored-XSS, unmapped-ID, and mapping-authorization paths; they were not reportable on the declared NodeBB version.

findings.title: Embedded pagination skips replies after the first extra page
findings.body:
The comment widget skips replies after the first “Load more” request and creates larger gaps on later pages. The browser increments `pagination` from 0 for each request, but the handler asks NodeBB for inclusive ranges `p * 10 .. 9 + p * 9`; page 1 is 10..18 and page 2 starts at 20, so reverse-set position 19 is never returned.

**Evidence:** `library.js:40` calculates mismatched bounds. `topics.getTopicPosts` forwards them to NodeBB's inclusive reverse sorted-set range, so the successive ranges are 0..9, 10..18, and 20..27. The widget increments the page number on each click in `public/lib/general.js:108-119` and requests it at `public/lib/general.js:177-180`.

**Impact:** A topic with at least 20 replies permanently omits comments from the embedded discussion view until the user visits the forum directly. This is contained display/data-completeness loss and is recoverable, so severity is low under the review policy.

**Fix:** Use one normalized pagination value for both bounds and request fixed ten-item inclusive ranges: `page * 10` through `page * 10 + 9`.

findings.title: Malformed publish tags terminate the NodeBB worker
findings.body:
A publisher can terminate a NodeBB worker by submitting malformed JSON in `tags`. The handler waits for asynchronous administrator/group checks, then calls `JSON.parse(tags)` without handling exceptions. Because that callback runs after Express has returned from the route handler, the `SyntaxError` is uncaught; NodeBB's uncaught-exception handler shuts down and exits the process.

**Preconditions:** The caller is an administrator or a member of `publishers`, has normal topic-create permission, and submits a valid CSRF token.

**Evidence:** The publish route is CSRF protected at `library.js:252`, and the GET response/form supplies a token at `library.js:100-106` and `public/templates/comments/comments.tpl:81-90`. After asynchronous authorization (`library.js:166-176`), `library.js:182` parses the client-controlled non-empty `tags` in the callback. NodeBB 1.12 defers group-membership results and exits on uncaught exceptions, so a request with `cid=1` and `tags={` reaches an uncaught `SyntaxError`.

**Impact:** A privileged publisher can take down a worker; the service restarts, so this is a broad but recoverable outage. The trigger requires an already trusted role, which discounts the policy severity to low.

**Fix:** Parse and validate `tags` before starting async work, or catch parse errors in the callback and return a 4xx response. Pass errors to Express rather than throwing.

findings.title: Published topics never show their source linkback
findings.body:
The configured linkback never appears on NodeBB 1.12, which this package declares compatible. Publishing stores the source URL under the new post’s numeric PID, but the registered profile-info hook receives only a user ID and profile array. `post.pid` is therefore `undefined`, so the later lookup reads `post:undefined` and never finds the stored URL.

**Evidence:** `library.js:186-187` stores `blog-comments:url` for the created post, and `library.js:203-207` reads it using `post.pid`. The hook is registered as `filter:posts.custom_profile_info` in `plugin.json:11-13`; NodeBB 1.12 calls that hook with `{ profile: [], uid }`, not a post object. As a result `library.js:208-221` skips the only code that appends the “Posted from” profile entry. The declared compatibility range includes NodeBB 1.12 at `package.json:30-32`.

**Impact:** Every published article lacks its promised source linkback on the supported NodeBB release. This is a contained, recoverable presentation defect, so severity is low under the review policy.

**Fix:** Use a hook that receives the post PID, or store/resolve the source URL from the user-profile hook's actual input model rather than reading `post.pid`.

summary:
Reviewed the added `server.js` and its HTTP/WebSocket paths.

Updated existing finding `fnd_rf0hcnbdiurn034h` to **high**: on Windows, an absolute-form HTTP request can bypass the new traversal filter and read arbitrary service-account-readable files outside `__dirname` (`server.js:10`). The root demo URL issue was already recorded separately.

The PR fixes the straightforward POSIX traversal case, but its path construction remains unsafe across supported platforms.

Reviewed the added generated parser and its public `Parser.parse` integration, lexer behavior, build flow, and generated-source consistency. I recorded one medium finding: the committed Jison 0.4.17 output conflicts with the lockfile’s Jison 0.4.18, so regenerating the parser breaks the advertised browser UMD build. The formula-array `eval` path is reachable but already has an open finding for this repository and file, so I did not duplicate it.

findings.title: Regenerating the parser breaks the browser build
findings.body:
Running the repository's documented parser generator makes the advertised browser build fail. The committed parser was generated by Jison 0.4.17, but the lockfile installs 0.4.18. That version emits a CommonJS CLI `main` which imports Node's `fs`; webpack follows the parser import while producing the UMD bundle and cannot resolve `fs` for the browser target.

**Evidence:** `package.json:15-20` exposes `generate-parser` and includes the UMD builds in `build`. The generator version recorded in the added file differs from the locked version (`src/grammar-parser/grammar-parser.js:1`, `package-lock.json:5515-5518`). After `npm run generate-parser`, `npm run build` fails in `build:umd` with `Module not found: Can't resolve 'fs'`; the generated parser is included through `src/parser.js:3`, and the browser bundle is configured by `webpack.config.js:9-20`. The README advertises that UMD browser artifact at `README.md:23-29`.

**Impact:** Contributors cannot regenerate the parser and build the browser package with the committed dependencies. This affects all releases made through the supported build path, but restoring the intended generator output/configuration recovers it. Severity is medium under the broad/recoverable policy.

**Fix:** Pin the generator to the version that produces browser-safe output, or configure/update generation so its output has no Node CLI imports, then commit that reproducible output and verify `generate-parser && build`.

summary: Review complete. The PR restores the serializer implementation and includes the intended UID-based placeholder fix, but it needs revision before merge: I recorded seven findings, including clean-install failure, code-generation injection paths, and serialization correctness defects. The package cannot currently load in this checkout because `randombytes` is undeclared, so the normal test suite could not run unmodified.

findings.title: Clean installs cannot load the serializer
findings.body:
A clean consumer installation cannot load this package. `index.js` imports `randombytes` during module initialization, but the published manifest declares only development dependencies, so npm does not install that module.

**Evidence:** `package.json:5` makes `index.js` the entry point and `index.js:9` imports `randombytes` before exporting the serializer. `package.json:27-32` contains no production dependency. Packing this revision and installing the tarball into an empty project installs only `serialize-javascript`; `node -e 'require("serialize-javascript")'` then fails with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` at `index.js:9`.

**Impact:** Every consumer installed without a coincidentally hoisted `randombytes` copy loses the package's only API. This is broad but recoverable by publishing a corrected manifest, so it is medium severity under the reach × persistence policy.

**Fix:** Add the `randombytes` version used by this implementation to `dependencies` (and regenerate the lockfile as appropriate).

findings.title: Function values bypass default inline-script escaping
findings.body:
Default serialization can emit a raw `</script>` from a function body, so the documented inline-script use permits injected browser code. For example, a server can construct but not invoke `new Function("return '</script><script>globalThis.xss=1</script>'")`; serializing it and placing the result in an inline `<script>` closes that element and executes the second script.

**Preconditions:** An attacker can supply callback/template source that the application compiles into a function and later serializes into an HTML script. Constructing the function does not execute its body.

**Evidence:** Functions become placeholders at `index.js:110-112`. The default escaping pass runs only on the JSON text at `index.js:188-193`, before replacement. Replacement returns `Function#toString()` verbatim through `index.js:125-139` and `index.js:234-236`, leaving `<`, `>`, and `/` in the final output. This conflicts with the default safe-script contract in `README.md:16-18` and `README.md:60-74`; only explicit `{unsafe: true}` should disable it (`README.md:100-106`).

**Impact:** The stated input condition crosses a trust boundary and runs arbitrary JavaScript in the embedding page's origin. The required application-specific compilation path discounts this one tier from high to medium under the reach × persistence policy.

**Fix:** Escape unsafe HTML and line-terminator characters in function source before inserting it, or apply the escaping pass after all placeholder replacements while preserving generated JavaScript syntax.

findings.title: Concise methods with nested functions serialize to invalid JavaScript
findings.body:
Concise object methods that contain an arrow or nested function serialize into invalid JavaScript. For example, serializing `{ method() { return () => 42; } }` returns `{"method":method() { return () => 42; }}`, which throws `SyntaxError: Unexpected token '{'` when deserialized as documented with `eval('(' + output + ')')`.

**Evidence:** Every function is sent to `serializeFunc` through `index.js:110-112` and `index.js:202-236`. The unanchored patterns at `index.js:17-18` match `=>` or `function` anywhere in a concise method body, so `index.js:131-139` returns `method() { ... }` unchanged. That source is invalid after an object property's colon. The conversion at `index.js:141-156` would emit a valid `function() { ... }`, but these early returns skip it. Simple concise methods are expected to use that conversion by `test/unit/serialize.js:120-134`.

**Impact:** A valid application value cannot be deserialized, which can prevent loading the serialized state. The failure is contained and recoverable by changing the input or serializer, so it is low severity under the reach × persistence policy.

**Fix:** Detect only function declarations and arrow functions at the start of the source, or normalize concise methods before testing their bodies.

findings.title: ignoreFunction deletes caller properties and rejects frozen objects
findings.body:
`ignoreFunction` changes its input while attempting to omit functions, and it rejects frozen inputs that `JSON.stringify` handles. `serialize({keep: 1, f: function () {}}, {ignoreFunction: true})` returns the expected text but permanently removes `f` from the caller's object; the same object after `Object.freeze` throws `TypeError: Cannot delete property 'f'`.

**Evidence:** With `ignoreFunction`, the replacer calls `deleteFunctions(value)` at `index.js:76-81`. That helper enumerates function-valued keys and deletes them from the original object at `index.js:46-55`. Strict mode is enabled at `index.js:7`, so deleting the non-configurable property on a frozen object throws. The option promises to treat functions like `JSON.stringify` (`README.md:108-115`), which omits object function properties without mutating or rejecting frozen objects.

**Impact:** A caller using this documented option can lose function properties or fail to serialize valid immutable state. The explicit non-default option discounts this contained permanent input mutation to low severity under the reach × persistence policy.

**Fix:** Do not delete caller properties. Have the replacer return `undefined` for function values when `ignoreFunction` is enabled, retaining JSON's array/object behavior without mutation.

findings.title: Modified RegExp flags become executable serialized source
findings.body:
A `RegExp` instance can make the serializer emit and later run arbitrary JavaScript because its `flags` property is inserted as raw source. An extensible native regexp needs no prototype modification: `Object.defineProperty(/safe/gi, 'flags', {value: '\"),globalThis.injected=1,(\"'})` serializes to `new RegExp("safe", ""),globalThis.injected=1,("")`. Evaluating the documented deserialization expression executes the assignment.

**Preconditions:** An attacker can provide a live, attacker-modified `RegExp` instance to a producer which serializes it and a consumer evaluates the returned JavaScript.

**Evidence:** The replacer stores every `instanceof RegExp` at `index.js:92-95`. During replacement, `index.js:215` safely serializes `.source` but concatenates `.flags` inside double quotes without string escaping. The earlier escaping pass is before placeholder expansion (`index.js:188-193`), so it cannot protect these characters. The package documents evaluated literal-JavaScript output (`README.md:16-18`, `README.md:119-124`).

**Impact:** Under the stated producer/consumer boundary, a modified live regexp crosses the boundary as code and executes in the consumer's evaluation context. Requiring this non-JSON, application-specific object path discounts the cross-boundary recoverable impact to medium under the reach × persistence policy.

**Fix:** Serialize the flags as a JavaScript string literal (or obtain and validate intrinsic regexp flags) rather than concatenating property text.

findings.title: A failed native-function request poisons the next serialization
findings.body:
A caught attempt to serialize one native function changes the result for the next request. Calling `serialize(Number)` throws as intended, but immediately calling `serialize(Boolean)` returns `function Boolean() { [native code] }` instead of throwing; that returned text cannot be parsed as JavaScript.

**Evidence:** `IS_NATIVE_CODE_REGEXP` is global at `index.js:16`, making `.test()` stateful. The first native match at `index.js:127-129` leaves `lastIndex` near the end of `Number`'s source. The next native source is tested from that offset, misses its earlier `[native code]` fragment, and falls through to the raw-source return at `index.js:131-134`. Native functions are expected to consistently throw by `test/unit/serialize.js:113-118`.

**Impact:** One caller can cause the next native-function serialization in the process to return unusable output rather than the documented error. The failure is transient, contained, and recoverable, so it is low severity under the reach × persistence policy.

**Fix:** Remove the `g` flag from this predicate or reset `IS_NATIVE_CODE_REGEXP.lastIndex` before testing.

findings.title: Classes with constructors serialize to malformed JavaScript
findings.body:
Classes with a constructor or method serialize to malformed JavaScript. For example, serializing `{Foo: class Foo { constructor() {} }}` produces `{"Foo":function() {} }}`, which throws `SyntaxError` when deserialized using the documented parenthesized `eval` form.

**Evidence:** Classes enter the function path at `index.js:110-112`. `serializeFunc` only recognizes ordinary functions and arrows at `index.js:125-139`. For class source containing `constructor()`, `index.js:141-155` takes that inner `(` as if it marked a concise method's argument list and prepends `function`, corrupting the source. The returned value is promised to be literal JavaScript at `README.md:4`, `README.md:16`, and its documented deserializer evaluates it at `README.md:119-124`.

**Impact:** Valid class values with ordinary constructors or methods cannot be restored, preventing affected serialized state from loading. The impact is contained and recoverable, so it is low severity under the reach × persistence policy.

**Fix:** Recognize class source before concise-method rewriting and return it unchanged, or reject unsupported classes explicitly.

summary:
Reviewed PR #1’s added HHVM package entrypoint and traced its deep-link, remote-connection, and debugger flows. The hostname safelist correctly addresses the CVE’s special-character host injection path, but I recorded three separate regressions: deep links can open and recursively watch `/` on saved remote hosts, breakpoint links throw before debugging starts, and cancelled connections leave stale progress UI.

No repository files were modified.

findings.title: Deep links can recursively watch the root of saved remote hosts
findings.body:
An external `atom://nuclide/attach-hhvm` link can select `/` as the initial directory for a host the victim has previously connected to. The normal connection dialog forbids this directory, but this handler sends it directly to saved-connection reuse. That creates a remote project rooted at `/` and starts a recursive watcher over the full accessible remote filesystem.

**Preconditions:** The victim has a reusable saved connection for the supplied valid hostname.

**Evidence:** The global URI handler forwards query parameters to the deep-link service without an origin check (`lib/main.js:356-365`). The handler accepts and decodes any string `hackRoot` (`pkg/nuclide-hhvm/lib/main.js:80-93`), then converts `hackRoot=/` to `cwd: "/"` for `createRemoteConnection` (`pkg/nuclide-hhvm/lib/main.js:127-144`). Saved connections reuse their credentials with the supplied CWD (`pkg/nuclide-remote-connection/lib/RemoteConnection.js:127-153`), and initialization recursively watches that root (`pkg/nuclide-remote-connection/lib/RemoteConnection.js:233-264`, `272-282`). In contrast, the interactive dialog rejects `/` (`pkg/nuclide-remote-projects/lib/ConnectionDialog.js:360-365`).

**Impact:** A link can make the victim's client and a saved remote host recursively watch the entire accessible filesystem and changes the project/CWD to `/`. This crosses the deep-link trust boundary but requires an existing saved connection and is recoverable by closing the project, so severity is medium.

**Fix:** Apply the same non-root initial-directory invariant before calling `createRemoteConnection` (and reject or normalize unsafe `hackRoot` values).

findings.title: Breakpoint deep links throw before HHVM debugging starts
findings.body:
A normal `attach-hhvm` deep link that asks for a breakpoint throws before it attaches the debugger. The remote debugger service returned by this provider lookup has no `addBreakpoint` method.

**Preconditions:** The link supplies `addBreakpoint=true` and an integer `line`.

**Evidence:** The handler obtains `nuclide-debugger.remote` and calls `debuggerService.addBreakpoint(...)` before `startDebugging` (`pkg/nuclide-hhvm/lib/main.js:172-185`). Both implementations registered for that service return `RemoteControlService` (`pkg/nuclide-debugger/lib/main.js:973-975`; `pkg/nuclide-debugger-new/lib/main.js:886-888`), and neither class exposes `addBreakpoint` (`pkg/nuclide-debugger/lib/RemoteControlService.js:39-45`; `pkg/nuclide-debugger-new/lib/RemoteControlService.js:34-62`). The call therefore raises `TypeError` and skips debugger startup.

**Impact:** Supported breakpoint deep links cannot attach a debugger. The failure affects one requested debugging operation and is recoverable by retrying without a breakpoint, so severity is low.

**Fix:** Expose a consistent breakpoint operation on both remote-control service implementations, or defer breakpoint creation through the debugger API after startup using its required line convention.

findings.title: Cancelled remote connections leave a stale Connecting notification
findings.body:
Cancelling the connection dialog leaves the earlier progress notification visible as “Connecting …”. The handler only dismisses that notification after all navigation and debugger work succeeds.

**Evidence:** The handler creates a dismissable connection notification (`pkg/nuclide-hhvm/lib/main.js:127-135`). If `createRemoteConnection()` returns `null`, it displays an error and returns without dismissing it (`pkg/nuclide-hhvm/lib/main.js:138-149`); the sole dismissal is on the success path (`pkg/nuclide-hhvm/lib/main.js:172-189`). A first-time connection can return `null` after the user cancels the dialog (`pkg/nuclide-remote-projects/lib/RemoteProjectsService.js:52-68`; `pkg/nuclide-remote-projects/lib/open-connection.js:94-97`).

**Impact:** A normal cancellation leaves misleading UI until the user manually closes it. The effect is contained and recoverable, so severity is low.

**Fix:** Dismiss the progress notification for every terminal result, such as with a `try`/`finally` around the connection and debugger sequence.

summary:
Reviewed PR #2 in full. The new HHVM deep-link handler accepts a doubly encoded hostname and renders it in an HTML-capable Atom notification, enabling renderer JavaScript execution from an attacker-controlled `atom://` link. I recorded the confirmed high-severity finding `fnd_mcnd7ekaqark4vxb`.

The adjacent fixed revision confirms that hostname validation is the required missing invariant.

findings.title: Attach-HHVM deep links execute HTML in Atom notifications
findings.body: An attacker who convinces an Atom user to open an `atom://nuclide/attach-hhvm` URI can execute HTML/JavaScript in Atom's renderer. The handler accepts a doubly encoded hostname, decodes it after its prefix-only remote-URI check, and interpolates it into an HTML-capable notification. **Evidence:** The root URI handler forwards the external URI query unchanged to the deep-link service (`lib/main.js:356-365`), which sends it to the `attach-hhvm` subscriber (`pkg/nuclide-deep-link/lib/DeepLinkService.js:74-97`). This handler checks only that the *pre-decoded* value starts with `nuclide://`, then calls `decodeURIComponent` (`pkg/nuclide-hhvm/lib/main.js:83-93`). `getHostname` accepts the decoded text before `/` without restricting hostname characters (`modules/nuclide-commons/nuclideUri.js:126-147`), and the handler embeds it in `atom.notifications.addInfo` (`pkg/nuclide-hhvm/lib/main.js:115-123`). For example, a query value that decodes first to `nuclide://%3Cimg%20src%3Dx%20onerror%3D%22...%22%3E/a.php` passes the prefix check and decodes again to an event-bearing `` hostname. Atom notifications accept HTML; the Nuclide notification integration renders notification text through `marked()` and `innerHTML` (`pkg/nuclide-atom-notifications/lib/main.js:63-76`). The adjacent fixed revision adds a hostname character allowlist at this exact point. **Impact:** Opening an attacker-controlled deep link crosses the external-link trust boundary and runs attacker JavaScript in the Atom renderer, with the user's editor privileges. This is high severity under the review policy. **Fix:** After decoding and extracting the hostname, reject any character outside the valid hostname set before creating the notification or remote connection.

summary:
Reviewed the full new `index.js` entry point and recorded three medium-severity availability findings. The PR restores the vulnerable brace-option detector and also permits nonterminating numeric sequence inputs.

`npm test` passes all 172 existing assertions. The working tree is clean.

findings.title: Untrusted brace patterns can block the event loop
findings.body:
An application that passes an untrusted pattern to `expand()` can have its Node.js event loop blocked for seconds by a short, balanced input such as `"{" + ",".repeat(26) + "\\nX}"`. The added entry point is the package's `main`, so this is the normal exported path.

**Evidence:** `expand()` passes every balanced brace body to `/^(.*,)+(.+)?$/` at `index.js:103-110`. The repeated `.*` can partition each comma many ways; `.` cannot consume the final newline, so the match backtracks exponentially before returning false. On Node 24, 22 commas took 98 ms and 26 commas exceeded a four-second timeout. The fixed PR branch replaces the regex with `m.body.indexOf(',') >= 0`.

**Impact:** A remote caller whose input is used as a brace pattern can repeatedly stall the single-threaded process and deny service to all its requests. This has broad, recoverable availability impact, so severity is **medium** under the review policy.

**Fix:** Detect option groups without an ambiguous backtracking regex, for example `m.body.indexOf(',') >= 0`, and add a regression test with comma runs followed by a newline.

findings.title: Zero-step sequences never terminate
findings.body:
A pattern with a zero sequence increment, such as `{1..3..0}`, never returns from `expand()`. Bash expands that same pattern to `1`, `2`, `3`, so callers that accept a user-provided pattern can be permanently blocked by an otherwise valid sequence.

**Evidence:** The sequence grammar accepts `..0` at `index.js:106`. `Math.abs(numeric(n[2]))` therefore sets `incr` to zero at `index.js:153-155`; the loop at `index.js:166` keeps testing the unchanged initial value and never terminates when the range is nonempty. `timeout 2s node -e "require('./')('{1..3..0}')"` did not complete, while `bash -c 'printf "<%s>\\n" {1..3..0}'` produced `<1>`, `<2>`, and `<3>`.

**Impact:** A remote caller whose input is used as a brace pattern can indefinitely block the single-threaded process, denying service to all requests until it is restarted. This is broad, recoverable availability impact, so severity is **medium** under the review policy.

**Fix:** Treat a parsed zero increment as the default increment of one before entering the loop, or reject it as a non-sequence, and cover `{1..3..0}` and reverse/alphabetic zero-step ranges.

findings.title: Overlong numeric sequences never terminate
findings.body:
A numeric sequence whose endpoints have 310 or more digits, for example `{<310 nines>..<310 nines>}`, never returns from `expand()`. This requires only a short input and does not need the range to contain multiple representable values.

**Evidence:** The numeric-sequence expression accepts arbitrary-length digits at `index.js:106`. `numeric()` accepts `parseInt(str, 10) == str` at `index.js:12-16`; for a 310-digit all-nine endpoint both conversions are `Infinity`, so the comparison succeeds. The loop then starts with `i` and `y` both `Infinity`; `lte(i, y)` is always true (`index.js:92-94`) and `i += incr` cannot change `Infinity` (`index.js:166`). `timeout 2s node -e "require('./')('{'+ '9'.repeat(310) +'..'+ '9'.repeat(310) +'}')"` did not complete.

**Impact:** A remote caller whose input is used as a brace pattern can indefinitely block the single-threaded process, denying service to all requests until it is restarted. This is broad, recoverable availability impact, so severity is **medium** under the review policy.

**Fix:** Reject sequence endpoints or increments that are not finite safe integers before the expansion loop. Use bounded integer parsing rather than the loose `parseInt(...) == str` test.

summary:
Reviewed the full added `index.ts` and recorded six findings. The most serious issue is that cross-origin redirects still send credentials configured through client defaults or built-in credential handlers. I also found TLS verification state leaking through `https.globalAgent`, plus redirect, keep-alive, response-lifecycle, and typed-404 correctness failures.

`npm run build` succeeded. The test suite was run, but most network-dependent httpbin tests failed or timed out with upstream `503` responses; local proxy tests passed.

findings.title: Cross-host redirects send client-level credentials
findings.body:
A redirect to a different host still receives credentials configured on the client or supplied by the bundled credential handlers. A server that can return a redirect for a privileged request can therefore capture the bearer token, PAT, or Basic credential at its target.

**Preconditions:** The caller uses `requestOptions.headers.Authorization` or a bundled credential handler, and the first server returns a followed cross-host redirect.

**Evidence:** The redirect branch deletes `Authorization` only from the per-call `headers` map at `index.ts:389-396`, then prepares the target request at `index.ts:399-401`. `_prepareRequest` rebuilds headers by merging the unchanged `requestOptions.headers` at `index.ts:553` and `index.ts:570-583`; it then calls every handler again at `index.ts:560-565`. The Basic, Bearer, and PAT handlers each unconditionally set `Authorization` in `auth.ts:12-16`, `auth.ts:41-43`, and `auth.ts:69-72`. A local 302 from `127.0.0.1` to `localhost` confirmed that all four credential sources reach the target; the existing test only covers per-call headers (`__tests__/basics.test.ts:182-223`).

**Impact:** This crosses a trust boundary and permanently discloses reusable credentials. Severity is high under the review policy: automatic redirects are enabled by default (`index.ts:106`, `index.ts:363-367`) and the issue was reproduced.

**Fix:** Carry redirect-origin state into request preparation and remove sensitive credentials from the final headers after default headers and handlers have run whenever the target origin differs. Add tests for default headers and each built-in credential handler.

findings.title: ignoreSslError disables verification for later clients
findings.body:
Enabling `ignoreSslError` on one direct HTTPS client disables certificate validation for later clients in the same process. Those later callers did not opt into insecure TLS, but share the mutated global agent.

**Preconditions:** A direct HTTPS request uses `ignoreSslError: true`; a later HTTPS request uses the default global agent.

**Evidence:** The constructor accepts `ignoreSslError` at `index.ts:124-127`. Without a proxy or keep-alive, `_getAgent` selects `https.globalAgent` at `index.ts:659-662`, then mutates its `options.rejectUnauthorized` to `false` at `index.ts:664-670`. Later ordinary clients select the same singleton, and `dispose()` neither restores it nor destroys it (`index.ts:424-429`). A local self-signed HTTPS server confirmed that, after an insecure client's request succeeds, a new default client also accepts the self-signed certificate.

**Impact:** An on-path attacker or invalid TLS endpoint can intercept a later caller's HTTPS traffic despite that caller requiring normal certificate validation. This is medium under the review policy: it crosses a trust boundary, but requires the non-default insecure option to have been enabled first.

**Fix:** Use a private HTTPS agent configured with `rejectUnauthorized: false` only for this client/request. Never modify `https.globalAgent`.

findings.title: Relative redirects target port 80 instead of the response origin
findings.body:
The client follows a standard relative `Location` as if it were an absolute URL. For example, an HTTP server returning `Location: /target` causes the next request to be sent to a null host on port 80 instead of the original host's `/target`; HTTPS requests instead reject the relative reference as a downgrade.

**Evidence:** The redirect loop parses the header by itself at `index.ts:369-374` and passes it directly to `_prepareRequest` at `index.ts:399-401`. It never resolves the reference against the effective request URL. `_prepareRequest` derives the protocol, host, port, and path from that incomplete value (`index.ts:540-552`), so a relative value has no hostname/protocol and defaults to HTTP/80. A local HTTP 302 with `Location: /target` reproduced an `ECONNREFUSED` to port 80; the origin never received `/target`. Existing tests use only absolute Locations (`__tests__/basics.test.ts:131-152`).

**Impact:** Normal, same-origin redirects fail, breaking clients against servers that use relative redirect targets. Severity is low under the review policy because this is a recoverable request failure.

**Fix:** Resolve `Location` against the URL of the response before protocol, origin, and request-option checks, and update that effective URL after each hop.

findings.title: Keep-alive clients cannot switch between HTTP and HTTPS
findings.body:
One keep-alive agent is reused for every direct destination, even when a later request uses the other protocol. After an HTTP request, an HTTPS request receives the cached `http.Agent` and rejects with `ERR_INVALID_PROTOCOL`; the inverse order has the corresponding failure. Proxy tunnel agents have the same problem because all four target/proxy TLS combinations share `_proxyAgent`.

**Preconditions:** The client enables `keepAlive` and sends requests to both HTTP and HTTPS endpoints.

**Evidence:** `_getAgent` returns `_agent` for any direct request or `_proxyAgent` for any proxied request before considering the target scheme (`index.ts:600-616`). The required agent is selected by scheme only after that return (`index.ts:618`, `index.ts:624-656`). A local HTTP request followed by HTTPS on one keep-alive client reproduced `ERR_INVALID_PROTOCOL: Protocol "https:" not supported. Expected "http:"`.

**Impact:** A supported keep-alive client cannot mix HTTP and HTTPS requests. Severity is low under the review policy: it is a recoverable request failure requiring the non-default keep-alive option.

**Fix:** Cache agents by target protocol and, for proxies, proxy endpoint/protocol plus target protocol; or construct a compatible agent whenever those properties differ.

findings.title: Typed 404 responses resolve before their headers are available
findings.body:
Typed JSON methods resolve a 404 before the response has been consumed. Callers therefore receive empty headers, and the returned object can mutate later when its body arrives.

**Evidence:** `_processResponse` resolves the newly created response immediately for 404 at `index.ts:698-709`, then awaits `readBody`, parses it, and assigns headers at `index.ts:714-727`. Later settlement has no effect, but these mutations remain observable. A local 404 with `X-404-Metadata: present` and a JSON body returned `{statusCode: 404, result: null, headers: {}}` immediately after `await getJson`; later the same object contained the header and parsed body. The typed response contract exposes headers (`interfaces.ts:95-99`), while the existing test checks only the null result (`__tests__/basics.test.ts:307-313`).

**Impact:** Consumers cannot reliably inspect 404 headers such as rate limits or application metadata, and the result changes after the promise resolves. Severity is low under the review policy because this is a contained, recoverable API correctness failure.

**Fix:** Consume the response and populate headers before resolving the special 404 result; preserve `result: null` for that response instead of parsing and mutating it later.

findings.title: Discarded redirect and 401 responses exhaust keep-alive pools
findings.body:
Two paths replace or reject a response without consuming it. With a bounded keep-alive pool, an unread response retains the only socket and the next request waits indefinitely.

**Preconditions:** The client uses `keepAlive: true` with a bounded `maxSockets`, and the discarded response body exceeds Node's buffered amount.

**Evidence:** A forbidden HTTPS-to-HTTP redirect throws at `index.ts:375-382` before the drain at `index.ts:385-387`. A 401 accepted by a supported authentication handler is passed to `handleAuthentication` at `index.ts:339-355` without draining it; the handler is not given the discarded response by its interface (`interfaces.ts:59-67`). In contrast, ordinary redirects and retries explicitly consume responses before replacing them at `index.ts:385-387` and `index.ts:412-414`. A local 128-KiB redirect or 401 response with `{keepAlive: true, maxSockets: 1}` retained the only socket and left the next request queued.

**Impact:** A server can make a client stop issuing later requests until the peer closes the unread response. Severity is low under the review policy because it requires non-default pool settings and is recoverable by recreating the client.

**Fix:** Drain or destroy every response before throwing it away: before the downgrade error and before invoking an authentication retry handler.

summary:
Reviewed the full `index.js` addition and its public expansion path. The option detection change removes the known catastrophic regex, but a separate malformed-brace recovery regex still has quadratic behavior; I recorded one medium-severity finding: `fnd_2c1nl4zbxxhpbsqn`.

`npm test` passes all 172 tests. The change is not ready to approve until the remaining recovery-path ReDoS is fixed.

findings.title: Malformed brace patterns can still block the event loop
findings.body:
A malformed pattern with one closed non-option group followed by comma-separated text can still block the Node.js event loop. For example, `expand('{x}' + ',a'.repeat(100000))` returns the literal input, but took about 15 seconds on Node 24.

**Evidence:** `expandTop()` passes public input to `expand()` at `index.js:79`. After `balanced()` separates `{x}`, its body is neither a sequence nor an option group, so the recovery branch calls `m.post.match(/,.*\}/)` at `index.js:110-114`. When `m.post` contains many commas and no closing brace, the unanchored match starts at each comma and `.*` scans the remaining suffix before failing to find `}`. This takes quadratic time: 10,000 `,a` pairs took about 164 ms, 30,000 took about 1.44 s, and 100,000 took about 15.4 s. The function then simply returns the original string.

**Impact:** A remote caller whose pattern reaches this API can repeatedly occupy its single-threaded Node.js process. This is broad, recoverable availability impact, so severity is **medium** under the review policy.

**Fix:** Replace the backtracking recovery test with a linear check for a comma followed by a closing brace, or scan `m.post` once without an ambiguous `.*` expression.

summary: Reviewed the new Git-backed filesystem implementation, including public input flows, process execution, binary output handling, and tree parsing. I recorded three findings: one high-severity command-execution issue and two low-severity correctness/availability issues. The legacy test toolchain could not run under the sandbox’s Node 24 environment; I recorded an environment report and used direct reproductions and independent verification instead.

findings.title: Public Git arguments can execute shell commands
findings.body:
`open()` accepts repository paths and refs from its caller, while `readFile()` accepts a repository filename. `_buildCommand()` interpolates all of them into a single string and every operation passes that string to `child_process.exec()`, which runs it through a shell. For example, `open("not-a-repository; touch /tmp/poc; #").then(g => g.showRef())` creates `/tmp/poc`; an injected final command also makes the promise resolve even though Git failed.

**Evidence:** `open()` stores unvalidated `path` and `ref` in `FSGit` (lib/index.ts:7-17). `readFile()` adds the supplied filename to `git show` (lib/index.ts:61-64), and `revParse()` adds the ref to `git rev-parse` (lib/index.ts:82-86). `_buildCommand()` joins these values without quoting (lib/index.ts:125-126), and the resulting strings reach `exec()` (lib/index.ts:38, lib/index.ts:64, lib/index.ts:86, lib/index.ts:102).

**Impact:** A consumer that passes request, configuration, or repository-controlled values through this public API gives an untrusted actor arbitrary commands as the Node process account. This crosses a trust boundary and can make persistent changes, so it is **high** under the review severity policy. The public path requires no valid Git repository.

**Fix:** Do not construct a shell command. Invoke `execFile("git", args, ...)` (or `spawn` with `shell: false`) and pass each Git option and operand as a separate array element.

findings.title: Binary Git blobs are decoded and corrupted
findings.body:
`readFile()` promises a `Buffer` when called without an encoding, but it lets `exec()` decode Git's blob output as UTF-8 before resolving it. Binary blob bytes that are not valid UTF-8 are replaced and cannot be recovered; callers also receive a string rather than the declared `Buffer`. Supplying `{ encoding: "hex" }` does not help because `String.prototype.toString()` ignores that argument.

**Evidence:** The overload declares `readFile(path: string): Promise<Buffer>` (lib/index.ts:57), but the `exec()` call has no `encoding: "buffer"` option (lib/index.ts:61-64) and resolves `stdout` unchanged when no options are supplied (lib/index.ts:66-72). Node's default `exec` encoding is UTF-8. For a Git blob containing bytes `80 ff 41`, the call returns `"��A"`; converting that result back to bytes produces `ef bf bd ef bf bd 41`, not the source bytes.

**Impact:** Any normal caller reading a binary Git object receives corrupted data. The effect is limited to that requested object and retrying cannot recover its bytes through this API, so it is **low** under the review severity policy.

**Fix:** Request raw output (`encoding: "buffer"`) and only call `Buffer#toString(opts.encoding)` for the encoding overload. The shell-free process invocation should preserve that buffer as well.

findings.title: Newline filenames crash tree enumeration
findings.body:
A repository with a tracked filename containing a newline makes `fileList()` throw from an asynchronous callback, which can terminate the Node process. Git permits newline bytes in filenames and `ls-tree -z` emits them unchanged. `exists()` also fails for every query because it first enumerates the complete tree.

**Evidence:** `fileList()` calls `_lsTree(this.ref, ".")` (lib/index.ts:31-33), which requests NUL-delimited output (lib/index.ts:98-102). After splitting on NUL, the parser uses anchored `(.+)` (lib/index.ts:106-108); JavaScript `.` does not match a newline, so a record for `line\nbreak.txt` yields `null`. The following accesses to `matches[1]` through `matches[4]` throw (lib/index.ts:109-115). A committed file named `line\nbreak.txt` reproduces `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null` in `fileList()`.

**Impact:** A repository contributor can cause consumers that enumerate that repository to fail, including unrelated `exists()` checks. This is a contained availability failure with no demonstrated data or privilege impact, so it is **low** under the review severity policy.

**Fix:** Parse the fixed metadata prefix separately from the remaining NUL-delimited filename (for example, use `([\\s\\S]+)` for the filename) and reject malformed records through the returned promise rather than dereferencing a failed match.

summary: Reviewed the full added `index.ts` implementation, including redirects, credentials, retries, streams, response parsing, TLS agents, proxy handling, and keep-alive behavior. I recorded four new confirmed findings and marked one duplicate 404 finding as duplicate of the existing canonical report. The build succeeds; the selected Jest suites could not pass because their `httpbin.org` integration requests returned HTTP 503 in this environment. Overall, the change has serious redirect-related credential and request-body disclosure flaws, plus several lower-severity reliability defects.

findings.title: 303 redirects forward POST bodies to the redirect target
findings.body:
A `303 See Other` after `post()` or `postJson()` resends the original POST body to the redirect target instead of retrieving it with a bodyless GET. A redirecting service or open redirect can therefore make the client disclose request data to a different origin; ordinary POST/redirect/result flows also repeat a write.

**Evidence:** Redirects are enabled by default at `index.ts:106` and include `SeeOther` at `index.ts:57-63`. The redirect loop prepares the target with the unchanged `verb` and sends the unchanged `data` at `index.ts:399-401`; raw requests set a content length and write string data at `index.ts:470-472` and `index.ts:508-520`. A local server that returned `303 Location: http://127.0.0.1:<other-port>/result` after `POST /submit` received a second `POST /result` with the full `secret=payload` body. RFC 9110 requires a 303 target to be retrieved with GET or HEAD. Existing 303 coverage uses only GET (`__tests__/basics.test.ts:143-153`).

**Impact:** This crosses a trust boundary and can permanently disclose request contents to the redirect target. Severity is high under the review policy: redirect following is default and the cross-origin body replay was reproduced.

**Fix:** For a 303, replace the redirected method with GET (or retain HEAD) and clear the body and body-specific headers before preparing the next request. Cover a cross-origin POST 303 regression case.

findings.title: getJson returns 404 responses before their headers are available
findings.body:
`getJson()` resolves its 404 response before reading the body and assigning response headers. Callers that inspect the object immediately after `await` therefore see `{}` for headers; the same object is later mutated after the response ends.

**Evidence:** `_processResponse` initializes empty headers at `index.ts:700-704` and resolves immediately for 404 at `index.ts:706-709`. It reads the body and assigns `res.message.headers` only at `index.ts:714-727`, then continues after the first resolve. A local 404 server sent `X-Proof: present-before-body-end` and delayed `end` by 250 ms: `await getJson()` returned in 9 ms with empty headers, then the returned object acquired `x-proof` after the body ended. The existing 404 test checks only the immediate null result (`__tests__/basics.test.ts:307-313`).

**Impact:** Callers cannot reliably use headers such as rate-limit, cache, or application metadata on a normal not-found response. This is a contained, recoverable API correctness failure, so severity is low under the review policy.

**Fix:** Handle 404 after consuming the response and populating headers, then resolve exactly once with `result: null`; do not continue parsing or mutate an already resolved response.

findings.title: Same-host redirects disclose Authorization to another port
findings.body:
A redirect to the same hostname on a different port retains `Authorization`, even though that port is a separate origin. A service that can redirect a credentialed request to an attacker-controlled service on the same host can therefore disclose the caller's bearer, PAT, or Basic credential.

**Evidence:** The redirect branch decides whether to remove `Authorization` by comparing only `hostname` at `index.ts:389-397`, omitting scheme and effective port, then sends the redirected request at `index.ts:399-401`. A local request from `http://127.0.0.1:<source-port>` to a 302 target on `http://127.0.0.1:<sink-port>` delivered `Authorization: Bearer secret` to the sink. This occurs for per-call headers, `requestOptions.headers`, and bundled credential handlers. The existing redirect tests cover only a changed hostname (`__tests__/basics.test.ts:182-223`).

**Impact:** This crosses a trust boundary and permanently discloses reusable credentials. Severity is high under the review policy: redirects are enabled by default and the disclosure was reproduced.

**Fix:** Resolve each Location against the current request URL, then compare scheme, normalized hostname, and effective port before forwarding sensitive headers. Suppress credentials from all header sources when that origin changes, and add a different-port regression test.

findings.title: Truncated responses leave JSON and redirect requests pending
findings.body:
A server that closes a response before its advertised body completes leaves `readBody()` pending forever. This stalls `getJson()` and stalls redirect or retry handling that tries to drain such a response.

**Evidence:** `readBody()` resolves only on `end` and never handles `error`, `aborted`, or `close` at `index.ts:79-90`. `_processResponse()` awaits it for JSON requests at `index.ts:714-716`; redirect and retry paths do the same at `index.ts:385-387` and `index.ts:412-414`. A local server sent `Content-Length: 100`, wrote a partial JSON body, then destroyed the socket. `getJson()` and requests draining a redirect or retryable response remained pending after 300 ms.

**Impact:** A remote endpoint or intermediary can indefinitely stall one client operation instead of producing a recoverable transport error. This is a contained, re-triggerable availability failure, so severity is low under the review policy.

**Fix:** Settle `readBody()` exactly once: resolve on `end` and reject on `error`, `aborted`, or premature `close`. Propagate that rejection through JSON, redirect, and retry paths.

findings.title: Retries reuse consumed stream bodies
findings.body:
Retrying a streamed GET reuses an already consumed readable stream. The retry can send an empty body or remain pending until the socket timeout when the caller supplied a content length.

**Preconditions:** The caller uses `sendStream('GET', ...)` with retries enabled and the first response is 502, 503, or 504.

**Evidence:** `sendStream` passes one stream into `request` at `index.ts:209-215`. GET is retryable at `index.ts:69`, and the retry loop invokes `requestRaw(info, data)` repeatedly with that same object at `index.ts:328-337` and `index.ts:405-415`. Each attempt pipes the stream at `index.ts:512-517`. A local stream containing `ABC123` was fully received on the first attempt, which returned 503; the second attempt received an empty body. When it waited for the supplied `Content-Length: 6`, it remained pending until the client timeout.

**Impact:** A supported retry configuration can corrupt an uploaded request or stall it for up to the three-minute default timeout. This is a contained, recoverable failure requiring the non-default retry option, so severity is low under the review policy.

**Fix:** Do not retry requests with non-replayable stream bodies, or accept a factory that creates a fresh stream for each attempt. Add a streamed retry regression test.

summary: Reviewed the new `extend` implementation, its public import path, package metadata, and prototype-pollution behavior. I recorded two findings for this PR. Direct functional tests pass (83/83), but the required lint/test workflow does not complete.

findings.title: Clean installs cannot load node.extend
findings.body:
A production-only install cannot load this library. `lib/extend.js` now imports `has`, but the package manifest does not install it; every `require('node.extend')` reaches that import through `index.js`.

**Evidence:** `lib/extend.js:13` unconditionally calls `require('has')`; `index.js:3` exports that module; and `package.json:14-16` declares only `is` as a production dependency. In an otherwise empty consumer, installing the packed tarball with `--omit=dev` and then running `node -e "require('node.extend')"` throws `Cannot find module 'has'` from `lib/extend.js`.

**Impact:** This affects every clean consumer install and prevents the package from loading. The failure is recoverable by publishing a corrected package, so severity is medium under the reach × persistence policy.

**Fix:** Add `has` to `dependencies` (not only dev dependencies) and verify a production-only tarball install can require the package.

findings.title: The test command fails on the new property helper
findings.body:
