**Evidence:** `Object.keys(obj)` includes JSON's enumerable own `__proto__` key at `lib/deep-extend.js:104`. `safeGetProperty` turns that source value into `undefined` (`lib/deep-extend.js:105-106`, `lib/deep-extend.js:146-148`), after which the scalar branch writes `target[key] = val` (`lib/deep-extend.js:113-118`). For example, `deepExtend(Object.create(null), JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"x":1}}')).__proto__` is `undefined`; the unfixed implementation produces `{x: 1}`. The target prototype remains `null` in both cases.

**Impact:** A caller loses a supplied configuration/map member in a contained, recoverable operation. This is `info` under the review policy because it requires a non-default null-prototype target.

**Fix:** Explicitly skip `__proto__` keys before the assignment/merge paths, rather than converting them to `undefined` and writing them. That retains the prototype-pollution protection without materializing or overwriting a target data property.

summary: Reviewed PR #1 and recorded four findings. The added renderer restores rendering and screenshot routes, but it exposes local Chrome-readable files, mishandles failed targets and invalid screenshot dimensions, and interpolates render URLs into page-context JavaScript. I also checked the changed file for whitespace errors; no automated test suite ran because dependencies and a Chrome executable are absent in this checkout.

findings.title: Render callers can read files available to Chrome
findings.body:
The new renderer accepts `file:` URLs and returns their contents. With the default empty configuration, `isRestricted()` does not apply a protocol check, so an unauthenticated request such as `GET /render/file:///etc/passwd` reaches this new `Page.navigate` call. Chrome renders files readable by its service account, and `serialize()` returns the document HTML to the caller. The repository's tests already rely on navigating `file://` URLs at `test/app-test.js:114-125`.

**Evidence:** `src/main.js:65-74` permits every URL when `renderOnly` is unset; both public routes forward the wildcard URL at `src/main.js:91-100` and `src/main.js:110-124`. This code navigates it at `src/renderer.js:74`, then serialization returns `document.firstElementChild.outerHTML` at `src/renderer.js:184-193`.

**Impact:** An unauthenticated remote caller can disclose any file readable by Chrome (including application files and normally `/etc/passwd`). This crosses a trust boundary and disclosure persists once received, so severity is high.

**Fix:** Before routing to the renderer, parse the requested URL and reject every protocol other than `http:` and `https:`, regardless of whether `renderOnly` is configured.

findings.title: Negative screenshot dimensions leave renderer requests pending
findings.body:
A caller can make the screenshot request never settle by passing a negative dimension, for example `GET /screenshot/https://example.com/?width=-1`. `parseInt('-1')` is retained and sent to `Emulation.setDeviceMetricsOverride`, which Chrome rejects because dimensions must be positive. That `await` occurs in an `async` Promise executor before the `try`/`catch`; the executor's rejected promise is ignored, so `captureScreenshot()` remains pending. The route awaits it and never sends a response.

**Evidence:** The public route passes query values directly and waits for the result at `src/main.js:110-130`. Negative values survive the upper-bound-only parsing at `src/renderer.js:211-213`; the rejecting CDP calls are at `src/renderer.js:213-214`, before error handling starts at `src/renderer.js:216`. The same `new Promise(async ...)` pattern means neither outer `resolve` nor `reject` runs (`src/renderer.js:201-225`).

**Impact:** Unauthenticated callers can hold renderer requests and Chrome targets open repeatedly. In the standalone error policy, unhandled rejections also make the process exit after more than five errors (`src/main.js:164-174`). This broadly denies the service until restarted, so severity is high.

**Fix:** Validate dimensions as positive bounded integers, and remove the async Promise executor (or wrap all awaited setup in a `try`/`catch` that rejects and closes the target).

findings.title: Render URLs can inject script into the loaded page
findings.body:
`serialize()` turns an untrusted render URL into JavaScript source without escaping it. A percent-encoded quote in an otherwise allowed URL can close the string at line 187 and run attacker code in the loaded page's origin. For example, a URL ending in `%27);document.body.setAttribute(%27data-injected%27,%27yes%27);//` produces a valid extra statement; placing it after a `#` keeps it out of the navigation request. The injected code runs after scripts are stripped and before the DOM is returned.

**Evidence:** The public wildcard route passes `request.params.url` unchanged at `src/main.js:91-100`. The renderer navigates to it at `src/renderer.js:74`, then constructs `Runtime.evaluate` source by interpolating it in a single-quoted literal at `src/renderer.js:187`. The resulting DOM is serialized and sent to the requester at `src/renderer.js:189-193`. This also defeats the documented `renderOnly` domain boundary (`README.md:197-199`) for a URL that begins with an allowed origin.

**Impact:** A caller can execute arbitrary script in an allowed target origin, read its DOM and script-readable same-origin storage, make same-origin requests, and alter the rendered response. This is a cross-origin trust-boundary violation; without evidence of authenticated browser state, severity is medium.

**Fix:** Do not interpolate the URL into an expression. Pass it as a CDP argument or encode it with `JSON.stringify(url)` before building the call.

findings.title: Failed renders leave Chrome targets open
findings.body:
Every failed render leaves its newly created Chrome target open. Both methods create a tab before loading the request, but call `CDP.Close` only after the entire happy path succeeds. Their error handlers reject without closing the tab. An unauthenticated caller can repeatedly request an invalid URL such as `/render/abc`—the repository test confirms it fails—and accumulate targets until Chrome or the process exhausts resources.

**Evidence:** `serialize()` creates the target at `src/renderer.js:178-179`, closes it only at `src/renderer.js:190`, and rejects without cleanup at `src/renderer.js:194-196`. `_loadPage()` rejects invalid navigation through `Page.navigate(...).catch(reject)` at `src/renderer.js:74`, so that path reaches the leaking catch. `captureScreenshot()` has the same create/success-close/error path at `src/renderer.js:202-224`. The unauthenticated routes expose both operations at `src/main.js:91-124`, and `test/app-test.js:136-140` shows `/render/abc` is an expected failure.

**Impact:** Any remote caller can consume Chrome targets with repeatable failed requests, eventually denying the renderer to all users until it is restarted. The failure has broad, recoverable availability impact, so severity is high.

**Fix:** Always close the target in a `finally` block after creation, including setup, navigation, evaluation, and screenshot failures.

summary: Reviewed PR #1 and updated the existing open finding `fnd_yfq0h3onpla5ztdg` with evidence from the patched code. The new hostname check is intended to constrain the shell argument, but its JavaScript regex escaping leaves the command-execution flaw reachable. The remaining changed surface and its helper flow were covered; no separate issues were identified.

Reviewed the new Chrome renderer and its public render and screenshot paths. I recorded four findings:

- High: local files readable through `file://` render URLs.
- Medium: URL interpolation allows script injection in allowlisted pages.
- Medium: failed requests leak Chrome targets.
- High: negative screenshot dimensions can hang requests and terminate the renderer.

The renderer otherwise follows the expected render, status, serialization, and screenshot flow.

findings.title: Render callers can read files available to Chrome
findings.body:
An unauthenticated caller can read files that the Chrome process can read. With the default empty configuration, `isRestricted()` permits every URL scheme; the render route passes the supplied `file://` URL to the new renderer, which navigates Chrome to it and returns the resulting document HTML.

**Evidence:** `src/main.js:65-74` returns unrestricted when `renderOnly` is absent and `src/main.js:91-100` forwards the route parameter to `serialize()`. The new `src/renderer.js:75` navigates to that value and `src/renderer.js:185-194` serializes and returns the loaded document. Existing tests deliberately render `file://` fixtures at `test/app-test.js:114-125`, proving this navigation path is supported. For example, `/render/file:///etc/passwd` returns Chrome's rendered representation of that file.

**Impact:** This crosses a trust boundary: any HTTP caller can disclose arbitrary local files accessible to the renderer service account. Per the review policy, network-reachable, permanent confidentiality loss is **high**.

**Fix:** Reject non-HTTP(S) URLs before dispatching to Chrome (parse the URL and require `http:` or `https:`), rather than relying on the optional prefix allowlist.

findings.title: Render URLs can inject script into an allowlisted page
findings.body:
When an allowlist is configured, an unauthenticated caller can execute arbitrary JavaScript in an allowlisted page's origin. `serialize()` places the decoded request URL in a single-quoted JavaScript expression without escaping it after Chrome has loaded the page.

**Preconditions:** `renderOnly` is configured and the render endpoint is reachable.

**Evidence:** The route passes the decoded wildcard parameter to `serialize()` after only a `startsWith()` allowlist check (`src/main.js:65-74`, `src/main.js:91-100`). The new code builds `...})('${url}')` and evaluates it in the page at `src/renderer.js:172-175,188`; it serializes that same page afterwards at `src/renderer.js:190`. A URL such as `https://allowed.example/page#');document.title="injected";//` passes a prefix allowlist, loads `https://allowed.example/page` because the payload is in the fragment, then terminates the string and executes the assignment in that allowed origin. The same payload can read that page's DOM and non-HttpOnly cookies or make same-origin requests.

**Impact:** The caller gains code execution in an origin the allowlist was meant to protect. This is a cross-trust-boundary confidentiality/integrity risk, discounted one tier because it requires the non-default `renderOnly` configuration; under the review policy it is **medium**.

**Fix:** Pass `url` as a protocol argument or serialize it with `JSON.stringify(url)` when building the expression; do not interpolate it into a quoted JavaScript literal.

findings.title: Failed renders leave Chrome targets open
findings.body:
Failed requests leave their newly created Chrome targets open. An unauthenticated caller can repeatedly request a malformed or unreachable URL and accumulate Chrome tabs until the renderer exhausts browser resources.

**Evidence:** Both methods create a target before rendering (`src/renderer.js:178-182`, `src/renderer.js:202-206`), while `_loadPage()` rejects for failed navigation (`src/renderer.js:75`, `src/renderer.js:96-101`). Their catch paths only reject (`src/renderer.js:184-197`, `src/renderer.js:217-225`); `CDP.Close` occurs only on success at `src/renderer.js:191,221`. The public routes expose both methods without authentication (`src/main.js:91-131`). A mock that forces `_loadPage()` to reject after `CDP.New` reaches the catch without invoking `CDP.Close`.

**Impact:** Repeated public requests can consume the shared renderer's tabs and deny rendering to all users. Restarting Chrome recovers the service, so broad, recoverable availability loss is **medium** under the review policy.

**Fix:** Put target creation through rendering in `try`/`finally` and close the target (and disconnect the client if needed) whenever `CDP.New` succeeded.

findings.title: Negative screenshot dimensions can terminate the renderer
findings.body:
A caller can make screenshot requests hang and then terminate the renderer with invalid dimensions. The async executor passed to `new Promise` drops rejected `await`s instead of rejecting the promise returned to the route.

**Evidence:** `captureScreenshot()` uses `new Promise(async ...)` at `src/renderer.js:202`; rejected awaits before its `try` are not caught (`src/renderer.js:203-215`). Negative `width` or `height` survives parsing and the upper-only clamp (`src/renderer.js:212-213`) and is sent to `Emulation.setDeviceMetricsOverride` at `src/renderer.js:214`, which requires non-negative dimensions. Its rejection leaves the outer promise pending, so `src/main.js:118` never sends a response. The process-level unhandled-rejection handler increments a counter and kills Chrome then exits after more than five errors (`src/main.js:164-180`). Thus six requests such as `/screenshot/http://example.test?width=-1` can deny service.

**Impact:** An unauthenticated caller can stop the shared renderer. This crosses a trust boundary and disrupts all users until the process is restarted, a recoverable outcome; under the review policy it is **high**.

**Fix:** Do not use async Promise executors: make the method `async` or catch every setup failure and reject. Validate dimensions as finite integers in the protocol range before sending CDP commands.

summary: Reviewed the new `index.js` serializer implementation and its documented serialization paths. Recorded two findings: unsafe RegExp code insertion and `ignoreFunction` input mutation/immutable-object failure. `npm test` passed (61 tests), and `npm run benchmark` completed successfully.

findings.title: Attacker-controlled RegExps inject JavaScript into serialized output
findings.body:
A caller that serializes an attacker-controlled `RegExp` can emit arbitrary JavaScript into the generated value. For example, assigning `re.toString = () => '(()=>{globalThis.pwned=1})()'` makes `serialize({re})` return `{"re":(()=>{globalThis.pwned=1})()}`; evaluating that documented output executes the expression.

**Preconditions:** The application accepts a `RegExp` object across a trust boundary and evaluates, serves, or embeds the returned JavaScript, as the package documents.

**Evidence:** The replacer stores the original `RegExp` at `index.js:79-82`. HTML escaping runs before placeholder expansion at `index.js:171-175`, then the `R` expansion directly inserts the instance's mutable `toString()` result at `index.js:190-192`. The README says the output is literal JavaScript for `.js` files or inline `<script>` elements (`README.md:14-18`) and demonstrates evaluation (`README.md:117-124`).

**Impact:** This crosses the consumer's input-to-code boundary and enables arbitrary JavaScript execution in the process/browser that consumes the serialized value. Per the review policy, cross-boundary execution that persists until the generated output is removed is **high** severity.

**Fix:** Do not emit `RegExp#toString()`. Serialize the regexp's `source` and `flags` as escaped string literals and reconstruct it with `new RegExp(source, flags)`.

findings.title: ignoreFunction mutates inputs and rejects immutable objects
findings.body:
`ignoreFunction` changes the object supplied by the caller and throws for immutable objects, despite being documented as JSON.stringify-like. `serialize({nested: {fn(){}}}, {ignoreFunction: true})` removes `nested.fn`; serializing the same shape with `nested` frozen throws `TypeError: Cannot delete property 'fn'`. It also converts an array function element into an `undefined` hole, producing `[undefined]` rather than JSON.stringify's `[null]`.

**Preconditions:** A caller uses the documented `ignoreFunction` option on an object graph with enumerable function properties.

**Evidence:** Every replacer call invokes `deleteFunctions` when the option is set (`index.js:63-68`). The helper enumerates function-valued properties and deletes them from the original value (`index.js:34-42`); strict mode is enabled at `index.js:7`, so deletion of a non-configurable property throws. The resulting array holes use the undefined placeholder (`index.js:101-103`) and are emitted as `undefined` (`index.js:202-204`). The README promises to treat functions as JSON.stringify does (`README.md:108-115`).

**Impact:** Serialization can remove callbacks from application objects shared with later code, or fail to serialize immutable state. This is a contained, recoverable application-integrity and availability failure; the opt-in option discounts it to **low** severity.

**Fix:** Make the replacer return `undefined` for function values without deleting properties. Preserve JSON.stringify array behavior by returning `null` for function array elements, or otherwise delegate that case to JSON.stringify-compatible handling.

summary: Reviewed the added CommonJS entry point and its classifier paths, including package and browser distribution behavior. The change blocks the CVE’s non-function constructor-name payload, but I recorded one info-level runtime compatibility issue. `npm test` passes: 36 tests.

findings.title: Stateful constructor accessors make kindOf throw
findings.body:
`ctorName` evaluates an observable `constructor` property three times. Since `isBuffer` has already evaluated it once, a value with a stateful accessor can make the newly shipped package entry throw instead of returning a type.

**Preconditions:** The caller passes an object whose `constructor` is an accessor (or Proxy trap) that returns different values across reads.

**Evidence:** `kindOf` calls `isBuffer` before `ctorName` (`index.js:16-23`), and `isBuffer` reads `val.constructor` once (`index.js:124-128`). `ctorName` then reads it for the truthiness check, the `typeof` check, and `.name` (`index.js:68-70`). For example, an accessor that returns `undefined` on its first read, a function on reads two and three, and throws on the fourth makes `kindOf(value)` throw. The unfixed helper read the property twice, while the intended fixed form only needs `typeof val.constructor === 'function' ? val.constructor.name : null`.

**Impact:** A crafted value can terminate a type-checking operation for one call. This is a contained, transient failure, so the severity is info.

**Fix:** Remove the separate truthiness read and test the constructor with `typeof` before reading its name.

summary: Reviewed all 566 added lines in `lib/main.js` and traced deploy, update, watch, Docker, delete, and invoke paths. I recorded three findings: one high-severity command-execution issue and two low-severity deployment compatibility/path-resolution regressions. The FunctionName validation blocks the original direct name-injection path, but the change is not ready to merge because the remaining high-severity deploy-path issue is reachable.

findings.title: Deployment package manifests can execute commands on the deployer
findings.body:
A function project's `package.json` can run shell commands on the machine that deploys it. The deploy command reads `files` from the configured code directory, joins entries without quoting, and puts the result in a string executed by `child_process.exec`.

**Preconditions:** The deployment project contains a `package.json` with a malicious `files` entry, such as `"index.js; touch /tmp/owned #"`.

**Evidence:** `deploy` changes into the configured project directory and reads its `package.json` at `lib/main.js:173-182`. It joins `files` with literal spaces at `lib/main.js:184`, concatenates that value into `$zipCmd` at `lib/main.js:190`, and sends the string to shell-backed `exec` at `lib/main.js:192`. This produces `zip ... index.js; touch /tmp/owned #`; the shell runs `touch`. The CLI exposes this path through `lambda deploy <file>` at `bin/lambda:9-15`, and the README documents deploying an arbitrary function config at `README.md:93-104`.

**Impact:** A project contributor can execute commands in the deployer's context. That process commonly has the AWS credentials resolved from environment variables by this tool (`lib/main.js:126-147`), so commands can read or export deployment credentials. This crosses from project metadata to the deploy host and can permanently disclose its credentials; severity is **high** under the reach/persistence policy. The command was reproduced with an isolated project and local AWS/ZIP stubs.

**Fix:** Do not build a shell command from manifest entries. Invoke `zip` with an argument array (for example, `execFile` or `spawn`) and pass each `files` entry as one argument; also reject non-string entries.

findings.title: Absolute config paths resolve relative code directories under the wrong root
findings.body:
Deploying a documented absolute config path with a relative `PATH` resolves the source directory below the invocation directory instead of beside the config. For example, `/tmp/function.lambda` with `PATH: ./code` should package `/tmp/code`, but from the repository root this code resolves `<cwd>/tmp/code`.

**Evidence:** The README defines `PATH` as relative to the config file (`README.md:22-23`) and documents `lambda deploy /path/to/my-function.lambda` (`README.md:93-104`). After removing the suffix, `deploy` derives `/tmp` as `$configPath` (`lib/main.js:101-103`, `lib/main.js:156`), but the relative branch unconditionally prefixes `process.cwd()` (`lib/main.js:159-163`). It then validates and changes into that incorrect directory before archiving (`lib/main.js:168-190`). Thus the usual case exits with “No such directory”; if `<cwd>/tmp/code` exists, it deploys that unintended code instead.

**Impact:** Any user following the documented absolute-path form with a relative code path cannot deploy, or can deploy the wrong directory if the accidental path exists. The error is recoverable by changing the config or invocation path, so severity is **low** under the reach/persistence policy.

**Fix:** Resolve relative `PATH` against `path.dirname(path.resolve(config_file))`, rather than concatenating `process.cwd()` and the textual config path. Use the same helper in `_parse_config_file` and `deploy` so `start` and Docker mounts use the identical path.

findings.title: Valid Lambda ARNs are rejected before deployment
findings.body:
The new function-name check rejects valid Lambda function ARNs before any AWS call. This prevents deployments that identify an existing function by its ARN, even though the subsequent create and update requests accept the configured value as their `FunctionName`.

**Preconditions:** `FunctionName` is a valid full or partial Lambda ARN, for example `arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:123456789012:function:my-function`.

**Evidence:** The validation at `lib/main.js:139-142` permits only a bare name and optional qualifier, so the colon-delimited ARN fails and the process exits. In contrast, the deployment requests pass the value unchanged to `createFunction` (`lib/main.js:221-240`) and to the existing-function update APIs (`lib/main.js:252-283`). Lambda documents a function name, full ARN, or partial ARN as valid `FunctionName` input for these APIs. The CLI calls this path directly at `bin/lambda:9-15`.

**Impact:** Deployments configured with a valid ARN fail locally instead of updating the selected function. This needs a non-default identifier format and is recoverable by changing the configuration to a bare name, so severity is **low** under the reach/persistence policy.

**Fix:** Validate against Lambda's documented `FunctionName` grammar, including full and partial ARNs, or leave identifier validation to the Lambda API while retaining the shell-safe archive invocation.

summary: Reviewed the added `index.js` implementation and its classification paths. I recorded one low-severity finding (`fnd_t7hi8ooxue3j3tfw`) and found no other confirmed PR-specific regressions. `npm test` passes: 36 tests passing.

findings.title: Objects with data constructors are reported as native collections
findings.body:
An ordinary object with an own, non-function `constructor` is treated as though it were a native object constructor. For example, `kindOf(JSON.parse('{"constructor":{"name":"Map"}}'))` returns `"map"`, although the input is an ordinary object. A `name` getter can also throw and prevent classification entirely.

**Evidence:** `kindOf` uses `ctorName` to select native collection and typed-array labels at `index.js:23-46`. `ctorName` only tests that `val.constructor` is truthy before reading `.name` at `index.js:68-70`. On the PR head, the JSON example above returns `"map"`; an object whose constructor has a throwing `name` getter throws before the `[object Object]` fallback at `index.js:53-65`. The package documents ordinary object support (`README.md:57-64`).

**Impact:** A caller that dispatches deserialized values by this API can take its Map/Promise/typed-array path for attacker-controlled plain data, or fail the request with a throwing accessor. This is a contained, recoverable incorrect type decision, so the severity is low under the review policy.

**Fix:** Only use a constructor name when `typeof val.constructor === 'function'`; otherwise return `null` and continue to the normal tag fallback.

summary:
Reviewed the full `index.js` addition and recorded one high-severity finding: attacker-controlled regular expressions can break out of inline scripts because `RegExp.source` is inserted without JavaScript or HTML escaping.

The implementation differs from upstream `serialize-javascript` 2.1.1 only at that escaping step. `npm test` also fails seven existing regexp/map/set assertions; the relevant round-trip failure is that escaped regexp backslashes are lost.

findings.title: Attacker-controlled RegExps can inject scripts into serialized output
findings.body:
The default-safe serializer still lets an attacker-controlled `RegExp` terminate an inline script and execute a second one. This leaves the CVE-2019-16769 path exploitable for applications that compile user input to a `RegExp` and embed the documented serializer output in a page.

**Preconditions:** The application serializes an attacker-influenced regular expression into an inline `<script>`, a documented use at `README.md:14-18` and `README.md:60-74`.

**Evidence:** RegExps are replaced by placeholders at `index.js:79-82`; the generic unsafe-character pass completes at `index.js:171-175`; then `index.js:190-192` inserts `.source` between quotes without escaping. For example, `serialize({re: /[</script><script>globalThis.pwned=1//]/})` emits a raw `</script><script>` sequence. The browser closes the host script and executes `globalThis.pwned=1`; `//` comments out the remaining generated text. The same defect also breaks ordinary patterns: `serialize(/\..*/)` emits `new RegExp("\..*", "")`, which evaluates to `/..*/` instead of the original `/\..*/`.

**Impact:** This crosses the trust boundary from an attacker-controlled pattern to JavaScript executing in every viewer's page. Under the review severity policy, that is high.

**Fix:** Serialize the source as a JavaScript string during placeholder expansion, as in `new RegExp(" + serialize(regexps[valueIndex].source) + ", ...)`, so it receives quote, backslash, and HTML-character escaping. Add the dangerous-regexp and escaped-backslash round-trip cases.

summary: The change restores the static server and adds lexical checks for direct `..` traversal. I recorded five findings, including a remaining symlink-based webroot escape and remotely triggerable server crashes. I also marked the pre-existing literal-parent traversal finding fixed because the new checks block its reproduction.

findings.title: Requests through in-root symlinks disclose files outside webroot
findings.body:
An HTTP request for a file beneath an in-root symlink is served from the symlink target, even when that target is outside `webroot`. Thus a webroot containing (for example) `out -> /etc` lets a remote caller read `/out/passwd` if it is readable by the server account.

**Preconditions:** A symlink under the served root targets an outside path. The server process can read the requested target.

**Evidence:** `express.static(webroot)` runs before the catch-all at `simplehttpserver/simplehttpserver.js:44`, so it serves regular files below the symlink without executing the later lexical checks. Those checks only use `path.join` and `path.relative` (`simplehttpserver/simplehttpserver.js:70-78`), and the fallback also uses symlink-following `fs.stat`/`fs.readdir`/`send` operations (`simplehttpserver/simplehttpserver.js:80-97`). For `GET /out/passwd`, the lexical relative path is `out/passwd`, but filesystem resolution reaches `/etc/passwd`.

**Impact:** Remote callers cross the configured webroot boundary and can disclose any filesystem file readable by the server account. Under the review policy this is medium: disclosure crosses a trust boundary and persists while the symlink remains, discounted because a local/webroot-writing actor must first create the symlink.

**Fix:** Resolve the configured root and every requested target to real paths before serving, and reject targets outside the resolved root; apply the invariant to both static serving and the directory fallback.

findings.title: Dot-prefixed indexed directories can terminate the server
findings.body:
A request for an existing dot-prefixed directory with an `index.html` terminates the process. Static middleware declines dot paths, which makes the fallback execute, but its `send` call passes the response instead of the required request object. `send` later reads `req.headers.range` from that response and throws.

**Preconditions:** The served root contains a dot-prefixed directory with `index.html`.

**Evidence:** Static serving is registered before the fallback (`simplehttpserver/simplehttpserver.js:44`). The fallback finds the directory and index at `simplehttpserver/simplehttpserver.js:80-87`, then calls `send(res, indexpath)` at `:89`; the declared `send` 0.13.x API requires the request as its first argument (`simplehttpserver/package.json:9`). With `.hidden/index.html` present, `GET /.hidden` makes static middleware fall through for the dot path and the fallback call throws when `send` accesses the missing `res.headers.range`.

**Impact:** Any remote caller can stop the server while such a directory exists. Under the review policy this is low: service availability is broadly affected but recoverable by restart, discounted because the dot-prefixed indexed directory must already exist.

**Fix:** Pass `req` to `send` (or rely on `express.static` after configuring its intended dot-file policy), and handle stream errors rather than allowing them to terminate the process.

findings.title: Unstatable directory entries can terminate the server
findings.body:
Listing a directory that contains an entry which disappears or cannot be statted terminates the process. The error path invokes the queue callback but falls through and dereferences the absent `stat` object.

**Preconditions:** A listed entry is removed between `readdir` and `stat`, is a dangling symlink, or otherwise cannot be statted.

**Evidence:** The fallback passes directory entries from `fs.readdir` to `directoryHTML` (`simplehttpserver/simplehttpserver.js:95-97`). Its worker calls `cb()` when `fs.stat` has no result (`:142-145`) but does not return, then executes `stat.isDirectory()` (`:147`). A root containing `list/dangling -> /no/such/file` causes a normal `GET /list/` to take this path and throw a `TypeError`.

**Impact:** A remote request can stop the server whenever such an entry exists. Under the review policy this is low: the availability loss is recoverable by restart and requires a pre-existing filesystem error state or another local writer.

**Fix:** Return immediately after the error callback (and report or skip the entry); ensure each queue task invokes its callback exactly once.

findings.title: Supported Node 0.10 runtimes return 500 for fallback requests
findings.body:
The advertised Node 0.10 runtime cannot execute the fallback route because it lacks `String.prototype.startsWith`. A normal request for a missing path therefore receives a 500 rather than the expected 404.

**Evidence:** The package declares Node `>= 0.10.0` at `simplehttpserver/package.json:7`. After static middleware falls through (`simplehttpserver/simplehttpserver.js:44`), every non-traversal GET reaches `relative.startsWith(...)` at `:57-75`. Node 0.10.48 has no `String.prototype.startsWith`; `GET /does-not-exist` throws there and Express returns 500.

**Impact:** On a supported runtime, all fallback requests fail. Under the review policy this is low: it broadly affects the service but is transient and limited to the declared legacy runtime.

**Fix:** Use a Node-0.10-compatible prefix check, such as `relative.indexOf('..' + path.sep) === 0`, or raise the supported Node version.

findings.title: A raw GET asterisk request can terminate the server
findings.body:
A raw `GET *` request terminates the process. Node accepts and dispatches this request form, but it bypasses Express's normal response augmentation; after the filesystem lookup fails, the fallback calls `res.sendStatus`, which is absent on that response.

**Evidence:** The wildcard GET route takes its path from `req.url` (`simplehttpserver/simplehttpserver.js:57-58`) and calls `res.sendStatus(404)` when `fs.stat` finds no directory (`:80-82`). With an empty webroot, sending `GET * HTTP/1.1` makes `pathname` equal `*`, reaches that callback, and throws `TypeError: res.sendStatus is not a function`, terminating Node. This needs no filesystem setup or authentication.

**Impact:** Any network client that can send a raw HTTP request can stop the server. Under the review policy this is medium: service availability is broadly affected and recoverable by restart.

**Fix:** Reject non-origin-form request targets before filesystem handling and send errors through a response API that is valid for all accepted Node request forms; add a raw-request regression test for `GET *`.

summary:
Reviewed the new Lambda CLI implementation across deploy, invoke, watch, and Docker startup paths. I recorded two low-severity findings: watch mode terminates on asynchronous ZIP failures, and `invoke` exits successfully when the Lambda handler reports a function-level error. The existing high-severity shell-injection finding already covers the unquoted archive command in this change, so I did not duplicate it.

`npm test` could not run the integration suite because this host uses Node v24 and the repository has no `test/res/new-function-*-v24.lambda` fixture.

findings.title: ZIP failures terminate the watch process
findings.body:
`lambda start` exits when it cannot create an archive, so it cannot redeploy after the user fixes the package. For example, a configured code directory with `package.json` containing `{"files": []}` produces `zip -r -9 <tmpfile>` with no input files.

**Evidence:** `start` creates a watcher intended to redeploy changed code/configuration at `lib/main.js:461-495` and documents that behavior at `README.md:107-113`. Its initial deployment only catches synchronous exceptions at `lib/main.js:478-481`. `deploy` starts `exec` asynchronously at `lib/main.js:185-187`, then throws its error from that callback at `lib/main.js:189-191`; the surrounding `try` has already returned. Thus any ZIP failure (including missing `zip`, unreadable input, or an empty `files` list) is an uncaught exception and terminates the watcher instead of letting a later file change retry deployment.

**Impact:** This affects the one local watch process until the user restarts it after fixing the package. The failure is contained and recoverable, so severity is **low** under the reach/persistence policy.

**Fix:** Do not throw from the asynchronous ZIP callback. Report the error and return so the watcher remains active; propagate asynchronous deployment errors through a callback or promise if callers need to act on them.

findings.title: Handler failures make the invoke command succeed
findings.body:
`lambda invoke` returns success after the invoked Lambda itself fails. Lambda reports a handler failure in a successful `RequestResponse` API response through `data.FunctionError` and an error payload, but this command only checks the SDK-level `err`.

**Evidence:** The CLI exposes this path at `bin/lambda:26-31`. `invoke` requests `InvocationType: 'RequestResponse'` at `lib/main.js:441-446`. Its callback exits nonzero only for `err` at `lib/main.js:448-452`, then prints `data.Payload` and returns normally at `lib/main.js:453-457`; it never checks `data.FunctionError`. Consequently, a handler exception produces a zero command status, and scripts using this command treat a failed invocation as successful.

**Impact:** A local caller or CI job can continue after one function invocation failed. Rerunning after handling the error recovers the affected operation; severity is **low** for this contained, recoverable automation error under the reach/persistence policy.

**Fix:** Check `data.FunctionError` after a successful SDK request and exit nonzero (while still printing the payload/logs) when it is present.

summary:
Reviewed the new checkbox input and its flows through additional sign-up fields. Recorded two findings: the reachable untrusted-placeholder DOM XSS and missing validation feedback for custom checkbox fields.

The fixed branch confirms that normal placeholders should render as escaped text. I did not run tests because the fresh checkout has no installed dependencies.

findings.title: Untrusted checkbox placeholders execute script in the sign-up page
findings.body: A Lock integrator that obtains an additional-signup checkbox placeholder from an untrusted source can inject markup that executes in every visitor's sign-up page. For example, an `onerror` handler in an injected image executes when the browser renders the checkbox. **Preconditions:** The application uses a checkbox in `additionalSignUpFields` and an untrusted actor can control its `placeholder` value. **Evidence:** Options validation accepts any nonempty placeholder string unchanged (`src/connection/database/index.js:94-122`, `src/connection/database/index.js:197-204`). The sign-up pane forwards it to `CustomInput` (`src/engine/classic/sign_up_pane.jsx:38-52`), which forwards checkbox placeholders to this component (`src/field/custom_input.jsx:28-35`). This component inserts it with `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` at line 18. Thus a placeholder such as `` becomes executable DOM rather than label text. **Impact:** This is DOM XSS in the relying application's origin for each affected sign-up visitor. Under the review policy, untrusted configuration crosses a trust boundary and the execution persists until that configuration is corrected, so the severity is medium. **Fix:** Render the normal `placeholder` as a React text child (`{placeholder}`). If formatted labels are required, use a separately named HTML prop and require callers to sanitize it before use.

findings.title: Invalid custom checkboxes block sign-up without an error message
findings.body:
An invalid custom checkbox prevents sign-up but gives the user no error state or validator hint. This affects required-consent and other checkbox fields that use the supported `validator` option.

**Preconditions:** An `additionalSignUpFields` checkbox has a validator and the user submits it with an invalid value.

**Evidence:** Checkbox validators are accepted (`src/connection/database/index.js:144-169`), and every additional field participates in `validateAndSubmit` (`src/connection/database/actions.js:58-64`). A failed validation marks fields visibly invalid rather than calling the sign-up callback (`src/core/actions.js:167-177`). `CustomInput` computes `isValid` for the checkbox but passes neither `invalidHint` nor an error wrapper (`src/field/custom_input.jsx:9-16`, `src/field/custom_input.jsx:28-35`). The new component ignores `isValid` and renders only the input and label (`src/ui/input/checkbox_input.jsx:4-20`), whereas `InputWrap` provides the error class and hint (`src/ui/input/input_wrap.jsx:6-10`, `src/ui/input/input_wrap.jsx:31-45`).

**Impact:** One sign-up attempt is blocked without identifying the invalid checkbox or explaining its requirement. The user can recover by changing the field, so this is contained and recoverable; severity is low under the review policy.

**Fix:** Give checkbox rendering the same invalid-state contract as other custom inputs: pass `invalidHint`, render an error wrapper/message, and expose the invalid state to assistive technology.

error: stopped at the run's time limit before finishing
summary: **This run stopped early at the run's time limit, so its results are partial.**

findings.title: HTTP callers can enumerate directories outside the configured web root
findings.body:
An unauthenticated HTTP client can make the fallback inspect directories outside the configured web root. For example, with web root `/tmp/oz-root` and a sibling `/tmp/oz-outside/secret.txt`, `curl --path-as-is http://127.0.0.1:18991/../oz-outside/` returns 200 and lists `secret.txt`.

**Evidence:** The handler takes the raw request pathname and passes it directly to `path.join(dir, pathname)` without checking containment (`simplehttpserver/simplehttpserver.js:57-60`). `path.join('/tmp/oz-root', '/../oz-outside/')` normalizes to `/tmp/oz-outside`; the subsequent `fs.stat` and `fs.readdir` then build a listing for that external directory (`simplehttpserver/simplehttpserver.js:61-79`).

**Impact:** This crosses the web-root access boundary and lets remote callers enumerate directory names accessible to the server process outside the intended root. The disclosure cannot be recalled, so this is high severity under the reach/persistence policy.

**Fix:** Before any filesystem access, reject parent-path components and verify that the normalized candidate remains below the resolved web root (for example, with `path.relative`).

findings.title: In-root symlinks expose files outside the web root
findings.body:
A webroot entry that is a symlink lets HTTP clients read its target even when the target is outside the configured root. With `webroot/outside -> /tmp/external` and `/tmp/external/secret.txt`, `GET /outside/secret.txt` returned the external file with 200.

**Preconditions:** A symlink in the served tree targets an outside path readable by the server process.

**Evidence:** Static middleware is mounted on the root before the fallback (`simplehttpserver/simplehttpserver.js:40-44`). It follows the symlink while serving lexical child paths; when no index exists, the fallback also follows it through `fs.stat` and `fs.readdir` (`simplehttpserver/simplehttpserver.js:61-79`). The lexical `path.join` path remains under `dir`, but filesystem resolution does not.

**Impact:** Remote callers can read files outside the webroot that the server account can read. This crosses the web-root boundary; severity is medium under the policy after discounting for the pre-existing local symlink.

**Fix:** Resolve requested targets to real paths and reject targets outside the real webroot before both static and fallback handling; do not protect only the fallback.

findings.title: Unstatable directory entries terminate the server
findings.body:
A normal directory-listing request terminates the process when an entry cannot be statted. A root containing `list/dangling -> no-such-target` and no `list/index.html` caused `GET /list/` to return and then exit Node with `TypeError` at `stat.isDirectory()`.

**Preconditions:** A listed directory contains a dangling symlink, an entry removed after `readdir`, or another unstatable entry.

**Evidence:** The fallback reads directory entries (`simplehttpserver/simplehttpserver.js:74-79`). The queue worker calls `cb()` when `fs.stat` yields no `stat` but continues and dereferences `stat.isDirectory()` (`simplehttpserver/simplehttpserver.js:124-135`). The exception is uncaught from the async callback.

**Impact:** Any remote caller can stop the server while such an entry exists. Availability is recoverable by restart and requires the pre-existing filesystem condition, so this is low under the policy.

**Fix:** On `err` or missing `stat`, return immediately after completing the queue item; ensure each item calls `cb` once.

findings.title: Dot-prefixed indexed directories terminate the server
findings.body:
A request to a dot-prefixed directory containing `index.html` terminates the server. Static middleware ignores the dot path and falls through; the fallback then calls `send(res, indexpath)`, but `send` expects the request as argument one. With `.hidden/index.html`, `GET /.hidden` caused an uncaught `TypeError` when `send` accessed `res.headers.range`.

**Preconditions:** The served root contains a dot-prefixed directory with `index.html`.

**Evidence:** Static middleware precedes the fallback (`simplehttpserver/simplehttpserver.js:44,54-58`). The fallback finds an index and passes `res` to `send` (`simplehttpserver/simplehttpserver.js:65-71`); package.json declares `send` 0.13.x, whose first argument is the request. Dot paths reach this branch because the static layer falls through.

**Impact:** A remote caller can terminate the broadly used server while the directory exists. Restart recovers it, and the directory is a pre-existing condition, so this is low under the policy.

**Fix:** Pass `req` to `send` and handle stream errors, or keep dot paths out of this fallback.

summary: Reviewed the new GET implementation and its request, parsing, promise, and packaging paths. I recorded two low-severity correctness findings in `_read.js`; both affect specific valid request/response cases. The change correctly avoids disabling TLS certificate verification, but it needs the recorded fixes before approval.

findings.title: Headerless successful GET responses fail during parsing
findings.body:
A successful GET rejects when the server omits `Content-Type`. Headerless 2xx responses are valid, but the response handler calls `.startsWith` on an undefined header; the caught `TypeError` is then returned as the request error instead of the response body.

**Evidence:** `_read.js:44` accepts 2xx responses, then `_read.js:59` evaluates `res.headers['content-type'].startsWith(...)` without checking the header exists. A local `200 OK` response with body `ok` and no `Content-Type` makes `await _read({url})` reject with `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'startsWith')`. `_write.js:46-50` shows the needed guarded header check.

**Impact:** Any caller fetching a normal headerless success response loses that request result. This is contained to a request and retrying after the server adds a header recovers it, so it is **low** under the review reach/persistence policy.

**Fix:** Treat an absent content type as non-JSON before calling `.startsWith`, then return the decoded body normally.

findings.title: GET data after a URL fragment never reaches the server
findings.body:
GET `data` parameters are silently omitted when the supplied URL contains a fragment. The implementation appends the query string after the complete URL, so the new parameters become part of `#...`, which HTTP never sends to the server.

**Preconditions:** The caller supplies both `options.data` and a URL containing a fragment.

**Evidence:** `_read.js:27-30` appends `?` or `&` directly to `options.url` and reparses it. For `http://host/resource?keep=1#fragment` with `{page: 2}`, this produces `http://host/resource?keep=1#fragment&page=2`; `http.get` at `_read.js:44` sends only `/resource?keep=1`. A local server reproduction confirmed that neither the fragment nor `page=2` reaches the server.

**Impact:** Filters, pagination, or other documented GET query values are lost for that request. This is contained and recoverable by using a fragment-free URL, so it is **low** under the review reach/persistence policy.

**Fix:** Add serialized data to the parsed URL's query/search component, then format it, so it precedes any fragment.

summary:
No findings.

The new checkbox component renders normal `placeholder` values as escaped React text rather than injecting them as HTML, preventing configured checkbox labels from executing markup. The raw `placeholderHTML` path has no supported caller in this revision; signup fields pass only `placeholder` through `SignUpPane` and `CustomInput`. The checkbox state remains consistent with the documented `"true"`/`"false"` string representation. Diff whitespace checks pass.

Reviewed the new serializer and its generated JavaScript paths, including cycles, repeated values, unsafe keys, and the documented `eval` round trip. The key-escaping change correctly preserves dangerous property names without literal HTML delimiters, but the related test expectation was not updated; `npm test` reports 44 passing tests and one failure. I recorded four findings covering the release-blocking test failure and confirmed serialization edge cases.

findings.title: The dangerous-key regression test fails after the escaping fix
findings.body:
`npm test` fails on a clean checkout: the dangerous-key assertion expects two source backslashes before `u003C`, but the serializer now emits one. One is required: JavaScript evaluates `"\\u003C"` to `<`, preserving the original key while keeping a literal `<` out of an HTML `<script>` block. The stale expected string instead decodes to a different key containing the literal characters `\\u003C`.

**Evidence:** `safeKey` now JSON-encodes the key and then replaces `<` with `\\u003C` (`src/index.ts:232-234`). For the input at `test/test.ts:92-94`, it returns `{"\\u003Csvg onload=alert(\\"xss_works\\")\\u003E":"bar"}`, whereas line 94 expects `{"\\\\u003Csvg ... \\u003E":"bar"}`. Running `npm test` yields 44 passing tests and this one failure. `prepublishOnly` runs `npm test` (`package.json:23-24`), so publishing also fails.

**Impact:** The project test suite and release command fail for every maintainer. This is broad but recoverable by correcting the assertion, so the severity is medium under the review policy.

**Fix:** Change `test/test.ts:94` to expect the single-backslash source escapes emitted by `safeKey`, and keep a round-trip assertion for the original property name.

findings.title: Repeated signed zeros deserialize as positive zero
findings.body:
A repeated mixture of signed and unsigned zero does not round-trip. For example, `devalue([-0, 0, -0, 0])` returns `(function(a){return [a,a,a,a]}(0))`; evaluating it produces four positive zeros. The serializer advertises support for `-0`.

**Evidence:** `walk` counts occurrences in a `Map` (`src/index.ts:21`, `src/index.ts:28-33`), whose SameValueZero matching treats `-0` and `0` as one key. Since the combined count exceeds one, `names` aliases every occurrence (`src/index.ts:79-88`) and initializes the shared value with the Map key at `src/index.ts:138-143`, which is `0`. This bypasses the otherwise correct negative-zero branch at `src/index.ts:213-216`.

**Impact:** Any caller serializing this uncommon but valid supported value receives corrupted numeric state. The effect is confined to that serialized value and can be corrected by reserializing after a fix, so the severity is low under the review policy.

**Fix:** Do not assign shared references to primitive values, or distinguish `-0` from `0` in occurrence tracking before creating aliases.

findings.title: Own __proto__ properties do not round-trip
findings.body:
An accepted own enumerable `__proto__` data property is not preserved by the generated expression. With `Object.defineProperty(obj, '__proto__', { value: 1, enumerable: true })`, serialization produces `{__proto__:1}`, which evaluates without an own `__proto__` property. If the object is repeated or cyclic, the generated `a.__proto__=...` invokes the inherited prototype setter instead; a self-reference throws `TypeError: Cyclic __proto__ value`.

**Evidence:** The POJO walk accepts all `Object.keys` keys (`src/index.ts:55-70`). `safeKey` and `safeProp` classify `__proto__` as an identifier (`src/index.ts:232-238`), then direct serialization emits it in an object literal (`src/index.ts:118-127`) and named-object reconstruction assigns it to `{}` (`src/index.ts:180-184`). Both forms trigger JavaScript's special `__proto__` behavior rather than creating the input data property.

**Impact:** A valid input object, including one obtained from JSON with an own `__proto__` key, changes shape or fails to deserialize. This is contained to the serialized state and recoverable after a code fix, so the severity is low under the review policy.

**Fix:** Treat `__proto__` as an unsafe key. Emit a quoted data-property key for direct objects, and use `Object.defineProperty` (or an equivalent own-property definition) when reconstructing named normal objects.

findings.title: Large repeated graphs produce an invalid null parameter
findings.body:
Serializing a graph with 2,266,392 distinct repeated values produces an invalid wrapper function. For example, `devalue(values.concat(values))` where `values` contains that many distinct numbers assigns the last alias the name `null`; the output contains `...,nulk,null){...` and evaluation throws `SyntaxError: Unexpected token 'null'`.

**Evidence:** Every repeated value gets an alias from `getName` (`src/index.ts:79-84`), and those aliases are emitted verbatim as IIFE parameters (`src/index.ts:133-140`, `src/index.ts:190`). `getName` only suffixes names matching `reserved` (`src/index.ts:196-204`), but that expression omits `null`, `true`, and `false` (`src/index.ts:3`). The 2,266,392nd generated name is `null`.

**Impact:** An unusually large but valid input cannot be deserialized. The effect is limited to that one serialization and needs a multi-million-reference graph, so the severity is info under the review policy.

**Fix:** Include literal words and all restricted identifiers in the generated-name exclusion set, or validate each candidate as an identifier permitted in formal parameters before using it.

summary: Reviewed the added GET implementation and its public API path. I recorded three findings: one high-severity TLS validation bypass and two low-severity response-handling failures. The changed file is otherwise clean under `git diff --check`; no repository files were modified during review.

findings.title: HTTPS GET requests accept forged certificates
findings.body:
`tiny.get` disables certificate verification for every HTTPS request. An active network attacker can present a self-signed or otherwise invalid certificate, receive headers and query data sent to the target, and supply the response the application accepts.

**Evidence:** `index.js:5` exposes this function as the public `get` API. `_read.js:33` selects `https.get` for HTTPS URLs, `_read.js:35` sets `rejectUnauthorized` to `false`, and `_read.js:41` passes those options to the client. A self-signed local HTTPS server succeeds through both `_read` and public `tiny.get`; native `https.get` and `origin/pr/fixed` instead fail with `DEPTH_ZERO_SELF_SIGNED_CERT`. The fixing ref removes only this assignment.

**Impact:** This crosses the network trust boundary and can permanently disclose bearer credentials or other sensitive request headers, as well as let the attacker alter consumed responses. Per the review severity policy, that is high.

**Fix:** Do not set `rejectUnauthorized` to `false`; preserve Node's default certificate and hostname verification (or make any exception an explicit, opt-in test-only setting).

findings.title: Headerless successful GET responses fail during parsing
findings.body:
A valid successful HTTP response may omit `Content-Type`, but this GET implementation treats that response as a failure. Applications cannot read the response body even though the server returned 2xx.

**Evidence:** After accepting any 2xx status at `_read.js:45`, the end handler unconditionally calls `.startsWith()` on `res.headers['content-type']` at `_read.js:60`. With a local `200` response that ends with ordinary text and no `Content-Type`, that value is `undefined`; the call throws and `_read.js:68-71` returns the `TypeError` with a null body.

**Impact:** A headerless successful response fails one caller request and can be retried or worked around, so this is low severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** Treat a missing content type as non-JSON, for example by checking that the header exists before testing its media type.

findings.title: Interrupted GET responses leave callers pending
findings.body:
A response that starts successfully but is interrupted never settles the GET operation. Callback callers never receive completion or an error, and Promise callers remain pending.

**Evidence:** For a 2xx response, `_read.js:52-72` installs only `data` and `end` listeners on the response stream; its only error listener is on the request at `_read.js:75`. The callback that resolves or rejects the no-callback Promise is invoked only from these paths (`_read.js:13-20`, `_read.js:56-71`). A local server that sends a `200` response with a larger `Content-Length`, writes a partial body, then destroys the socket emits `ECONNRESET`/`aborted` on the response while neither the callback nor Promise settled.

**Impact:** The loss is contained to the interrupted request, but callers can hang until their own timeout or indefinitely; it is low severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** Attach a response `error`/`aborted` handler that invokes the callback exactly once, alongside the existing request error handling.

summary: Reviewed the new `src/index.ts` serializer across value traversal, generated source, escaping, aliases, and reconstruction paths. I recorded confirmed issues, including executable source injection through forged type tags and several serialization correctness failures; I also folded duplicate findings and closed one stale finding that describes the alternate commit rather than this PR. `npm test` passes with 45 tests.

findings.title: Forged RegExp tags inject JavaScript into serialized output
findings.body:
A caller can pass an object with `Symbol.toStringTag = 'RegExp'` and a custom `toString` method to make the serializer return attacker-controlled JavaScript. For example, `devalue({ [Symbol.toStringTag]: 'RegExp', toString: () => '(()=>{globalThis.pwned=1})()' })` returns that expression; evaluating the documented output executes it.

**Preconditions:** Untrusted data can reach `devalue` and the resulting source is evaluated or embedded in a script, as documented.

**Evidence:** `getType` trusts `Object.prototype.toString.call` at `src/index.ts:220-222`, which honors `Symbol.toStringTag`. Both passes treat the forged object as a `RegExp` and skip the default branch that rejects symbol keys and functions (`src/index.ts:35-44`, `src/index.ts:55-70`). The RegExp serializer then inserts `thing.toString()` directly into the generated program (`src/index.ts:102-104`). The README documents evaluating this output (`README.md:84-87`).

**Impact:** An untrusted input crosses into executable script in the consumer's context. This is **high** under the review policy because it crosses a trust boundary and script execution is not recoverable by a supported action.

**Fix:** Validate native types by unforgeable brand/prototype checks before dispatching, and reject spoofed tagged objects; do not emit a user-overridable `toString()` result as source.

findings.title: Repeated empty collections produce invalid JavaScript
findings.body:
A repeated empty `Set` or `Map` produces source that cannot be parsed. For example, serializing `[set, set]` for `const set = new Set()` emits `(function(a){a.;return [a,a]}(new Set))`; the dangling `a.` raises `SyntaxError` when the documented consumer evaluates the result.

**Evidence:** A second reference makes the collection a named value (`src/index.ts:28-33`, `src/index.ts:79-84`). For named Sets and Maps, the reconstruction path unconditionally appends `${name}.` before joining `add`/`set` calls (`src/index.ts:170-178`). Empty collections have no calls to join, and the malformed statement is included in the IIFE (`src/index.ts:188-190`). The API documents both repeated references and Sets/Maps (`README.md:3-10`).

**Impact:** A normal supported input cannot be deserialized. The failure is contained to that serialized value and is recoverable by changing the input, so this is **low** under the review policy.

**Fix:** Only add a Set/Map mutation statement when the collection has at least one entry.

findings.title: Unsafe object keys are changed during serialization
findings.body:
Object keys containing unsafe characters do not round-trip. For input `{ '<': 42 }`, the serializer emits `{"\\u003C":42}`; evaluating it creates a key containing the six literal characters `\\u003C`, not `<`. Newlines and the other characters handled by `escapeUnsafeChars` fail the same way, including in the shared/cyclic-object path.

**Evidence:** Normal object output applies `safeKey` to every key (`src/index.ts:119`), and shared/cyclic reconstruction uses `safeProp` (`src/index.ts:182-184`). Both helpers call `JSON.stringify(escapeUnsafeChars(key))` (`src/index.ts:232-238`). Escaping first creates a backslash in the key, which `JSON.stringify` escapes again. The existing dangerous-key assertion expects this double-backslash output (`test/test.ts:91-95`) but does not evaluate it.

**Impact:** Supported POJOs lose property names after the documented evaluation step, causing contained incorrect data or failed lookups. This is **low** under the review policy.

**Fix:** JSON-stringify the original key first, then escape unsafe characters in the generated source text, so HTML-sensitive characters remain absent while the JavaScript literal reconstructs the original key.

findings.title: Own __proto__ values mutate reconstructed prototypes
findings.body:
An own enumerable `__proto__` data property is reconstructed as a prototype mutation instead of data. `devalue(JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"polluted":true}}'))` emits `{__proto__:{polluted:true}}`; evaluation yields an object with no own `__proto__` property and with `{ polluted: true }` as its prototype. For a repeated object, the emitted `a.__proto__=...` invokes the inherited legacy setter; a self-reference through that property throws `TypeError: Cyclic __proto__ value`.

**Evidence:** `walk` accepts all enumerable string keys (`src/index.ts:70`). Normal objects are emitted as object literals using `safeKey` (`src/index.ts:119-127`); `safeKey('__proto__')` treats the key as an identifier (`src/index.ts:232-234`). Named objects are initialized as `{}` and populated with assignments via `safeProp` (`src/index.ts:181-184`, `src/index.ts:236-238`), which produces `.__proto__`. JSON input normally creates this as an own enumerable data property.

**Impact:** A supported input loses data and can change the prototype of its reconstructed object; cyclic data cannot be restored. The effect is contained to the returned serialized record and is **low** under the review policy.

**Fix:** Special-case `__proto__` so reconstruction defines an own data property (for example with `Object.defineProperty`), rather than using object-literal or assignment syntax with legacy prototype semantics.

findings.title: Repeated zero values discard negative zero
findings.body:
A repeated mixture of `0` and `-0` loses the negative-zero value. Both `devalue([0, -0])` and `devalue([-0, 0])` produce `(function(a){return [a,a]}(0))`; after evaluation both elements are positive zero (`Object.is(result[1], -0)` is false). Standalone negative zero is correctly serialized as `-0`.

**Evidence:** The counting pass keys values in a `Map` (`src/index.ts:21`, `src/index.ts:28-33`), whose SameValueZero comparison treats `0` and `-0` as one value. That entry is named when its count exceeds one (`src/index.ts:79-84`), and `stringify` substitutes the name for both elements (`src/index.ts:86-93`, `src/index.ts:109-112`). The parameter is initialized from the normalized Map key as `0` (`src/index.ts:138-143`). This bypasses the otherwise correct negative-zero handling at `src/index.ts:214`.

**Impact:** A supported primitive value is changed within the returned record. The effect is contained and recoverable by avoiding the mixed repeated values, so this is **low** under the review policy.

**Fix:** Do not alias primitive values, or use equality that distinguishes `-0` from `0` when collecting aliases.

findings.title: NUL followed by an octal digit serializes as an octal escape
findings.body:
A NUL character followed by an octal digit produces a different string or invalid source. For `devalue('\0' + '1')`, the generated JavaScript string literal is `"\\01"`. In the README's indirect `eval` consumption it is parsed as the legacy octal escape U+0001, yielding a one-character string instead of NUL followed by `"1"`; strict parsing rejects it. The same applies to following digits `1` through `7`.

**Evidence:** The escape table maps NUL to `\\0` (`src/index.ts:14`), and `stringifyString` emits it without considering the following character (`src/index.ts:247-250`, `src/index.ts:266-267`). The README documents evaluating returned source (`README.md:84-88`).

**Impact:** Ordinary strings containing this sequence cannot be faithfully deserialized. The wrong value is limited to the serialized record and is recoverable, so this is **low** under the review policy.

**Fix:** Emit NUL as `\\u0000` when the next character is a decimal digit, or always use that unambiguous form.

summary:
Reviewed PR #2 and recorded one high-severity finding: `fnd_6391q7rvqr8b59ca`.

The new entry point memoizes `path.relative` and invalidates its cache after cwd changes. The cache uses prototype-bearing objects, allowing specially named path inputs to corrupt process-wide object state; the PR should not merge until cache storage uses safe own-key maps.

findings.title: Path arguments can pollute Object.prototype
findings.body:
An attacker who controls path arguments can pollute `Object.prototype`. For example, `relative('__proto__', 'isAdmin')` reaches the assignment at line 39 through the inherited `cache['__proto__']` object and creates `Object.prototype.isAdmin = '../isAdmin'`. Later code in the same process can then treat an ordinary object as privileged through a truthy inherited `isAdmin` property. The shim exposes the same behavior through global `path.relative`.

**Preconditions:** The consuming application passes attacker-controlled path strings to this package (or its shim).

**Evidence:** `cache` is a prototype-bearing object at `lib/index.js:13`. With `from === '__proto__'`, the cache lookup at `lib/index.js:34` resolves to `Object.prototype`; line 38 does not replace that truthy inherited value, and line 39 writes the result to it. In a fresh Node process, `require('./lib')('__proto__', 'isAdmin')` makes `({}).isAdmin` equal `'../isAdmin'`. The result is also retained after the cwd cache reset at `lib/index.js:28-31` because that reset does not undo the prototype write.

**Impact:** This crosses the boundary from supplied path data to process-wide object state. A caller can add arbitrary truthy property names to every normal object until restart, which can alter authorization or application control flow. Under the review severity policy, cross-boundary, recoverable process-wide state corruption is **high**.

**Fix:** Store both cache levels in null-prototype maps (and use a null-prototype map when invalidating on cwd changes), or otherwise use own-property-safe storage. This must ensure `__proto__`, `constructor`, and `toString` are always data keys rather than inherited properties.

summary:
Reviewed PR #1 and recorded one medium-severity finding: `fnd_pg3d76rbcq31p3pg`.

The change adds the cached `path.relative` implementation and uses a null-prototype initial cache. Direct runtime checks confirmed normal parsing and reproduced the remaining CWD-dependent cache flaw. The repository has no installed `tape` dependency, so the bundled test suite was not run.

findings.title: A CWD change restores prototype pollution
findings.body:
After a working-directory change, untrusted path arguments can again write arbitrary keys to `Object.prototype`, so the CVE fix is bypassed in applications that call `process.chdir()`.

**Preconditions:** The process changes its CWD after this module loads and passes attacker-controlled `from` and `to` values to this API.

**Evidence:** `cache` initially has no prototype (`lib/index.js:13`), but the CWD-invalidation branch replaces it with `{}` (`lib/index.js:28-31`). A subsequent `cachedPathRelative('__proto__', 'ozbenchPolluted')` makes `cache[from]` resolve to `Object.prototype`; lines 38-39 then assign the native relative-path string to `Object.prototype.ozbenchPolluted`. Reproduction confirmed that `({}).ozbenchPolluted` becomes `../ozbenchPolluted` after `process.chdir()`.

**Impact:** A caller who can supply these path arguments across the application's trust boundary can alter the prototype inherited by all ordinary objects. This is recoverable in-memory prototype pollution. The required, non-default CWD change discounts the impact one tier to medium under the review policy.

**Fix:** Preserve the null-prototype invariant whenever the cache is reset: replace `cache = {}` with `cache = Object.create(null)`. Consider using null-prototype objects for per-`from` buckets as well.

summary:
Reviewed the new `index.js` implementation across parsing, verification, and stream APIs. I recorded four findings, including a strict-mode regex denial of service, and verified each with focused reproductions.

`npm test` does not pass: strict-mode expectations fail in `test/integrity.js` and `test/stringify.js` because short test digests are now rejected. Overall, the PR needs fixes before merge.

findings.title: Strict integrity parsing permits exponential regex backtracking
findings.body:
A strict parse of a valid digest followed by question marks and one non-VCHAR byte blocks the event loop exponentially. For example, `sha256-LXEWQrcmsEQBYnyp+6wy9chTD7GQPMTbAiWHF5IaSIE=` plus 28 `?` characters and `\x7f` takes about 1.8 seconds to reject; 24, 26, and 28 question marks took 115 ms, 460 ms, and 1.84 s respectively.

**Preconditions:** The application parses attacker-controlled integrity metadata with the documented, recommended `strict` option.

**Evidence:** `Hash` applies `STRICT_SRI_REGEX` when strict is enabled (`index.js:17-25`). In `index.js:12`, the outer `*` repeats a group beginning with `?`, while the inner `*` also accepts `?` through its `[\x21-\x7E]` VCHAR class. A failing final byte makes the regex try every partition of the run. Exported `parse()` sends each input token to this constructor (`index.js:123-151`); verification APIs also parse caller-supplied SRI (`index.js:215-231`, `index.js:243-249`).

**Impact:** An attacker who supplies integrity metadata can synchronously consume CPU and stall the Node.js process. This crosses the metadata trust boundary, but requires the optional strict mode, so the severity is **medium** under the review reach/persistence policy.

**Fix:** Parse options without overlapping repetitions, or make the repeated option body exclude the `?` delimiter and validate its contents separately. Ensure a rejected suffix has linear-time handling.

findings.title: Malformed strict SRI values make checkData throw
findings.body:
Malformed metadata is retained in strict mode and then makes `checkData` throw instead of return `false`. Both `sha256-A=` followed by 42 `A` characters (padding in the middle) and a valid SHA-256 digest followed by a bare `?` parse under `{strict: true}`. `checkData('x', sri, {strict: true})` then throws `Error: No algorithms available for ""`.

**Evidence:** The strict regex accepts `=` at every digest position and permits an empty option (`index.js:12`). The constructor stores those matches without further validation (`index.js:22-33`). Strict serialization rejects them because Base64 padding must be terminal and an option must contain at least one VCHAR (`index.js:41-60`). `checkData` treats the initial parse as nonempty (`index.js:215-220`), but `match` reparses it; the strict serialization is empty, so `pickAlgorithm` throws (`index.js:96-116`, `index.js:221-222`). This conflicts with strict parsing's promise to discard invalid components and `checkData`'s documented false-on-failure behavior (`README.md:104-110`, `README.md:379-386`).

**Impact:** A malformed SRI string can turn a normal verification failure into an uncaught synchronous exception in callers using strict mode. The affected operation is recoverable and strict mode is optional, so the severity is **low** under the review reach/persistence policy.

**Fix:** Make strict parsing use the same Base64 and nonempty-option rules as strict serialization, so invalid entries are discarded before verification.

findings.title: Single-mode stream verification throws for valid metadata
findings.body:
Passing the documented `single` option together with valid integrity metadata makes stream verification throw before it returns a stream or Promise. For example, `checkStream(Readable.from([data]), fromData(data), {single: true})` fails with `TypeError: sri.pickAlgorithm is not a function`.

**Evidence:** `parse` returns a `Hash`, rather than an `Integrity`, when `opts.single` is set (`index.js:137-142`). `integrityStream` passes those options while parsing `opts.integrity`, then unconditionally invokes the `Integrity`-only `pickAlgorithm` method (`index.js:247-250`; the method exists only at `index.js:109-120`). `checkStream` forwards caller options and constructs this stream before creating its Promise (`index.js:225-232`). The API documents both `opts.single` and `opts.integrity` for `integrityStream` (`README.md:448-465`).

**Impact:** A supported stream-verification configuration rejects valid data synchronously rather than verifying it. This is a contained, recoverable API failure, so severity is **low** under the review reach/persistence policy.

**Fix:** Always parse verification metadata as an `Integrity` (for example, omit `single` from the parse options); apply `single` only to the generated output.

findings.title: Empty integrity metadata makes checkStream accept unverified data
findings.body:
`checkStream` accepts empty integrity metadata and resolves `undefined` after consuming arbitrary bytes instead of rejecting the failed verification. For example, `checkStream(Readable.from(['untrusted']), '').then(console.log)` prints `undefined`.

**Evidence:** `checkStream` passes its `sri` argument as `opts.integrity` without validating it (`index.js:225-231`). An empty string is falsy, so `integrityStream` does not parse or select verification metadata (`index.js:247-250`), and its mismatch branch is skipped because it also tests `opts.integrity` for truthiness (`index.js:270-285`). No `verified` event fires, leaving the wrapper's result undefined (`index.js:236-240`). In contrast, `checkData` explicitly returns false for empty parsed metadata (`index.js:215-220`), and its test covers that behavior (`test/check.js:72-75`).

**Impact:** A caller that treats successful Promise resolution as verified content can accept an arbitrary stream when a required integrity value is missing or empty. This requires the caller to pass an empty value rather than reject it and is recoverable, so severity is **low** under the review reach/persistence policy.

**Fix:** Have `checkStream` reject when parsing produces no integrity entries, before creating the transform; retain no-integrity generation mode only for direct `integrityStream` callers.

summary:
Reviewed PR #1 and recorded two findings:

- **High:** The published `dist/js` bundle still injects untrusted tooltip HTML without sanitization, so the CVE fix does not reach normal package consumers.
- **Medium:** `js/src/tooltip.js` imports a missing `./tools/sanitizer` module, causing standard JavaScript builds to fail.

The added source matches Bootstrap’s intended sanitizer backport, including default sanitization and protected data attributes. However, the required sanitizer source and regenerated distribution artifacts are both absent. I confirmed `npm run js-compile-standalone` fails on the unresolved import.

findings.title: Tooltip's missing sanitizer module stops JavaScript builds
findings.body:
The normal JavaScript build now fails because the new Tooltip source imports a module that this change does not add. `npm run js-compile-standalone` terminates with `Could not resolve './tools/sanitizer' from js/src/tooltip.js`, so no updated bundle can be produced.

**Evidence:** `js/src/tooltip.js:8-11` imports `./tools/sanitizer`, but there is no `js/src/tools/sanitizer.js` (or equivalent resolution target). The normal Rollup entry imports Tooltip through `js/src/index.js:12` and uses that entry at `build/rollup.config.js:38`; the standard compile script is `package.json:48`. The new symbols are required for both defaults and rendering at `js/src/tooltip.js:72-74` and `js/src/tooltip.js:446-451`.

**Impact:** Every normal source build fails before it emits the package bundle. This is broad but recoverable by a source correction, so severity is **medium** under the review policy.

**Fix:** Add Bootstrap's sanitizer module at `js/src/tools/sanitizer.js` (or correct the import to an included equivalent), then regenerate and test the JavaScript artifacts.

findings.title: Published bundle still injects untrusted tooltip HTML
findings.body: The package still publishes the pre-fix Tooltip implementation, so applications that consume the normal bundle remain vulnerable when they render untrusted tooltip HTML. For example, an application using `$('#trigger').tooltip({ html: true, title: '' })` passes that string to the shipped jQuery `.html()` sink when the tooltip is shown. **Preconditions:** An application renders attacker-controlled tooltip or Popover text with the documented `html: true` option. **Evidence:** The package entry is `dist/js/bootstrap` (`package.json:90`), but this change modifies only `js/src/tooltip.js`. The published bundle's Tooltip forwards the title into `setElementContent` at `dist/js/bootstrap.js:2969-2972`, then uses `$element[html ? 'html' : 'text'](content)` without sanitization at `dist/js/bootstrap.js:2975-2989`. The separate published Tooltip artifact has the same sink at `js/dist/tooltip.js:428-442`. In contrast, the added source intends to sanitize HTML at `js/src/tooltip.js:446-451`, but it is neither reflected in these artifacts nor currently buildable because its import is unresolved. **Impact:** An attacker who can supply tooltip content can execute script in a viewer's origin. This crosses the application's trust boundary; severity is **high** under the review policy. **Fix:** Include the sanitizer dependency, rebuild all published Tooltip/Popover and main bundle artifacts from the fixed source, and commit those generated outputs so the package entry uses the sanitizer by default.

summary:
Reviewed the full added `index.js` surface and traced its parsing, verification, stream, and generation paths. The strict parser’s ReDoS is confirmed, but an identical open finding already exists for this repository and line (`fnd_x1erxqjgyfk5ih86`), so I did not create a duplicate.

`npm test` passes: lint and all six test files succeed. I also checked the fixed branch; its strict-regex change removes the unbounded ambiguous parsing behavior.
