No findings recorded.

The PR restores the Text Encoding Brute Force operation and applies the upstream CVE-2019-15532 fix by HTML-escaping each input-derived value before inserting it into the HTML result table at `src/core/operations/TextEncodingBruteForce.mjs:81`. This prevents the output renderer’s `innerHTML` path from parsing supplied text as markup. I also checked the encoding and presentation paths; the remaining malformed closing table tag is cosmetic in the current renderer and does not create a concrete security or functional failure. The test suite could not run because dependencies are not installed (`grunt: not found`).

Reviewed the full added MooTools extension and its runtime consumers. I recorded four findings: two stored XSS paths exposed by restoring the extension, plus two low-severity plain-editor/preferences behavior failures.

The file restores required Haddock functionality, but it also enables unsafe existing consumers and contains unsafe text-to-HTML conversion. I found no duplicate findings for this repository.

findings.title: Plain editor renders page headings as executable HTML
findings.body: A page heading is treated as HTML when the plain editor builds its section menu. An attacker can save `!` in page source; when another user opens that page in the plain editor, the image is inserted into the menu and its handler runs in the victim's JSPWiki origin. **Preconditions:** The victim can open the crafted page in the default plain editor. **Evidence:** `jspwikiSectionParser` extracts a heading title and only removes wiki syntax; it never HTML-escapes it (`jspwiki-war/src/main/scripts/wiki-edit/Wiki.Edit.js:263-274`). `Snipe.Sections.menu` passes that title as Slick's `html` property and adopts the result (`jspwiki-war/src/main/scripts/wiki-edit/Snipe.Sections.js:140-161`), which reaches `innerHTML`. Before this PR, the missing `ifClass` makes the earlier `body` behavior fail, so the editor behavior never initializes. This file supplies `ifClass` at `jspwiki-war/src/main/scripts/moo-extend/Element.Extend.js:47-53`, making the sink reachable. **Impact:** A contributor who can supply page text can execute script in a plain-editor user's authenticated session. This is stored cross-user XSS; user interaction (opening the editor) discounts it to medium under the review policy. **Fix:** Escape the final parsed heading title before storing it in the section data (as upstream's `escapeHtml()` remediation does), rather than passing source text to an HTML sink.

findings.title: Caps blocks reparse escaped page text as executable HTML
findings.body: The new text mapper turns escaped page text back into markup in the existing `.caps` behavior. A page author can put an event-bearing tag inside a `%%caps ... %%` block; with raw HTML disabled, the server safely emits it as a text node, but this method reparses the lower-cased text as HTML and inserts an executable element on every page view. **Evidence:** Raw page text is escaped when HTML is disabled (`jspwiki-main/src/main/java/org/apache/wiki/parser/JSPWikiMarkupParser.java:527-537`), and class markup creates an element with the author-chosen class (`jspwiki-main/src/main/java/org/apache/wiki/parser/JSPWikiMarkupParser.java:2154-2171`). The existing `.caps` behavior calls `mapTextNodes(s => s.toLowerCase())` (`jspwiki-war/src/main/scripts/wiki/Wiki.Behaviors.js:214-218`). The added method detects any `<`, assigns the callback result to `innerHTML`, then replaces the safe text node with that fragment (`jspwiki-war/src/main/scripts/moo-extend/Element.Extend.js:525-537`). Lowercasing preserves ``. **Impact:** A page author can cause stored script execution for every viewer of that page, crossing the content-author/viewer trust boundary. Rendering the crafted page is required, so this is medium under the review policy. **Fix:** Do not infer HTML from a callback result. Keep callback output as text for transformations such as `.caps`, or require callers that intentionally emit markup to construct DOM nodes from trusted, escaped pieces.

findings.title: The local-draft Delete button leaves the saved draft intact
findings.body:
The plain editor's local-draft dialog labels its danger button “Delete,” but clicking it only closes the dialog. The saved draft remains in `localStorage` and the same prompt appears again after reload, so a user cannot discard a stale draft without leaving the editor through another action.

**Evidence:** The editor opens `.localstorage` with a callback that only restores the cached value (`jspwiki-war/src/main/scripts/wiki-edit/Wiki.Edit.js:95-103`), while the template supplies Restore as `.btn-success` and Delete as `.btn-danger` (`jspwiki-war/src/main/webapp/templates/default/editors/plain.jsp:95-100`). `openModal` invokes its callback only for `.btn-success`; the danger button only removes modal classes (`jspwiki-war/src/main/scripts/moo-extend/Element.Extend.js:289-295`). No delete handler removes the cache in this path.

**Impact:** A user who selects Delete cannot remove a locally saved edit from the recovery prompt. The draft persists until the user saves, switches editors, or abandons the edit through a separate form action, making this a contained, recoverable low-severity data-control failure.

**Fix:** Give the dialog a distinct delete callback that calls `localStorage.removeItem(LocalCache)` (and closes the modal), rather than treating all non-success buttons as Cancel.

findings.title: Radio preference changes do not trigger the unsaved-changes warning
findings.body:
Changing either radio preference is never considered an unsaved change. The warning compares every radio's immutable `value` with this method's immutable `defaultValue`, not the selected state, so navigating away loses a changed Layout or Orientation choice without warning.

**Evidence:** The added method returns `defaultValue` for radios (`jspwiki-war/src/main/scripts/moo-extend/Element.Extend.js:406-411`). The preferences form has `fluid`/`fixed` and `fav-left`/`fav-right` radio pairs (`jspwiki-war/src/main/webapp/templates/default/PreferencesTab.jsp:167-189`). On unload, `Prefs.js` uses `el.value` for every non-checkbox and compares it with `getDefaultValue()` (`jspwiki-war/src/main/scripts/wiki/Prefs.js:43-45,59-68`). Selecting the other radio changes `checked` but neither value, so neither pair can make the form dirty.

**Impact:** One user's unsaved preference change can be silently lost on navigation. It is contained and recoverable by changing and saving it again, so low severity.

**Fix:** Compare radio groups by their initially checked and currently checked member, or have `getDefaultValue()` return `defaultChecked` for radios and make the caller use `checked` for them.

summary:
Recorded two findings:

- **Medium:** The new constructor allowlist makes an existing `new Array(2)` test fail.
- **Low:** Quoted and numeric object keys evaluate under `"undefined"` instead of their source keys.

The change adds the upstream security-hardened evaluator, but omits its matching test updates and a later upstream literal-key correction. I also attempted `npm test`; lint and build completed, but the old `esm` dependency crashes under the available Node 24 runtime before Mocha runs.

findings.title: The security allowlist leaves the existing test suite failing
findings.body:
The full test suite cannot pass after this change. `new Array(2)` resolves `Array` as a built-in, but this handler returns `null` because `Array` is deliberately absent from `callAllowed`; the existing test still expects an array.

**Evidence:** `src/get-static-value.js:55-98` allowlists `Array.isArray`, not `Array`, and `src/get-static-value.js:362-373` rejects constructors outside that list. `test/get-static-value.js:78` expects `{ value: new Array(2) }`, so its assertion at `test/get-static-value.js:138-141` fails when it receives `null`. The matching upstream security fix changed this exact expectation to `null`.

**Impact:** The normal `npm test` path fails for every contributor and CI run. This is broad but recoverable by correcting the stale assertion, so severity is medium under the review policy.

**Fix:** Update the `new Array(2)` test expectation to `null` (and port the upstream security regression tests); do not re-allow `Array` construction merely to satisfy the obsolete test.

findings.title: Literal object keys evaluate as an undefined property
findings.body:
Quoted and numeric object-literal keys are evaluated as the property name `"undefined"`. Consumers of `getStaticValue` therefore receive a different value from the source expression; for example, `({"x": 1}).x` evaluates to `undefined` rather than `1`.

**Evidence:** For every noncomputed property, the new evaluator takes `propertyNode.key.name` at `src/get-static-value.js:384-387`, then assigns it at `src/get-static-value.js:391`. Espree represents quoted and numeric keys as `Literal` nodes, which have `value` but no `name`, so the assignment creates `object["undefined"]`. `MemberExpression` subsequently reads this malformed object at `src/get-static-value.js:346-359`. The project’s own `getPropertyName` distinguishes literal keys and uses `String(node.key.value)` (`src/get-property-name.js:17-25`); upstream later fixed this exact branch and added literal-key tests.

**Impact:** Any plugin or internal caller that relies on this public static evaluator can misclassify an individual AST expression. The incorrect result is contained and recoverable, so severity is low under the review policy.

**Fix:** Preserve `Identifier.name` for noncomputed identifier keys, but convert noncomputed `Literal` keys from their value (including BigInt spelling) before assigning them. Add quoted and numeric key cases to `test/get-static-value.js`.

summary:
Reviewed the complete new `st.js` implementation and recorded six low-severity findings covering mount isolation, middleware state reuse, autoindex behavior, filtering/cache interaction, and HTTP compression caching.

The CVE-2017-16224 redirect payload is blocked: encoded traversal segments now return `403` before the autoindex redirect path. `npm test` ran most tests successfully but exits nonzero because the old Tap 10 runner crashes under Node 24 while handling child-process exceptions.

findings.title: Adjacent routes are served by a static mount
findings.body:
A mount at `/static` also handles URLs such as `/static-secret`. Thus a route that is outside the configured static prefix can be intercepted and served from the static root instead of reaching the application.

**Evidence:** `getUriPath()` uses only `u.indexOf(this.url) !== 0` to test mount membership, then strips `this.url` unconditionally (`st.js:188-204`). With `url: '/static'`, `/static-secret` becomes `/-secret`; `serve()` joins that with the static root and handles the request if the file exists (`st.js:227-247`). A local server with a `-secret` file returned `200 LEAKED_STATIC_CONTENT` for `GET /static-secret`.

**Impact:** A request to an adjacent application route can receive static-root content and bypass the application's route handling. This is a contained, recoverable routing/content exposure, so severity is low.

**Fix:** Require the mount prefix to end at a path boundary: accept only an exact mount URL or a URL whose next character is `/` (with root handled separately).

findings.title: Chained mounts serve files without validating their own URL prefix
findings.body:
When an earlier passthrough mount calls `next()`, it leaves its mount-relative `req.sturl` on the request. A later mount trusts that value rather than validating the original URL against its own prefix, so it can serve a file for a URL outside its mount.

**Preconditions:** Two `st` middleware mounts are chained and the first uses `passthrough: true`.

**Evidence:** `serve()` only parses the URL when `req.sturl` is falsey (`st.js:227-230`), while the ENOENT passthrough branch calls `next()` without clearing it (`st.js:255-258`). The second mount then joins that stale value with *its* root (`st.js:247`). Reproduction: first mount `/first` was empty; second mount `/second` contained `secret.txt`. `GET /first/secret.txt` returned `200 SECOND-SECRET` from the second root. Re-parsing for `/second` would reject `/first/secret.txt` at `st.js:188-190`.

**Impact:** Chained middleware can expose a second mount's file through an unrelated route. The issue requires this non-default chaining/passthrough setup and affects one request at a time, so severity is low.

**Fix:** Keep the parsed path mount-local (or key it by mount) and always validate `req.url` for each mount before constructing its filesystem path.

findings.title: Empty autoindexed directories leave requests pending
findings.body:
An autoindex request for an empty directory never receives a response. The readdir loader only completes from a per-entry stat callback, but no callback exists when filtering leaves zero entries.

**Evidence:** After filtering, `_loadReaddir()` sets `len = files.length` (`st.js:544-551`) and invokes `next()` only from `files.forEach()`'s stat callback (`st.js:552-560`). `next()` is the sole success path to `cb(null, data)` (`st.js:563-565`). A local `GET /` against an empty default-mounted directory received no response after 750 ms. The same holds for a directory containing only dotfiles with the default `dot: false`.

**Impact:** Requests to such an otherwise ordinary autoindexed directory remain pending, and later readers of the same in-flight cache key also wait. This is contained availability loss, so severity is low.

**Fix:** Call `cb(null, data)` immediately when the filtered entry count is zero.

findings.title: Autoindex redirects discard the mount prefix
findings.body:
The slash-adding redirect for an autoindexed directory drops the configured mount prefix. Clients following it leave the mount and usually receive the application's fallback response.

**Evidence:** `getUriPath()` strips `this.url`, leaving `req.sturl` mount-relative (`st.js:188-204`). For a directory without a trailing slash, `autoindex()` writes that relative value directly to `Location` (`st.js:351-356`). With `url: '/test'` and an existing `dir/`, `GET /test/dir` returned `301 Location: /dir/`; following `/dir/` returned the fallback 404 because it no longer matched `/test` (`st.js:188-190`, `st.js:239-245`).

**Impact:** Every slashless autoindex-directory request on a non-root mount redirects to the wrong URL. The result is recoverable request failure, so severity is low.

**Fix:** Build the redirect from the external mount URL plus the mount-relative path, preserving `/test/dir/` in this example.

findings.title: Filtered responses poison the shared content cache
findings.body:
A response filter is applied before the shared content cache is populated, but cached responses neither apply nor distinguish that filter. Consequently the first filtered request determines the bytes returned to later unfiltered or differently filtered requests for the cache lifetime.

**Preconditions:** The documented `res.filter` integration is used with a request-specific filter.

**Evidence:** `streamFile()` replaces the input with `stream.pipe(res.filter)` (`st.js:407-415`), and that resulting stream feeds both the response and `bufs`, which is stored under a key consisting only of size and ETag (`st.js:437-472`; key at `st.js:370-384`). On a cache hit, `cachedFile()` directly ends the prior bytes and never reads `res.filter` (`st.js:387-404`). In a local reproduction, the first request used an uppercase Transform; later unfiltered and differently filtered requests returned the uppercase bytes with `x-from-cache: true`, and the second filter was never invoked. The API documents attaching `res.filter` before calling the mount (`README.md:263-270`).

**Impact:** Request-specific transformations can leak or corrupt a prior response for up to the default ten-minute content-cache lifetime. The issue needs a non-default, request-specific filter, so severity is low.

**Fix:** Do not place filtered output in the shared source-content cache. Cache unfiltered bytes and apply the current filter after retrieving them, or include a stable filter variant in the cache key.

findings.title: Compressed responses omit the Accept-Encoding cache variance
findings.body:
The handler sends a public cacheable response in either gzip or identity form based on `Accept-Encoding`, but does not declare `Vary: Accept-Encoding`. A compliant shared HTTP cache can therefore reuse a gzip response for a client that did not accept gzip, or reuse identity bytes for a gzip-capable client.

**Evidence:** The default response policy is `public, max-age=600` (`st.js:108-115`) and is set before serving the file (`st.js:303-305`). `getGz()` selects gzip from the request header (`st.js:595-601`), and the response conditionally sets `content-encoding: gzip` (`st.js:387-403`, `st.js:412-442`). None of those header paths sets `Vary`. The test suite itself exercises identity then gzip representations of the same resource (`test/gzip-after-no-gzip.js:13-43`).

**Impact:** Behind a shared proxy cache, one client can prime a representation that is incorrectly reused for other clients for ten minutes. This requires a shared cache outside the handler, so severity is low.

**Fix:** Add `Vary: Accept-Encoding` whenever gzip negotiation is enabled, preserving any Vary values the application already set.

summary:
Reviewed the new static AST evaluator and recorded one high-severity finding: `fnd_dqwrbrlxx9b4k1q2`.

The implementation adds broad expression evaluation but invokes resolved functions and constructors directly, which is unsafe for linted source. I also confirmed the quoted/numeric object-key issue, but it was already recorded as `fnd_6ko2ccuseaihof20`. `npm test` could not complete in this environment because the legacy `esm` loader fails before Mocha runs.

findings.title: Linted source can execute code in the ESLint process
findings.body:
A rule that calls the public `getStaticValue(node, context.getScope())` API can execute JavaScript embedded in the source being linted. For example, parsing `Function("global.__ozbench_static_eval = \\"ran\\"")()` through ESLint and passing its expression statement to the API sets the marker in the ESLint process; `({}).constructor.constructor(...)()` works without resolving the `Function` identifier.

**Evidence:** `Identifier` resolves unshadowed built-ins, including `Function`, to the live Node global at src/get-static-value.js:207-219. `CallExpression` then invokes every resolved function at src/get-static-value.js:165-186; arbitrary member reads at src/get-static-value.js:265-273 expose the constructor-chain variant. The public API only catches errors after evaluation at src/get-static-value.js:411-416. `getStaticValue` is exported at src/index.js:52, and the supported ESLint caller pattern passes `context.getScope()` (test/get-static-value.js:121-136).

**Impact:** This crosses the boundary from code supplied for linting into the linter process. A malicious repository file can read its environment, alter files, or run subprocesses with the privileges of a developer or CI job that uses a rule built on this API. This is **high** severity because arbitrary process code execution can cause permanent secret disclosure or modification.

**Fix:** Never invoke arbitrary resolved values. Restrict calls and constructors to a vetted pure-function allowlist, treat `Object.freeze`/`seal`/`preventExtensions` as non-mutating pass-throughs, and reject getter-backed member reads and arbitrary tagged-template functions.

summary:
Reviewed PR #2 and recorded two findings: a high-severity shared-recipe XSS and a low-severity memory-exhaustion path for large inputs.

The change adds the missing encoding enumeration operation and integrates with existing generated configuration and tests. I did not run the full npm test suite because dependencies are not installed.

findings.title: Shared recipes execute script embedded in encoding results
findings.body:
A shared recipe can execute arbitrary JavaScript in the recipient's CyberChef origin. The app accepts the sender-controlled recipe and Base64 input from the URL fragment and auto-bakes it. In Decode mode, an ASCII payload such as `<script>window.__xss=1</script>` remains unchanged in the UTF-8 result, is inserted unescaped into the HTML table, and `OutputWaiter` explicitly evaluates script elements after assigning the table to `innerHTML`.

**Evidence:** `present()` interpolates `Utils.printable()` output directly into a table cell at `src/core/operations/TextEncodingBruteForce.mjs:82-83`; `printable()` does not escape printable HTML metacharacters (`src/core/Utils.mjs:176-186`). UTF-8 is among the enumerated formats (`src/core/lib/ChrEnc.mjs:12-14`), and the browser sink assigns the result to `innerHTML` then evaluates each script (`src/web/OutputWaiter.mjs:73-80`). A recipient opening `#recipe=Text_Encoding_Brute_Force('Decode')&input=PHNjcmlwdD53aW5kb3cuX194c3M9MTwvc2NyaXB0Pg` executes `window.__xss=1` when auto-bake runs.

**Impact:** This crosses a trust boundary: anyone who can send a shared recipe link can run code as a recipient who opens it. Under the review severity policy, cross-boundary, recoverable script execution is **high**.

**Fix:** HTML-escape both encoding names and rendered values before interpolation (for example, with `Utils.escapeHtml`), or construct table cells as text nodes. Do not rely on `printable()` for HTML encoding.

findings.title: Large inputs exhaust memory while enumerating encodings
findings.body:
Opening or dropping a moderately large file and running Decode makes the operation retain a full decoded copy for every supported encoding before any output-size safeguard runs. For a 20 MiB ASCII file, the 44 conversions retain about 850 MiB of text, followed by a JSON clone and a full rendered HTML table. This can exhaust the worker or browser process. The existing output threshold runs only after these allocations and the raw JSON is still posted back to the main thread.

**Preconditions:** A user runs this operation on a large file or pasted input.

**Evidence:** The operation loops through every `IO_FORMAT` entry and stores each complete result (`src/core/operations/TextEncodingBruteForce.mjs:52-66`); `present()` then processes and concatenates every value (`src/core/operations/TextEncodingBruteForce.mjs:78-87`). File loading has no size cap (`src/web/InputWaiter.mjs:322-329`) and allocates the entire file (`src/web/LoaderWorker.js:26-45`). `Chef` clones the JSON and applies its display threshold only after `recipe.present()` (`src/core/Chef.mjs:92-115`), while the worker posts the unpresented JSON too (`src/core/ChefWorker.js:104-109`).

**Impact:** A supplied or locally selected large input can make one browser tab or worker unavailable until it is terminated or restarted. This is contained and recoverable; under the review severity policy it is **low**.

**Fix:** Impose an input/output byte budget before enumerating charsets, or cap each conversion and avoid retaining/rendering every full result. Apply any display threshold before cloning or serializing the result.

summary:
Reviewed PR #2 and recorded two findings:

- `fnd_sv8ezo4dim37djvq` — high: tar archives can write outside the extraction directory through unfiltered symlinks.
- `fnd_68hxaj4sl6jten2f` — low: standalone `.gz` archives always fail because extraction writes to a directory path.

The change restores archive extraction, but the tar symlink filter uses the ZIP callback shape and never rejects `tar-fs` symlinks. I reproduced the external write with a crafted tar.gz. I also reproduced the plain-gzip failure (`EISDIR`). `eslint lib/util/extract.js` passes; targeted resolver tests had 30 passing, with two legacy stream failures under the current Node runtime.

findings.title: Tar packages can write through unfiltered symlinks
findings.body:
A package archive can create a symlink and then write a later tar member through it outside Bower's temporary extraction directory. `tar-fs` calls `ignore(name, header)`, but this predicate receives only `name` and looks for the ZIP-library value `SymbolicLink`; it therefore never filters tar symlink entries. `tar-fs` creates accepted symlinks and writes subsequent members using the symlinked path.

**Evidence:** `extractTar` and `extractTarGz` install `isSymlink` as `tar-fs`'s `ignore` callback (lib/util/extract.js:62-70, 90-101), while `isSymlink` accepts one argument and checks `SymbolicLink` (lib/util/extract.js:133-135). The installed `tar-fs` invokes `ignore(name, header)` (node_modules/tar-fs/index.js:231-239), creates `header.type === 'symlink'` entries (node_modules/tar-fs/index.js:250-254), and writes regular members to their resolved `name` (node_modules/tar-fs/index.js:273-283). I reproduced this with a tar.gz containing `link -> /tmp/.../escaped` followed by `link/owned.txt`; extraction created `/tmp/.../escaped/owned.txt`. Remote URL resolution reaches this code for recognized archives (lib/core/resolvers/UrlResolver.js:228-249).

**Impact:** A malicious package can write files at arbitrary locations writable by the user running Bower. This crosses the package-to-local-filesystem trust boundary and persists until manually removed, so the severity is high under the review policy.

**Fix:** Make the tar callback accept `(name, header)` and reject `header.type === 'symlink'`. Keep the separate `SymbolicLink` check only for `decompress-zip`.

findings.title: Plain gzip archives always fail extraction
findings.body:
Every supported plain `.gz` archive fails instead of installing its decompressed file. `extract()` creates a temporary directory and passes it to every extractor, but `extractGz()` passes that directory as the file target to `fs-write-stream-atomic`. Its final rename therefore attempts to replace the existing directory with a file and rejects with `EISDIR`.

**Evidence:** The extractor table routes `.gz` and `application/x-gzip` to `extractGz` (lib/util/extract.js:21-33). `extract()` creates `tempDir` with `tmp.dir` and invokes `extractor(src, tempDir)` (lib/util/extract.js:225-246). `extractGz` calls `createWriteStream(dst)` (lib/util/extract.js:119-124); that module writes to a temporary file then renames it to its target (node_modules/fs-write-stream-atomic/index.js:39-46, 87-105). I reproduced a call with an existing destination directory and a valid gzip stream; it rejected with `EISDIR` at that final rename. Both local-file resolution and URL resolution call `extract` with their existing `_tempDir` (lib/core/resolvers/FsResolver.js:105-115; lib/core/resolvers/UrlResolver.js:228-249).

**Impact:** Users cannot install a package distributed as a standalone gzip stream. The failed request is recoverable by using a supported archive format, so this is low severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** Derive an output filename inside the temporary directory (for example, the archive basename without `.gz`) and pass that file path to `createWriteStream`, then let the existing relocation code move it.

summary:
Reviewed the new static-file middleware across URI handling, access checks, indexing, caching, streaming, and descriptor lifecycle. I recorded three findings: two medium-severity access/redirect issues and one low-severity aborted-download resource leak.

I also ran the test suite after installing dependencies. Most tests ran successfully, but `npm test` failed under Node 24 in legacy `tap` handling, including the no-cache and CLI cases; the working tree was left clean.

findings.title: Root-mounted autoindex redirects to attacker-controlled origins
findings.body:
A root-mounted server redirects a request containing a terminal encoded `..` to an attacker-controlled scheme-relative URL. An unauthenticated client can make a victim follow `//attacker.example/%2e%2e`, which receives `Location: //attacker.example/%2e%2e/` and resolves off-origin.

**Preconditions:** The middleware uses its default root mount and directory indexing is enabled (both defaults).

**Evidence:** `getPath()` converts `%2e` to `.` but rejects `..` only when another slash follows it (`st.js:171-184`). Thus `//attacker.example/%2e%2e` normalizes to `/`, passes the root-mount check, and resolves to the served directory (`st.js:189-206`). `serve()` retains the raw request path (`st.js:224-228`), and `autoindex()` appends `/` to that raw value in its redirect (`st.js:348-353`). A raw HTTP request to a local default mount returned `301 Location: //attacker.example/%2e%2e/`; the fixed branch returns 403.

**Impact:** This is a network-reachable, unauthenticated open redirect from a trusted origin. Under the review policy it is **medium**: it crosses the origin trust boundary, but its effect is transient phishing/redirect abuse rather than data access or code execution.

**Fix:** Reject terminal `..` path components after normalizing encoded separators, and build redirect locations from a validated canonical URI rather than the raw request target.

findings.title: Encoded dots bypass the default dotfile access restriction
findings.body:
The default dotfile restriction is applied to the raw URL while file resolution decodes encoded dots first. An unauthenticated request for `/%2ehidden` therefore returns a file named `.hidden` from the served root even though `dot` defaults to `false`.

**Evidence:** `getPath()` turns `%2e` into `.` before joining the result beneath the static root (`st.js:171-175`, `st.js:202-206`). The authorization check instead tests the unchanged `req.sturl` for a literal dot (`st.js:224-228`, `st.js:238-244`), so `/%2ehidden` does not match. A local mount with `dot: false` and a `.hidden` file returned HTTP 200 and its contents for that request. The documented default is to return 403 for dot-file URL parts (`README.md:149-150`), and the fixed branch canonicalizes the URI before this check.

**Impact:** An unauthenticated caller can read dot-prefixed configuration or credential files that the default policy is meant to withhold. Under the review policy this is **medium**: the disclosure crosses the caller's access boundary and cannot be undone once secret content is exposed, but it is limited to dotfiles placed under the configured static root.

**Fix:** Apply the dotfile policy to the same decoded, canonical URI used for filesystem resolution, before opening the file.

findings.title: Aborted uncached downloads retain file descriptors
findings.body:
A client that closes a download before completion leaves its checked-out file descriptor referenced indefinitely. Repeating aborted requests can exhaust the server's descriptor limit and make later opens fail.

**Preconditions:** `cache: false` is enabled (a supported configuration), and the client aborts before a large response completes.

**Evidence:** A served file descriptor is checked out before streaming and is returned only through `end` (`st.js:257-263`). `streamFile()` replaces the source stream's `destroy()` with a no-op (`st.js:404-407`), calls `end` only on source error or source `end` (`st.js:420-424`, `st.js:441-443`), and does not handle response close. With `cache: false`, content caching is disabled by the `none` configuration (`st.js:118-129`), so a client abort leaves the source stream short of `end`. A local test serving a 256 MiB file with `cache: false` and `gzip: false` left five distinct managed descriptors checked out after five requests that closed after the first chunk. The `fd` manager retains a pending descriptor while its reference count remains nonzero (`node_modules/fd/index.js:65-81`).

**Impact:** An unauthenticated client can cause a recoverable availability failure by exhausting file descriptors. Under the review policy this is **low**: the outcome can affect the service broadly, but it requires the documented non-default `cache: false` setting, which discounts the otherwise medium broad/recoverable impact.

**Fix:** On response close or abort, destroy the source stream and call the idempotent `end` function; do not replace normal stream destruction without equivalent cleanup.

summary:
Reviewed PR #1 and recorded three findings: the reserved-key guard remains bypassable, and the new implementation has two memoization correctness defects.

The change adds the `set-value` entry point and attempts to block prototype-pollution path segments. `npm test` passes (26 tests), but the prototype-pollution fix is incomplete, so the PR should not merge as-is.

findings.title: Coercible array segments bypass the prototype-pollution guard
findings.body:
The new guard can be bypassed with an array-form path containing a nested JSON array. For example, `set({}, JSON.parse('[["__proto__"], "isAdmin"]'), true)` leaves the first segment in `keys`: it is an array, so it is not strictly equal to the blocked string. When the loop later uses it as `target[prop]`, JavaScript coerces it to `"__proto__"`, traverses into `Object.prototype`, and writes `isAdmin` there. All ordinary objects created afterward inherit the attacker-controlled value.

**Preconditions:** An application forwards an attacker-controlled array path to this library. Array paths are a supported API (`test.js:112-115`) and the payload is JSON-representable.

**Evidence:** `index.js:28` filters before property-key coercion. `isValidKey` only compares values by strict equality (`index.js:101-103`), while the traversal performs computed property access at `index.js:40` and `index.js:49`. On the reviewed commit, the JSON payload above makes `({}).isAdmin === true`.

**Impact:** This is process-wide prototype pollution. Under the review policy, it is **medium**: it affects all ordinary objects in the process but is recoverable by restart; downstream impact depends on how the host application consumes inherited properties.

**Fix:** Require every parsed or array path segment to be a primitive string before validation, then reject the entire path if any segment is `__proto__`, `constructor`, or `prototype`. Do not coerce segment objects after the reserved-name check.

findings.title: Memo cache can redirect later property assignments
findings.body:
The process-global split cache uses an ambiguous key. A normal call such as `set(obj, 'profile.role', 'first', {merge: true})` caches `['profile', 'role']` under `profile.role;merge=true`. A later call without options, `set(obj, 'profile.role;merge=true', 'second')`, has the same cache ID, so it overwrites `obj.profile.role` instead of setting `obj.profile['role;merge=true']`.

**Evidence:** `split` returns a process-global cached segment array before parsing (`index.js:63-65`, `index.js:84`, `index.js:109`). `createKey` creates the collision by appending unescaped option text to one path (`index.js:88-98`), and `set` uses those cached segments to select the write location (`index.js:28`, `index.js:37-50`). I reproduced the two calls above on the reviewed commit; the result was `{"profile":{"role":"second"}}` rather than a separate `role;merge=true` property.

**Impact:** A prior call can cause a later valid path to modify a different property. Under the review policy this is **low**: it is a recoverable, contained integrity error, although hosts that accept paths from callers can expose it across requests because the cache is module-global.

**Fix:** Use an unambiguous cache key, such as a nested cache keyed separately by the path and options identity/serialized tuple, or disable memoization when options are supplied.

findings.title: Inherited memo names make valid string paths throw
findings.body:
A valid one-segment string path that names an inherited `Object.prototype` member throws instead of setting an own property. For example, `set({}, 'toString', value)` obtains the inherited `Object.prototype.toString` function from `set.memo`, returns it as the parsed key list, then calls its missing `.filter` method.

**Evidence:** `split` treats any truthy inherited `set.memo[id]` member as a cache hit (`index.js:63-65`), and the memo uses a normal object (`index.js:109`). String paths are supported (`index.js:18-20`), but the new filtering call assumes the returned value is an array (`index.js:28`). On the reviewed commit, both `'toString'` and `'hasOwnProperty'` throw `TypeError`; the supported array form `set({}, ['toString'], value)` succeeds (`test.js:112-115`).

**Impact:** Requests that set one of these valid property names fail if the error is not caught. Under the review policy this is **low**: the failure is contained and recoverable.

**Fix:** Store memo entries in a null-prototype object or a `Map`, and only return an own cached array entry.

summary: Implemented `tar-fs` bindings in the new `index.js`. I recorded four findings: two high-severity extraction-root escapes and two low-severity correctness/availability issues. `npm test` fails at the existing absolute-hardlink regression test, confirming the vulnerable behavior remains.

findings.title: Archive hardlinks let later entries overwrite files outside the extraction root
findings.body:
A crafted archive can overwrite a file outside the extraction root. A hardlink entry can name an absolute or `..`-escaping source; a later file entry for that same archive path writes through the hardlink.

**Evidence:** `onlink` resolves the attacker-controlled `header.linkname` with `path.resolve(cwd, ...)` and passes it to `xfs.link` without containment validation (`index.js:261-273`). The destination itself is under `cwd` (`index.js:235-239`). A following file entry opens that destination for writing (`index.js:277-289`), which truncates the shared inode outside the root. This is reproducible with a hardlink to an external file followed by a file entry of the same name; the included regression fixture constructs that sequence at `test/index.js:315-335`.

**Impact:** An archive supplier crosses the extraction-root trust boundary and permanently modifies any linkable file writable by the extraction process. Per the review policy, this is high severity.

**Fix:** Reject hardlink sources that do not resolve inside `cwd` before calling `xfs.link`; build and validate the source path with the same rooted-path invariant as entry destinations.

findings.title: Archive directory entries create paths through prior symlinks outside the extraction root
findings.body:
A crafted archive can create directories outside the extraction root by first creating a symlink and then placing a directory entry beneath it. Directory entries never check that their path components are real directories.

**Evidence:** Symlink extraction creates the attacker-controlled link target without a containment check (`index.js:254-258`). For a later directory entry such as `pivot/created`, the directory branch directly calls `mkdirfix` (`index.js:291-296`), which passes that path to `mkdirp` (`index.js:337-338`). `mkdirp` follows the prior `pivot` symlink. A reproducer with `pivot -> /tmp/outside` and a `pivot/created` directory entry creates `/tmp/outside/created`. The `validate` check that detects a symlinked intermediate path appears only in the non-directory branch (`index.js:298-320`).

**Impact:** An archive supplier crosses the extraction-root trust boundary and persistently creates arbitrary directories wherever the extraction process has permission. Per the review policy, this is high severity.

**Fix:** Apply component validation before handling directory entries, and create paths without following untrusted symlink components.

findings.title: Extraction creates directories with the host filesystem instead of opts.fs
findings.body:
Extraction ignores the supplied filesystem for directory creation. This breaks virtual or policy-enforcing filesystem backends and can create directories in the host filesystem instead.

**Preconditions:** The caller uses the documented `opts.fs` override.

**Evidence:** `extract` stores that override in `xfs` (`index.js:172-176`), and both callers pass it as `fs` to `mkdirfix` (`index.js:291-295`, `index.js:304-306`). `mkdirfix` instead reads the nonexistent `opts.xfs` and gives `undefined` to `mkdirp` (`index.js:337-338`), so `mkdirp` falls back to its native `fs`. A custom `fs.mkdir` that returns an error is never called while extraction still creates the target directory on the host.

**Impact:** A caller that relies on a custom backend for isolation or directory policy can have extraction bypass that backend for parent creation. The issue requires the non-default custom-filesystem option and is low severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** Pass `opts.fs` to `mkdirp` (and ensure related ownership handling uses the same backend where supported).

findings.title: Dereferenced directory symlink cycles expand until packing fails
findings.body:
Packing with `dereference: true` expands directory-symlink cycles until the process emits many duplicate entries and finally fails with `ELOOP`.

**Preconditions:** The caller enables `dereference: true` on a source tree containing a directory symlink to an ancestor.

**Evidence:** Dereferencing switches traversal from `lstat` to `stat` (`index.js:69`). The walker queues every child of each resolved directory with no visited-directory or depth tracking (`index.js:21-45`), so `loop -> .` produces `loop/loop/...`. It emits files from each repeated visit (`index.js:115-120`, `index.js:138-147`) until a path lookup fails and destroys the stream (`index.js:96-97`). A one-megabyte file with `loop -> .` emitted about 40 MiB before `ELOOP` in reproduction.

**Impact:** A source-tree author can cause an opted-in packaging job to consume excess output, memory, and time, then fail. The non-default option and filesystem symlink-depth bound reduce this to low severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** Track visited dereferenced directory identities, or impose and document a traversal limit before reading and queuing children.

summary:
Reviewed the new authentication router and its integration with Passport, user groups, password resets, and initial installation. I recorded four findings: unauthenticated administrator creation, a first-user initialization race, reset-driven login denial, and malformed reset requests that leave connections open.

The working tree remains clean, and `git diff --check` passes. I did not run the test suite because dependencies are not installed.

findings.title: Unauthenticated callers can create all-permissions administrators
findings.body:
An unauthenticated caller can create and log in as an all-permissions administrator through `POST /admin/signup`, even when public registration is disabled. A new email, username, and password are enough; no existing user or special request field is needed.

**Evidence:** The added route exposes `local-signup` without an authorization or installation-state check (`server/apps/routes/auth.js:13-15`). The strategy saves a `User` built from the request body after checking only email uniqueness (`server/utils/passport.js:25-36`). When `usergroup` is omitted, the schema assigns the `admin` group (`server/models/UserSchema.js:39-47`), and startup creates that group with every permission enabled (`server/utils/create-admin-usergroup.js:9-19`). The separate public signup route is gated by `Site.allowPublicRegistration`, which defaults to false (`server/utils/public-registration.js:12-26`, `server/models/SiteSchema.js:22-25`), but this route bypasses that gate.

**Impact:** This crosses the authentication and authorization boundary: an Internet caller can gain administrative control over the CMS and its data. Under the review severity policy, unauthorized privileged access with recoverable persistence is **high**.

**Fix:** Do not expose this signup route independently. Require the same public-registration gate and assign a configured non-admin group, or remove the route and retain only the installation-only first-user flow.

findings.title: Malformed password-reset requests leave connections open
findings.body:
Requests that omit a reset identifier never receive a response. For example, posting `{"password":"x"}` to `/admin/setpassword` leaves `token` undefined and throws at `token.toString()`; the equivalent missing `email` and `t` cases affect the other public reset endpoints.

**Evidence:** `setpassword` validates only `password` before dereferencing `token` (`server/apps/routes/auth.js:50-60`); `/forgotpassword` and `/verify` unconditionally dereference `email` and `req.query.t` (`server/apps/routes/auth.js:78-80`, `server/apps/routes/auth.js:103-105`). These are `async` Express 4.15.5 handlers with no `try/catch` or `next` forwarding (`package-lock.json:5158-5161`), and the application has no error middleware (`server/index.js:29-61`). Express 4 does not handle the rejected handler Promise, so the request stays open instead of reaching a 4xx response.

**Impact:** An unauthenticated caller can retain connections with tiny malformed requests until the server or an intermediary times them out, enabling resource exhaustion. The effect is transient and requires concurrent requests, so the review policy rates this **low**.

**Fix:** Validate each required identifier before coercion and return 400 for absent or invalid values; forward unexpected async errors to Express error handling.

findings.title: Concurrent initial setup creates multiple administrators
findings.body:
Two callers can both become administrators during initial setup. They can submit different valid identities to `/admin/firstuser` while the users collection is empty: both requests can finish the existence check before either performs its save.

**Preconditions:** The instance is in its normal initial state (the startup-created `admin` group exists, but no user has been created yet), and requests overlap.

**Evidence:** The public handler performs `User.findOne()` and then independently saves a new user (`server/apps/routes/auth.js:20-33`), with no transaction or conditional insert. It explicitly assigns each saved user to `admin` (`server/apps/routes/auth.js:30-31`). Only email and username have unique constraints (`server/models/UserSchema.js:12-26`), so distinct identities do not conflict. Startup creates the all-permissions admin group before the server accepts this flow (`server/utils/database.js:50-53`; `server/utils/create-admin-usergroup.js:9-19`).

**Impact:** An unauthenticated caller racing a legitimate installer can obtain administrator access. This crosses the authorization boundary and persists until an administrator removes the account. The review policy starts this at high; the unreproduced timing interleaving discounts it to **medium**.

**Fix:** Make initialization a database-enforced singleton, such as an atomic conditional update/insert on an installation record, and create the first user only when that operation succeeds.

findings.title: Anyone can repeatedly block a user's password login
findings.body:
Any caller who knows a user's email can prevent that user from starting a password login. Each request to `/admin/forgotpassword` replaces the user token; the login strategy rejects every user with a token, while the caller does not need to possess the reset link.

**Evidence:** The public route finds the submitted email and persists a new token (`server/apps/routes/auth.js:78-90`). Local login rejects a user whenever `user.token` is present, before password validation (`server/utils/passport.js:40-45`). The only normal path that clears the token requires the emailed token (`server/apps/routes/auth.js:50-65`), and repeated reset requests replace it. This route has no authentication or rate-limit middleware (`server/apps/admin.js:10-13`).

**Impact:** An unauthenticated caller can repeatedly deny new password logins and invalidate a victim's reset links. Existing sessions remain usable, and the victim can recover if the requests stop, so the contained, recoverable availability impact is **low** under the review policy.

**Fix:** Keep the current credential usable until a reset token is redeemed, or otherwise rate-limit and bind reset requests so third parties cannot repeatedly invalidate a user's login and recovery state.

summary:
Reviewed PR #2 and recorded three findings: prototype pollution through unfiltered path segments, cache aliasing across path parser configurations, and inherited memo keys breaking valid property assignments.

The change adds the package implementation and passes the existing suite (`npm test`: 26 passing). The PR still needs fixes for the recorded issues before approval.

findings.title: Untrusted paths can pollute Object.prototype
findings.body:
Calling the public setter with an untrusted path can modify `Object.prototype` for the entire Node process. For example, in a fresh process, `set({}, '__proto__.polluted', true)` makes `({}).polluted === true`; `constructor.prototype.polluted` and equivalent array paths do the same.

**Preconditions:** The host passes an untrusted path to this library's public API.

**Evidence:** String paths are split at `index.js:28`, while array paths are used directly. The loop reads `target[prop]` and follows it without requiring an own property (`index.js:37-49`). Thus `__proto__` resolves to `Object.prototype`, and `constructor` then `prototype` resolves there as well; both pass `isObject` because it accepts objects and functions (`index.js:101-109`). `result` assigns the final attacker-controlled key to that shared object (`index.js:55-60`). `package.json:20` and `index.js:114` expose this function as the package API.

**Impact:** An untrusted caller can add arbitrary properties to all ordinary objects subsequently used in the process. This crosses the host application's input boundary and persists until restart, so the severity is **high** under the reach × persistence policy.

**Fix:** Reject `__proto__`, `constructor`, and `prototype` segments before traversing, for both parsed strings and array paths.

findings.title: Memo cache aliases distinct path parsers
findings.body:
The global parse cache can make a later call use keys selected by a different parser configuration, so it writes a different property shape. Two closure-created splitters have identical `String(fn)` text despite capturing different separators: after `set({}, 'a.b', 1, {split: make('.')})`, `set(target, 'a.b', 2, {split: make('/')})` creates `target.a.b` rather than the expected `target['a.b']`. The same root cause is reachable without a custom callback: priming `set({}, 'a/b', 1, {separator: '/'})` caches under `a/b;separator=/`; a subsequent default call with literal path `a/b;separator=/` wrongly writes `target.a.b`.

**Evidence:** `split` returns `set.memo[id]` before evaluating the current parser options (`index.js:63-65`) and retains every parse globally (`index.js:84-85`, `index.js:113`). `createKey` makes `id` by raw concatenation and `String(options[key])` (`index.js:88-98`), which neither encodes path/option boundaries nor preserves closure identity. On a cache miss, the custom callback or separator controls the expected keys (`index.js:67-75`); the traversal consumes the incorrectly cached keys at `index.js:37-49`.

**Impact:** One call can corrupt the output shape of later calls in the same process. This is a recoverable, contained integrity failure, so it is **low** under the reach × persistence policy.

**Fix:** Do not cache parses made by custom splitters, and use a collision-free cache structure that distinguishes the exact path and parser configuration.

findings.title: Inherited memo names break valid property assignments
findings.body:
Ordinary supported property names that exist on `Object.prototype` cannot be set with the default API. In a fresh module, `set({}, 'toString', 'VALUE')` leaves the target empty, while `set({}, 'constructor', 'VALUE')` creates `{'undefined': 'VALUE'}` rather than an own `constructor` property. This happens even on the first call and after resetting `set.memo = {}`.

**Evidence:** `set` sends string paths to `split` (`index.js:28`), but the cache is a normal object (`index.js:113`) and lookup accepts inherited values (`index.js:63-65`). For `toString`, that returns the inherited zero-arity function, so the assignment loop does not run (`index.js:29`, `index.js:37-50`). For `constructor`, it returns `Object`; the single-key shortcut uses `keys[0]`, which is `undefined`, and `result` assigns that key (`index.js:32-34`, `index.js:55-60`). The documented immediate-property behavior establishes that a string key should be assigned (`test.js:88-92`).

**Impact:** Callers cannot reliably store values under valid JavaScript property names, producing a contained, recoverable API correctness failure. Severity is **low** under the reach × persistence policy.

**Fix:** Use a null-prototype memo or an own-property check before returning a cached parse.

summary:
Reviewed all 345 added lines in `index.js` and traced packing, extraction, path validation, stream handling, and custom filesystem behavior. I recorded two findings: a high-severity extraction-root escape through symlink handling and a low-severity custom-filesystem directory-creation bug.

The existing test suite passes (`48/48`). The change fixes the intended hardlink CVE case, but it remains unsafe for crafted symlink entries and needs additional containment checks before approval.

findings.title: Archive symlinks allow writes outside the extraction root
findings.body:
A crafted tar can modify paths outside `cwd`. On Unix, it can create `victim` as a symlink to an absolute writable file, then provide a regular-file entry also named `victim`. The second entry validates only `cwd` and follows the final symlink, truncating and replacing the external file. A directory entry through that attacker-created (or a pre-existing) symlink also bypasses validation and creates or changes external directories.

**Preconditions:** The application extracts an attacker-controlled tar on a non-Windows host; the affected target is writable by the extracting process.

**Evidence:** `onsymlink` passes the archive-controlled `header.linkname` directly to `xfs.symlink` at `index.js:254-258`. For a following file, `validate` receives only `path.dirname(name)` at `index.js:298-304`, so it does not inspect `cwd/victim`; `onfile` opens that path with `xfs.createWriteStream` at `index.js:277-288`. A tar-stream reproduction changed an external target from `original` to `overwritten` while `cwd/victim` remained a symlink. Separately, directory entries call `mkdirfix(name, ...)` before the `validate` branch at `index.js:291-296`; `mkdirp` follows a symlinked component and the later `utimes`/`chmod` modify the resulting external directory at `index.js:207-231`. The existing regression test covers only hardlinks at `test/index.js:315-345`.

**Impact:** An untrusted archive crosses the extraction boundary and can permanently replace files or create and modify directories writable by the extraction process, outside the caller-selected destination. Under the review policy, cross-trust-boundary permanent data modification is **high**.

**Fix:** Enforce a separator-aware resolved-target containment check for archive symlinks, reject or unlink a final symlink before opening a file destination, and validate directory paths with the same no-symlink-ancestor invariant before `mkdirp`.

findings.title: Custom filesystem extraction creates parent directories on the host filesystem
findings.body:
Extraction with the supported `opts.fs` backend creates missing directories through Node's real filesystem instead. `extract` consistently selects `opts.fs` as `xfs` and passes it to `mkdirfix` as `fs`, but `mkdirfix` reads the nonexistent `opts.xfs`; `mkdirp` then falls back to native `fs`. A virtual or sandboxed backend therefore cannot extract an archive with a missing parent without creating host directories and usually fails when its write stream cannot find the corresponding backend directory.

**Preconditions:** The caller uses `tar.extract(destination, { fs: xfs })` and the archive contains a directory entry or a file under a missing directory.

**Evidence:** `extract` selects `opts.fs` at `index.js:176` and passes `{ fs: xfs }` to `mkdirfix` at `index.js:291-306`. `mkdirfix` instead supplies `opts.xfs` to `mkdirp` at `index.js:337-338`. In mkdirp 0.5.1, an undefined option selects native `fs`. A reproduction with a path-mapping `xfs` observed zero `xfs.mkdir` calls, created the host directory, and then failed the backend write with `ENOENT`.

**Impact:** Alternate-filesystem extraction is broken and can leave unwanted host directories. The affected caller can remove them and use the default filesystem, so this is a contained, recoverable failure and is **low** under the review policy.

**Fix:** Pass `opts.fs` to `mkdirp`.

summary: Reviewed PR #2’s new sequential installer downloader and its downstream installation flow. I recorded three findings: two high-severity network integrity issues and one low-severity lifecycle error-propagation issue. Tests passed with `npm test` after installing dependencies with `--force --ignore-scripts` because the package restricts installation to Windows.

findings.title: Network attackers can replace the Python installer
findings.body:
The default Python installer is fetched from HTTPS with certificate verification disabled, then executed by the elevated installation flow. A network-path attacker can serve a forged-certificate response containing an arbitrary MSI.

**Evidence:** `src/constants.js:1,9-14` constructs the default `https://www.python.org/.../python-2.7.11.msi` URL. This new downloader passes it to Nugget with `strictSSL: false` at `src/download.js:27-36`; Nugget forwards that option to request, where it disables TLS authorization. No integrity check follows at `src/download.js:38-52`. The later PowerShell script invokes `msiexec.exe /i python-2.7.11.msi` at `ps1/launch-installer.ps1:32-39` after requiring administrator privileges at `ps1/launch-installer.ps1:42-51`.

**Impact:** An active network attacker crosses the package user's trust boundary and gains code execution in the installer context. This is **high** under the review policy (trust-boundary compromise with persistent arbitrary code execution).

**Fix:** Do not set `strictSSL: false`; keep certificate validation enabled. Also validate downloaded installer signatures or pinned checksums before invoking either installer.

findings.title: Download failures make postinstall report success
findings.body:
A failed installer download is only printed, so the postinstall process exits successfully without installing either tool. This leaves users with a successful npm installation and a broken build environment.

**Evidence:** A Nugget error rejects `downloadTools()` at `src/download.js:38-47`. The callback that starts installation is attached only to the fully successful chain at `src/download.js:13-15`; the terminal handler at `src/download.js:16-17` logs the error but neither calls the callback nor rethrows or sets a failure status. `src/index.js:11-15` starts `install()` and `environment()` only through that callback. With no remaining work or nonzero exit, Node exits 0 and npm treats `postinstall` as successful.

**Impact:** A recoverable download or proxy failure silently leaves one installation without its promised tools. This is **low** under the review policy: the impact is contained and retrying the install restores it.

**Fix:** Propagate the rejection to the lifecycle process (for example, set a nonzero exit code or rethrow) instead of swallowing it; do not start installation after a failed download.

findings.title: Network attackers can replace the Build Tools installer
findings.body:
The newly reachable download path fetches the Visual C++ Build Tools executable over plaintext HTTP and executes it as part of the elevated install. An active network attacker can replace that executable in transit.

**Evidence:** The added code passes `installer.url` directly to Nugget at `src/download.js:38` and treats a successful response as a valid installer at `src/download.js:50-52`; it has no hash or signature check. For the first download, `src/constants.js:3-7` supplies the HTTP `download.microsoft.com` URL. After both downloads resolve, `src/index.js:11-15` starts the installation flow. `ps1/launch-installer.ps1:24-29` changes into the download directory and launches `BuildTools_Full.exe`, after the script's administrator check at `ps1/launch-installer.ps1:42-51`.

**Impact:** A network attacker crosses the package user's trust boundary and can execute an arbitrary EXE in the privileged installation flow. This is **high** under the review policy (trust-boundary compromise with persistent arbitrary code execution).

**Fix:** Fetch this installer over authenticated HTTPS and verify a pinned checksum or Authenticode publisher before launching it. Do not execute a download whose integrity was not verified.

summary:
Reviewed the added archive extraction utility and its resolver call paths. I recorded one high-severity finding: TAR hard-link entries remain unfiltered and can overwrite eligible files outside the extraction directory.

The symlink issue from the prior revision is fixed by the new `(name, header)` filter. I also ran `npm test`; 105 tests passed, but the legacy suite has 10 failures under the sandbox’s Node.js 24 runtime, which I recorded as an environment report.

findings.title: Tar packages can overwrite files through unfiltered hard links
findings.body:
A remote TAR package can overwrite a linkable file outside Bower's extraction directory. The TAR filter rejects symlinks but accepts `link` (hard-link) members; a later regular member with the same name then writes through the hard link.

**Preconditions:** The victim already exists on the same filesystem as Bower's temporary extraction directory and is linkable and writable by the Bower process. This affects Unix-like systems; `tar-fs` skips hard links on Windows.

**Evidence:** Both TAR paths pass `isSymlink` as the only `tar-fs` filter (lib/util/extract.js:65-69, lib/util/extract.js:95-99), and that function rejects only `entry.type === 'symlink'` (lib/util/extract.js:133-135). The committed lock resolves `tar-fs` to 1.15.3 (yarn.lock:4829-4837). In that version, `link` entries call `fs.link(path.resolve(cwd, header.linkname), name)` and normal file entries subsequently call `createWriteStream(name)`. I reproduced extraction through this module with a TAR containing `payload` as a hard link to an existing sibling `outside` file, followed by a regular `payload` entry. It changed `outside` to the regular entry's content; `outside` and the extracted `payload` had the same inode. URL resolution accepts an archive supplied by the remote package source and calls this extractor (lib/core/resolvers/UrlResolver.js:228-249).

**Impact:** A package source crosses the package-to-local-filesystem trust boundary and can persistently alter eligible files owned by the Bower user. This is high severity under the review policy; the same-filesystem and existing-linkable-file requirements are explicit limits, but were met in the reproduction.

**Fix:** Reject TAR hard-link entries as well as symlinks, preferably allow only regular files and directories before passing entries to `tar-fs`.

summary:
Found and recorded one high-severity issue: the new downloader accepts unverified installer content and the installation flow executes it.

The change downloads the Build Tools executable over HTTP and disables TLS certificate verification for downloads, without verifying hashes or publisher signatures before execution. `npm test` passes (after installing dependencies with `--force` on this non-Windows runner).

findings.title: Network attackers can replace installers before execution
findings.body:
A network attacker can replace either installer during a normal package installation and have it executed. The Build Tools URL is plaintext HTTP; the Python HTTPS request also accepts invalid certificates because this downloader sets `strictSSL: false`. No later step validates a hash or publisher.

**Evidence:** `downloadTools` disables certificate validation and saves the response as the installer at `src/download.js:29-38`. The Build Tools source is HTTP (`src/constants.js:3-6`), and completion invokes the installation flow (`src/download.js:14-16`, `src/index.js:11-14`). The PowerShell launcher executes that downloaded EXE directly at `ps1/launch-installer.ps1:24-29` and installs the downloaded MSI at `ps1/launch-installer.ps1:32-39`.

**Impact:** An on-path attacker crosses the network trust boundary to execute arbitrary code during installation, normally in the administrator PowerShell required by the launcher. This is high severity under the reach × persistence policy.

**Fix:** Fetch installers over authenticated HTTPS with certificate checks enabled and verify an expected digest or trusted Authenticode publisher before executing either file.

summary:
Reviewed the new Selectize accessibility plugin. The live-region change correctly avoids reparsing option text as HTML, addressing the injection path. I recorded two low-severity keyboard/accessibility regressions: Enter reopens default single-select dropdowns, and option refreshes can leave a dangling `aria-activedescendant` reference.

`node --check selectize-plugin-a11y.js` passes.

findings.title: Enter selection reopens single-select dropdowns
findings.body:
Pressing Enter to select an active option in an ordinary single-select closes the Selectize dropdown, then this handler clicks the control and focuses it again. With Selectize 0.12.4's default `openOnFocus`, the dropdown reopens immediately, so keyboard users cannot complete the normal Enter selection without an unwanted open/close cycle.

**Evidence:** The wrapper installs a bubbling `keydown` handler on the control after Selectize has installed its own handlers, and invokes `click()` for every Enter key (`selectize-plugin-a11y.js:103-114`). Selectize handles the same Enter on its focused input first: selecting an active option closes and blurs a full single-select; the bubbled event then reaches this handler. The synthetic control click refocuses that blurred control, which reopens it under the documented default. The handler neither checks whether Selectize already handled the key nor prevents this second action.

**Impact:** This affects keyboard selection in every default single-select using the plugin. It is contained to the current control and recoverable by closing it again, so this is low severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** Do not synthesize a control click for Enter events already handled by Selectize; either remove this handler or limit it to a state where Selectize has not selected/handled an active option.

findings.title: Option refreshes leave a dangling active-descendant reference
findings.body:
A normal `updateOption()` call can replace the currently active result while the dropdown remains open, leaving the input's `aria-activedescendant` set to the removed element's ID. Assistive technology then receives a dangling focus reference rather than the active result state.

**Evidence:** On an open dropdown, Selectize 0.12.4 calls `refreshOptions(false)` from `updateOption()`. Updating the option that is currently the sole filtered result removes that option, clears its active option, and keeps the dropdown open. This plugin observes only `class` attribute mutations (`selectize-plugin-a11y.js:59-64`) and only assigns `aria-activedescendant` when an option gains `active` (`selectize-plugin-a11y.js:45-55`). It does not observe the removed child or clear the attribute when the active option loses its class. Its only clearing path is dropdown close (`selectize-plugin-a11y.js:36-44`), which does not occur in this refresh path.

**Impact:** A screen-reader user of the affected open control gets an invalid active-descendant reference until the dropdown closes or another option becomes active. The failure is contained and recoverable, so this is low severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** Keep `aria-activedescendant` synchronized when options are removed or the active option is cleared, for example by observing child-list changes and clearing it unless the referenced active option still exists.

summary: Reviewed the new XMPP utility module and its transport, roster, presence, and SASL call paths. Verified that the updated `xmlEncode` replaces every XML-sensitive character occurrence, including repeated characters. Recorded one low-severity interoperability finding in the DIGEST-MD5 JID escaping path. `git diff --check` passed; this repository has no configured automated test script.

findings.title: DIGEST-MD5 rejects JIDs whose localpart contains #
findings.body:
A user with a legal localpart such as `alice#dev` cannot authenticate when the server selects DIGEST-MD5. `open()` retains that localpart, but the DIGEST-MD5 path sends and hashes `alice\\23dev`: `encodeJid()` maps `#` to `\\23`, although that is not an XMPP JID escape. The emitted DIGEST `username` also leaves that backslash unquoted.

**Preconditions:** The server offers DIGEST-MD5 before any supported alternative (or offers only DIGEST-MD5).

**Evidence:** `xmppSession.open()` accepts the supplied user and adds only the domain when needed (`xmpp/xmppSession.js:72-80`); the feature handler selects the first offered mechanism (`xmpp/xmppSession.js:202-205`). DIGEST-MD5 extracts the localpart and passes it to `encodeJid()` before using it in both the A1 hash and `username` directive (`xmpp/sasl.js:104-128`). `encodeJid()` changes `#` to `\\23` (`xmpp/util.js:35-37`). `#` is legal in an XMPP localpart, while `\\23` is not its defined escaped form, so the server computes the credential digest for `alice#dev` and rejects the client value.

**Impact:** The affected user's login fails for a legacy but supported authentication mechanism. This is a contained, recoverable interoperability failure, so severity is low under the review reach/persistence policy.

**Fix:** Do not apply XEP-0106-style escaping to the SASL simple username. Use the original localpart in the digest, and quote backslashes and quotes when serializing the DIGEST `username` directive.

summary: Reviewed the new admin authentication router and its session, model, Passport, and frontend flows. I recorded one high-severity finding for raw MongoDB selector input in the password-reset lookup. The upstream fixed branch confirms that request values must be converted to strings before use in these queries.

findings.title: Unauthenticated callers can reset and access an arbitrary account
findings.body:
An unauthenticated JSON request can supply a MongoDB operator instead of a reset token. For example, `{"token":{"$ne":"x"},"password":"attacker-password"}` reaches `findOne` as `{ token: { $ne: 'x' } }`. Since `token` is optional, this matches accounts with no reset token; `findOne()` then chooses a matching account.

**Evidence:** JSON parsing preserves the object before this unauthenticated router is mounted (`server/index.js:29-35`, `server/apps/admin.js:10-13`). The route puts raw `req.body.token` in the query at `server/apps/routes/auth.js:50-58`. The locked Mongoose 4.11.13 accepts `$ne` for a `String` query path (`package-lock.json:10080-10096`), and `User.token` is optional (`server/models/UserSchema.js:33`). After the match, the handler replaces the selected account's password, clears its token, saves it, and calls `req.login` (`server/apps/routes/auth.js:64-75`). Passport serializes that selected user's ID into the session (`server/utils/passport.js:14-16`).

**Impact:** A remote unauthenticated caller can take over a matching account and obtain its authenticated session. The injected predicate is not target-selective when several accounts match, but it deterministically compromises the account in a single-user deployment and otherwise compromises whichever account `findOne()` returns. This crosses an account trust boundary and is recoverable through a later password reset, so it is **high** under the review severity policy.

**Fix:** Require `token` to be a primitive nonempty string before querying, and use that string as the equality value. Apply the same type boundary to the other request values used as MongoDB selectors.

summary:
Reviewed the full new `classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js` implementation and its classifier, serialization, and multilabel integrations. Recorded four findings covering constructor availability, training arguments, persisted model state, and single-class behavior.

Overall, the new wrapper is not ready to merge: normal construction and established training calls fail, and supported model lifecycle paths are broken. I also ran a direct Node probe that confirmed the executable-check failure; the targeted npm test could not run because `mocha` is not installed in the fresh checkout.

findings.title: SvmLinear rejects normal LibLinear installations
findings.body:
Every `SvmLinear` construction rejects a normal LibLinear installation. `isInstalled` passes `"liblinear_train ."` as the executable name, so Node looks for a file with that entire name rather than running `liblinear_train` with `.` as an argument. The constructor throws whenever that probe fails.

**Evidence:** `execFileSync('liblinear_train .')` is used at `classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js:44-50`, and the constructor unconditionally calls this probe at `classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js:37-41`. `execFileSync('liblinear_train', ['.'])` succeeds with a `liblinear_train` executable on `PATH`; the current single-string form fails with `ENOENT`. The test suite gates all SvmLinear tests on this same broken probe, so it skips them instead of exposing the failure (`test/classifiersTest/SvmTest.js:90-93`).

**Impact:** This makes the newly exported classifier unavailable to every normal consumer with LibLinear installed. The loss is recoverable by a code fix, so this is medium severity under the reach/persistence policy.

**Fix:** Probe the configured trainer as a command plus argument array (or use a non-executing PATH lookup), and use `train_command` rather than a hard-coded command for custom configurations.

findings.title: String learn_args makes SvmLinear training throw
findings.body:
Training throws before invoking LibLinear for the string-form `learn_args` already used throughout this repository. String `.concat([learnFile, modelFile])` returns a string; the following `args.join(...)` then raises `TypeError`.

**Evidence:** `trainBatch` constructs and joins the arguments at `classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js:93-97`. Existing SvmLinear callers pass strings, including the binary tests (`test/classifiersTest/SvmTest.js:90-91`), multiclass tests (`test/classifiersTest/SvmMulticlassTest.js:16-19`), multilabel tests (`test/classifiersTest/multilabel/MetaLabelerSvmTest.js:95-96`), and the shipped demo (`classifiers/svm/SvmLinearDemo.js:16-23`). The current broken installation probe masks this path, but it is reached as soon as that probe is corrected or bypassed.

**Impact:** Existing documented examples and all checked-in SvmLinear integrations cannot train. This is broad and recoverable by a code fix, so it is medium severity under the reach/persistence policy.

**Fix:** Normalize `learn_args` to an argument array before appending the input and model paths, or migrate every caller and documentation example atomically to arrays.

findings.title: Serialized SvmLinear models lose their learned state
findings.body:
A trained SvmLinear model cannot survive the standard `EnhancedClassifier` JSON round trip. The implementation classifies from `mapLabelToMapFeatureToWeight`, but serializes the never-assigned `mapFeatureToWeight`; JSON therefore omits the classifier state. A restored classifier then tries to read the unserialized `modelFileString` and fails.

**Evidence:** Loading populates `mapLabelToMapFeatureToWeight` and `allLabels` (`classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js:109-114`), and `classify` consumes that map (`classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js:151-185`). `toJSON` and `fromJSON` instead use `mapFeatureToWeight`, which this file never sets (`classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js:222-228`). `EnhancedClassifier` delegates these hooks during serialization and restoration (`classifiers/EnhancedClassifier.js:491-505`). Reproducing that route after a successful classification produces an omitted `classifier` JSON field, then `fs.readFileSync(undefined)` on the restored classifier.

**Impact:** Any consumer that persists the newly added classifier loses its trained model and cannot classify after reload. The failure affects the supported serialization path and is recoverable by retraining/fixing, so it is medium severity under the reach/persistence policy.

**Fix:** Serialize and restore the label-to-weight map plus labels (or a durable model representation), and ensure the restored state satisfies `classify` without relying on an ephemeral file path.

findings.title: Single-class SvmLinear models throw during classification
findings.body:
Training a dataset with one class returns without creating a model, but the intended single-label classifier branch is checked only after an attempted model load. Thus the first ordinary `classify` call reads an undefined path and throws instead of returning the sole label.

**Evidence:** `trainBatch` assigns `allLabels` then returns for one label before assigning `modelFileString` (`classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js:83-104`). `classify` first calls `setModel(this.modelFileString)` when no map exists (`classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js:151-155`), and `setModel` reads that argument immediately (`classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js:109-114`); the single-label return at `classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js:156-167` is therefore unreachable. `getModelWeights` has the same missing-model load (`classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js:117-121`). This also reaches the SvmLinear-backed MetaLabeler single-class fixture: its binary child receives only label `1` (`classifiers/multilabel/BinaryRelevance.js:58-96`; `test/classifiersTest/multilabel/MetaLabelerSvmTest.js:31-40`) and is later classified (`classifiers/multilabel/BinaryRelevance.js:121-148`).

**Impact:** A valid single-class training set produces a classifier that fails every prediction rather than returning its known label. The affected model/request is contained and can be retrained after a fix, so this is low severity under the reach/persistence policy.

**Fix:** Test the single-label condition before lazy model loading, and preserve enough singleton state for model access and serialization.

summary: Reviewed the full 140-line plugin addition and its Selectize 0.12.4 integration paths. I recorded one high-severity finding for the unsafe live-region rendering path. Lifecycle behavior did not produce a separate reportable regression; the existing Enter-key issue is already tracked for this file.

findings.title: Attacker-controlled option labels execute script in the live region
findings.body:
An option label that an application renders as text is parsed again as HTML when the user makes that option active. An attacker who can supply a label such as `` can therefore execute script in every visitor's origin when that option is navigated to. **Preconditions:** The application exposes attacker-controlled option labels and uses a renderer that safely renders those labels as text (the normal mitigation before this plugin's second rendering). **Evidence:** The dropdown mutation observer takes an active option's text with `$target.text()` and sends it to `speak()` at `selectize-plugin-a11y.js:46-53`. `speak()` concatenates that text into `"
" + msg + "
