"`, which jQuery parses as HTML, then inserts the resulting node into the live region at `selectize-plugin-a11y.js:27-30`. The region is appended to `body` at `selectize-plugin-a11y.js:93-98`. Thus text that was inert in the option becomes live markup on keyboard navigation or hover. **Impact:** This crosses a trust boundary: a party allowed to provide an option label can run arbitrary JavaScript in another user's application origin, including exfiltrating that user's data. Per the review severity policy, the resulting permanent disclosure makes this **high**. **Fix:** Keep the announcement as text. Create an empty element and assign `msg` with `.text(msg)` (or a DOM `textContent` assignment) before adding it to the live region; never concatenate the label into HTML.

summary:
Reviewed the complete added `index.js` implementation and recorded five low-severity findings. The change replaces unsafe Buffer construction, but it also introduces compatibility and connection-lifecycle defects in proxy handling.

`npm test` could not complete under the current Node/OpenSSL runtime because the bundled TLS test certificate key is too small (`ERR_SSL...ee key too small`); this is a test-fixture environment failure before the request tests run.

findings.title: Authenticated proxies fail on early supported Node 4 releases
findings.body:
Authenticated proxy requests fail on Node 4.0–4.4, despite Node 4 being in the supported CI matrix. A proxy URI such as `http://user:pass@proxy:3128` is parsed into `proxy.auth`; the request callback then calls `Buffer.from(proxy.auth)`. In those Node releases `Buffer.from` is the inherited typed-array method and rejects strings, so the CONNECT request is never written.

**Preconditions:** The application runs on Node 4.0–4.4 and uses an authenticated proxy.

**Evidence:** The package has no `engines` exclusion and tests Node `4` in `.travis.yml:5-10`. The constructor accepts proxy URI strings at `index.js:25-26`; `url.parse()` supplies `auth`, which is copied at `index.js:35` and encoded at `index.js:205-207`. `Buffer.from('user:pass')` throws on Node 4.0–4.4; string support arrived in Node 4.5.

**Impact:** Authenticated requests through supported Node 4 versions fail synchronously rather than reaching the proxy. This affects a contained request and is recoverable by upgrading or changing the call, so severity is low under the review policy.

**Fix:** Use a string-compatible conversion on the supported runtime (for example, retain `new Buffer(proxy.auth)` here, where `proxy.auth` is a string), or raise the declared minimum Node version and CI coverage to Node 4.5 or newer.

findings.title: Incomplete CONNECT responses leave proxied requests pending
findings.body:
A proxy that closes its connection after a partial CONNECT response leaves the client request pending forever. After buffering a response that lacks `\r\n\r\n`, the callback waits for more data. A graceful `end` or `close` only logs, while only the `error` path completes the agent callback. `agent-base` therefore never attaches a socket or delivers an error to the request.

**Preconditions:** The configured proxy or an intermediary closes the CONNECT connection before completing its response headers.

**Evidence:** Partial data takes the wait path at `index.js:113-127`. `onend` and `onclose` do not call `fn` at `index.js:100-106`; only `onerror` does at `index.js:108-111`. The request has already sent CONNECT at `index.js:201-223`. A local proxy that replied `HTTP/1.1 200 Connection established\r\nX-Partial: yes` then closed produced no `socket`, `response`, or `error` event after 500 ms.

**Impact:** A failed proxied request stays open until the caller imposes its own timeout or destroys it. The effect is contained to requests routed through that failed proxy and recoverable, so severity is low under the review policy.

**Fix:** Treat `end` and `close` before a completed CONNECT response as an error: clean up and invoke `fn()` once with an appropriate connection/protocol error.

findings.title: IPv6 origins produce malformed CONNECT authorities
findings.body:
IPv6-literal destinations produce an invalid CONNECT authority. Node passes the request callback an unbracketed `opts.host` such as `::1`; this code serializes it as `::1:8081`, which a strict proxy cannot parse as an IPv6 authority. The same value is used for `Host`, so neither header identifies the intended target.

**Preconditions:** A proxied HTTP or HTTPS request targets an IPv6 literal.

**Evidence:** The CONNECT authority concatenates `opts.host + ':' + opts.port` at `index.js:201-202`, and `Host` begins with that unbracketed value at `index.js:212-216`. A local strict proxy rejected the actual emitted `CONNECT ::1:8081 HTTP/1.1` with 400 before attempting the target. `agent-base` supplies the callback this normalized request `host` value.

**Impact:** Requests to IPv6-literal origins fail through strict proxies. The outcome is a contained, recoverable compatibility failure, so severity is low under the review policy.

**Fix:** Detect IPv6 literals and bracket them when serializing the CONNECT authority and Host header (for example, `[::1]:8081`).

findings.title: Non-200 successful CONNECT responses never establish a tunnel
findings.body:
The agent treats a valid successful CONNECT response other than 200 as a proxy error. HTTP CONNECT defines the entire 2xx range as success, but the success branch only accepts 200; a proxy returning 201 or 204 is replayed as an HTTP response and the tunnel, including the destination TLS handshake, never starts.

**Preconditions:** The configured proxy returns a non-200 2xx response to CONNECT.

**Evidence:** Only `200` reaches the tunnel handoff at `index.js:130-157`; all other statuses take the response-replay branch at `index.js:158-169`. A local proxy that returned 201 or 204 while piping a live TLS target caused the caller to receive the proxy response and the target to receive no request. Changing the condition to a 2xx range completed the same tunnels. RFC 7231 §4.3.6 defines any 2xx CONNECT response as success.

**Impact:** Requests through standards-compliant non-200 proxies do not reach their origin. This is a contained, recoverable interoperability failure, so severity is low under the review policy.

**Fix:** Treat `statusCode >= 200 && statusCode < 300` as CONNECT success and keep replay only for non-2xx responses.

findings.title: HTTPS proxies receive an invalid HTTP/1.1 ALPN identifier
findings.body:
HTTPS-proxy connections advertise `http 1.1` as their ALPN protocol, but the registered HTTP/1.1 identifier is `http/1.1`. A proxy configured to require the standard identifier rejects TLS negotiation before the agent sends CONNECT.

**Preconditions:** The proxy uses TLS and requires or selects HTTP/1.1 with ALPN.

**Evidence:** The secure-proxy default is `['http 1.1']` at `index.js:46-48` and is passed to `tls.connect()` at `index.js:73-74`. A local TLS proxy with `ALPNProtocols: ['http/1.1']` rejected the agent offer with `ERR_SSL_TLSV1_ALERT_NO_APPLICATION_PROTOCOL`; offering `http/1.1` negotiated successfully. The existing TLS-proxy fixture has no ALPN requirement (`test/test.js:60-66`).

**Impact:** Connections to affected HTTPS proxies fail before any request reaches the proxy. This is a contained, recoverable compatibility failure, so severity is low under the review policy.

**Fix:** Set the default ALPN list to `['http/1.1']`.

summary:
Reviewed the new Linux backend and its public API call paths. Recorded one confirmed high-severity finding: `fnd_o99gctwo73rvvir8`.

Verified the issue through `macaddress.one()` with an injected interface name; the injected command ran and the callback reported success. `npm test` passes.

findings.title: Untrusted interface names execute shell commands on Linux
findings.body:
An application that passes an untrusted interface name to the documented `one(iface, callback)` API lets that input execute arbitrary shell commands with the Node process's privileges.

**Evidence:** The public API forwards an explicit `iface` without validation to the Linux backend (`index.js:78`, `index.js:107-109`). The backend concatenates it into a string passed to `child_process.exec` (`lib/linux.js:3-4`), which invokes a shell. For example, `one('missing; printf injected > /tmp/marker; #', cb)` runs the injected `printf`; the trailing `#` comments out the fixed `/address` suffix. This path was reproduced through `macaddress.one()`, and its callback reported success because the injected command was last and exited successfully.

**Impact:** An untrusted caller can gain the process's command-execution capability, crossing the application's input trust boundary. Per the review policy this is high severity; command execution persists until the affected deployment is corrected and can alter or disclose accessible data.

**Fix:** Do not use a shell to read the sysfs file. Validate that `iface` identifies an expected interface and use `fs.readFile` (or another non-shell API) for its `address` file.

summary:
**This run stopped early at the run's time limit, so its results are partial.**

Reviewed PR #2’s added `index.js`.

Recorded:
- **High:** Numeric proxy credentials can disclose uninitialized process memory on supported Node 4–7 releases (`index.js:207`).
- **Low:** Unterminated CONNECT responses can exhaust client CPU and memory (`index.js:113`).

I also confirmed the existing finding for incomplete CONNECT responses that leave requests pending; I did not duplicate it. I did not reach final verification of the IPv6 and ALPN hypotheses before the run ended.

`npm test` could not complete because the sandbox OpenSSL rejects the repository’s small test certificate; I recorded environment report `rpt_tcgcexqxzx3t0tp6`.

findings.title: Numeric proxy credentials disclose process memory
findings.body:
A caller that passes a numeric `auth` value causes the CONNECT request to disclose uninitialized process memory to the proxy on supported Node 4–7 releases. The options object is public API, so applications that forward untrusted proxy settings can expose memory to an attacker-selected proxy.

**Preconditions:** The process runs on Node 4–7, and `auth` is a non-zero number, for example `{ host: 'proxy.example', port: 8080, auth: 128 }`.

**Evidence:** The constructor accepts and shallow-copies arbitrary proxy options without validating `auth` (`index.js:25-35`). A truthy value is passed to `new Buffer(proxy.auth)` (`index.js:205-207`). On Node 4–7, the numeric `Buffer` form allocates uninitialized memory. Its Base64 encoding becomes `Proxy-Authorization` and is written to the proxy (`index.js:207`, `index.js:219-223`). The project tests Node 4 through 8 (`.travis.yml:5-10`). A Node 6.17.0 run with `auth: 128` sent a decoded 128-byte buffer containing non-zero uninitialized bytes to a local proxy.

**Impact:** The configured proxy receives process-memory contents that it should not receive. Once transmitted, the disclosure cannot be undone. This crosses the application-to-proxy trust boundary and is permanent, so severity is high under the review policy.

**Fix:** Require `auth` to be a string before encoding it, and use a safe string-to-buffer conversion compatible with every supported Node version. Reject other types rather than passing them to the numeric `Buffer` constructor.

findings.title: Unterminated CONNECT responses exhaust client resources
findings.body:
A proxy can keep every request using it in an unbounded pre-CONNECT parsing loop by streaming bytes without a header terminator. This retains attacker-controlled data and repeatedly copies the entire response until the client process runs out of memory or CPU.

**Preconditions:** The configured proxy is malicious or compromised, or an attacker can alter traffic to a plaintext HTTP proxy connection.

**Evidence:** Each incoming chunk is retained in `buffers` (`index.js:83-84`, `index.js:113-115`), then every chunk causes `Buffer.concat()` and ASCII decoding of all buffered bytes (`index.js:116-117`). If `\r\n\r\n` is absent, the code immediately reads again without a byte limit or error (`index.js:119-127`). Completion and cleanup occur only after the terminator (`index.js:156-169`); clean EOF also only logs (`index.js:100-106`). A local proxy streaming 8 MiB without a terminator caused 129 concatenations, about 524 MiB copied, and about 124 MiB RSS. The inherited agent timeout is unset by default (`node_modules/agent-base/index.js:38-42`).

**Impact:** A hostile proxy can exhaust resources in client processes that use it, interrupting their proxied requests. The proxy is normally a trusted configured service, which discounts this broad, recoverable availability failure to low under the review policy.

**Fix:** Set a bounded maximum CONNECT-response header size and fail and destroy the proxy socket when it is exceeded. Parse incrementally so each received byte is copied and scanned at most once.

summary:
Reviewed the new Linux backend and its call paths. I recorded three findings: a medium-severity sysfs path traversal, plus low-severity failures for restricted `PATH` environments and suppressed errors from `all()`.

`npm test` passed, and an explicit Linux lookup completed successfully in this environment. The PR should not merge until the recorded issues are addressed.

findings.title: Caller-supplied interface names can read files outside sysfs
findings.body:
A caller that supplies an interface name can make this library return a file outside sysfs. For example, after creating `/tmp/mac/address` as a symlink to a file readable by the application, `one('../../../tmp/mac', callback)` reads that target and returns its contents.

**Preconditions:** The application passes an attacker-controlled value to `one(iface, callback)`, and the attacker can arrange an `address` entry in a traversable writable directory.

**Evidence:** `one()` sends an explicit `iface` to the Linux backend without validation (`index.js:78-110`). The backend concatenates it into a pathname passed to `cat` (`lib/linux.js:3-4`). The three `..` segments in the example resolve `/sys/class/net/../../../tmp/mac/address` to `/tmp/mac/address`; `cat` follows the final symlink. `execFile` avoids shell parsing but does not constrain pathname resolution.

**Impact:** This discloses any text file readable by the application process through a public callback. The filesystem setup requirement discounts the cross-boundary, permanent disclosure by one tier under the review policy.

**Fix:** Reject interface names containing path separators or resolve the name from the enumerated interface set before constructing the sysfs path.

findings.title: Restricted PATH prevents Linux MAC lookups
findings.body:
The Linux backend fails even for a valid interface when the host service uses a restricted `PATH`. `execFile("cat", ...)` resolves the command through that environment, so `one('eth0', cb)` receives `spawn cat ENOENT` when `cat` is not on `PATH`.

**Evidence:** Linux unconditionally selects this backend (`index.js:55-64`) and explicit `one()` calls forward the interface to it (`index.js:78-110`). The new backend invokes bare `cat` (`lib/linux.js:1-4`) and returns execution errors (`lib/linux.js:5-7`). The package documents Linux and Node 0.8+ support (`README.md:18-23`), including releases that need this fallback.

**Impact:** A service with a hardened or minimal command path cannot retrieve MAC addresses. The failure is recoverable by restoring `PATH`; the non-default deployment setting discounts the broad availability failure to low severity.

**Fix:** Use the absolute system utility path expected by supported Linux targets, or avoid spawning `cat` and read the sysfs file with Node's filesystem API.

findings.title: Linux MAC lookup failures are reported as successful all() results
findings.body:
On Linux fallback paths, `all()` reports success after a MAC lookup fails and returns an interface without its MAC. For example, a missing sysfs mount or unavailable `cat` causes `linux.js` to call back with an error, but the public callback receives `(null, ifaces)`.

**Evidence:** `all()` schedules a backend lookup for each interface lacking `mac` (`index.js:114-123`), while the new Linux backend returns read/spawn errors (`lib/linux.js:4-8`). `parallel()` records such errors (`index.js:13-22`), but `all()` ignores its `err` argument and unconditionally calls `callback(null, ifaces)` (`index.js:134-140`). This PR makes that existing aggregator behavior reachable on Linux because it supplies the previously missing selected backend (`index.js:62-64`).

**Impact:** Callers can treat an incomplete MAC inventory as valid, causing recoverable incorrect behavior. A missing sysfs mount or command is a non-default environment condition, so the broad failure is low severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** Propagate the aggregate error from `parallel()` (or return per-interface errors) instead of reporting a successful complete result.

summary: Reviewed the new LibLinear wrapper and its training, inference, persistence, and higher-level multilabel paths. I recorded four findings covering model lifecycle, serialization, default construction, and binary decision-boundary behavior. `npm test` could not run because `mocha` is not installed; static inspection and controlled reproductions covered the reported paths.

findings.title: Single-class SvmLinear models throw during classification
findings.body:
Training on an all-one-label set records that label but creates no model. The first later classification tries to load `this.modelFileString` before checking the one-label shortcut, although that path was never set, so `fs.readFileSync(undefined)` throws instead of returning the sole label.

**Evidence:** `trainBatch` returns after setting `allLabels` at `classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js:85-93`, before the model path assignment at `:96-110`. `classify` calls `setModel(this.modelFileString)` at `:158-159` before its single-label branch at `:161-171`; `setModel` reads the supplied path at `:115-118`. The checked-in MetaLabeler SVM test includes a single-class input scenario (`test/classifiersTest/multilabel/MetaLabelerSvmTest.js:31-59`) that trains this path through `BinaryRelevance`.

**Impact:** Any all-positive, all-negative, or one-class model fails on first inference. The failure affects one trained classifier and can be corrected by retraining after the fix, so its contained, recoverable impact is low under the review policy.

**Fix:** Check `allLabels.length === 1` before lazy model loading, or initialize the one-label model map during training.

findings.title: Serialized SvmLinear models lose their learned state
findings.body:
Persisting an SvmLinear classifier drops the parsed model, so a restored classifier cannot classify. Training and loading populate `mapLabelToMapFeatureToWeight`, but `toJSON` and `fromJSON` use the unrelated `mapFeatureToWeight` property, which no other code in this file sets or reads.

**Evidence:** `setModel` builds `mapLabelToMapFeatureToWeight` and `allLabels` at `classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js:115-120`, and `classify` requires that map at `:158-176`. In contrast, `toJSON` returns `mapFeatureToWeight` and `fromJSON` restores only that field at `:227-233`. `EnhancedClassifier` delegates persistence to its base classifier at `classifiers/EnhancedClassifier.js:491-505`; after restoration the map and `modelFileString` are absent, so the first classification follows `:158-159` and tries to read an undefined path.

**Impact:** Every SvmLinear model saved through the supported wrapper persistence path loses its learned state and cannot serve predictions after a restart. The saved models must be retrained or re-saved after the fix; this broad recoverable loss is medium under the review policy.

**Fix:** Serialize and restore `mapLabelToMapFeatureToWeight` together with the label state required by `classify`, or use one consistent model field throughout the class.

findings.title: SvmLinear cannot be constructed with its documented defaults
findings.body:
The documented default configuration cannot be constructed. Although every option has a fallback and the documentation marks only the model prefix as optional, the constructor dereferences `opts` before applying any fallback, so `new SvmLinear()` throws a TypeError before it can check for LibLinear or use its defaults.

**Evidence:** The defaults are documented at `classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js:12-17`, but the first statement reads `opts.learn_args` at `:30`; the installation check is only reached at `:39-43`. The public classifiers module exports SvmLinear (`classifiers/index.js:11`). Existing tests bind an options object before construction (`test/classifiersTest/SvmTest.js:90-92`), which masks direct default construction.

**Impact:** Consumers using the public classifier with its documented defaults cannot create it. This is a contained, recoverable API failure, so it is low under the review policy.

**Fix:** Normalize the parameter at entry, for example `opts = opts || {}`, before reading option properties.

findings.title: Zero-margin binary predictions disagree with LibLinear
findings.body:
For a binary model with an exact zero decision value, the wrapper returns the opposite label from LibLinear. LibLinear selects the second header label when the decision value is zero, but this code sorts equal scores and returns the first enumerated label.

**Evidence:** LibLinear binary models contain one weight column; the parser maps it to the first header label and its negation to the second at `classifiers/svm/SvmLinear.js:265-291`. `classify` sorts those scores without a tie rule at `:175-193` and returns the first label at `:207-210`. For the valid header `label 0 1` and zero score, both computed scores are zero and JavaScript retains the integer-key enumeration order `0`, then `1`, so this method returns `0`. LibLinear's binary prediction rule is `decision > 0 ? label[0] : label[1]`, which returns `1` on the same input.

**Impact:** Inputs on the decision boundary receive a different class from the LibLinear model this wrapper exposes. Each result is confined to one prediction and a supported code correction removes the inconsistency, so this is low under the review policy.

**Fix:** Implement LibLinear's strict-positive binary decision rule instead of selecting the first label after sorting tied scores.

summary:
**This run stopped early at the run's time limit, so its results are partial.**

Reviewed the added XMPP utility and its transport, roster, presence, chat, SASL, and widget call paths. I recorded five findings: XML attribute/text injection and malformed outbound XML, Unicode SASL authentication failure, and a high-severity remote chat-message XSS enabled by the newly available XMPP dependency.

I also checked the JID encoding path; its defect overlaps an existing open finding, so I did not duplicate it. I did not run the manual Openfire/BOSH integration suite because it requires an external configured server; `htmlToPlain` has no in-repository caller and was not further tested.

findings.title: Repeated XML metacharacters escape roster attributes
findings.body:
A roster alias containing a second XML metacharacter escapes the `name` attribute and lets the caller append sibling XMPP stanzas to the authenticated BOSH request. For example, an alias beginning with `<>"` followed by ` ></item></query></iq><message xmlns="jabber:client" to="victim@example.test" type="chat"><body>x</body></message><iq><query><item x="` leaves the second quote and all later markup literal, while the fixed suffix closes the replacement roster IQ.

**Evidence:** `xmlEncode` uses non-global string replacements, so it encodes only the first instance of each character (xmpp/util.js:5-9). `addRosterItem` accepts `name`, places it in the quoted `item` attribute, and appends a predictable closing suffix (xmpp/RosterService.js:14-43); the supplied test page passes its alias input directly to this API (xmpp/tests/test_xmppService.html:384-391). The transport queues the constructed string, concatenates it inside the BOSH body without parsing or escaping, and posts it unchanged (xmpp/TransportSession.js:167-170, 225-229, 274-280, 283-306). Thus a well-formed injected `<message xmlns="jabber:client">` is framed as another outbound stanza.

**Impact:** An application user who can supply a roster alias can make their authenticated client send protocol actions beyond the roster update. This is contained to that session and actions are processed server-side, so it is low severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** Escape every XML metacharacter in `xmlEncode`, using a global replacement or equivalent single-pass encoder. Add a test with repeated quotes and angle brackets through the roster API.

findings.title: Raw contact attributes can inject XMPP stanzas
findings.body:
Several public XMPP APIs serialize caller-supplied attribute values without escaping them. A crafted contact value can close `to="..."` and insert a sibling XMPP stanza into the authenticated BOSH body. This is independent of `xmlEncode`: these paths do not call that helper.

**Evidence:** `createElement` appends each attribute value directly between quote delimiters (xmpp/util.js:81-98). `PresenceService._manageSubscriptions` passes its `contact` argument as `to` after only presence and `@` checks, and the public subscription methods expose it (xmpp/PresenceService.js:275-304). For example, a contact beginning `victim@example.test" /><message xmlns="jabber:client" to="attacker@example.test" type="chat"><body>x</body></message><presence to="` produces a direct message sibling followed by the intended presence stanza. The raw constructed string is queued, concatenated into the BOSH body, and posted without outbound parsing or escaping (xmpp/TransportSession.js:167-170, 225-229, 274-280, 283-306).

**Impact:** An application user who controls a contact value can cause their authenticated session to issue extra XMPP protocol actions. The effect is contained to that session and server processing, so this is low severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** Make the XML serializer escape every attribute value exactly once. Remove or reconcile the roster callers' pre-encoding so valid names are not double-encoded, and test quote and markup payloads through subscription and roster APIs.

findings.title: Remote chat messages execute markup in recipients’ browsers
findings.body:
An XMPP peer can execute script in a chat recipient's browser by sending XML-escaped HTML in a message body. The XML parser decodes the body before the chat widget appends it with `innerHTML`.

**Evidence:** The inbound handler assigns `n.firstChild.nodeValue` from an XMPP `<body>` directly to `message.body` (xmpp/xmppSession.js:241-261), then delivers that object to the registered chat instance or callback (xmpp/xmppSession.js:316-341; xmpp/ChatService.js:21-24). The supplied client test page connects that callback to `newMessage` and calls `displayMessage` (xmpp/tests/test_xmppService.html:220-240, 340-359). `displayMessage` concatenates `message.body` into `messages.domNode.innerHTML` (xmpp/widget/ChatSession.js:20-25). Thus `<body><img src=x onerror=alert(1)></body>` from a remote peer becomes executable markup. The added module makes the required XMPP transport dependency available (xmpp/TransportSession.js:1-4; xmpp/util.js:1); its `stripHtml` helper is used only for outbound messages (xmpp/ChatService.js:84-85) and does not protect reception.

**Impact:** A remote XMPP peer crosses a trust boundary and can run script in a recipient's authenticated browser context. Script execution can access application data and act as that user, which is high severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** Render chat content as text (for example, assign `textContent` or create text nodes), and separately sanitize any deliberately supported XHTML-IM content before rendering it.

findings.title: Common chat text produces malformed BOSH XML
findings.body:
Ordinary chat text containing `&` or a bare `<` creates an invalid BOSH XML document, so the message is rejected and can terminate the transport session.

**Evidence:** The chat widget passes the input value as `body` (xmpp/widget/ChatSession.js:34-40). `sendMessage` appends the raw body to the XHTML body and appends `stripHtml(body)` to the plain body (xmpp/ChatService.js:66-85, 101-114). `stripHtml` removes only complete tag-like spans and does not XML-escape text, so `AT&T` and `1 < 2` remain invalid XML (xmpp/util.js:100-108). The transport concatenates this raw stanza into the BOSH envelope and posts it without XML serialization (xmpp/TransportSession.js:219-229, 274-280, 283-312); HTTP client errors transition the transport to `Terminate` (xmpp/TransportSession.js:457-469).

**Impact:** A normal user can lose the active XMPP connection by sending common text. The failure is transient and limited to that session, so it is low severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** XML-escape all element text before concatenating it, or construct and serialize DOM/XML nodes rather than assembling strings.

findings.title: Unicode SASL credentials are encoded as invalid bytes
findings.body:
SASL PLAIN authentication sends non-ASCII credentials as JavaScript UTF-16 code units rather than UTF-8 bytes. A compliant server cannot recover the intended credential.

**Evidence:** PLAIN builds the authzid/NUL/authcid/NUL/password token and passes it to this helper (xmpp/sasl.js:50-63). `Base64.encode` pushes `charCodeAt()` values directly into a byte-array encoder (xmpp/util.js:128-136). For password `päss`, it emits byte `e4` for `ä`; UTF-8 requires `c3 a4` (RFC 4616 section 2). The session selects PLAIN from advertised mechanisms and treats an unsuccessful response as login failure (xmpp/xmppSession.js:171-231).

**Impact:** Users with non-ASCII account names or passwords cannot authenticate to compliant servers. This is a contained, recoverable login failure, so it is low severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** UTF-8 encode JavaScript strings before Base64 encoding, and decode SASL text as UTF-8 where required. Add a PLAIN test using non-ASCII credentials.

summary: Reviewed the new SSH public-key formatter and its parse, serialization, and CLI conversion paths. I recorded two findings: one authorization-impacting output-injection issue and one bounded ECDSA input-integrity issue. The regex change removes the demonstrated quadratic matching behavior; malformed 1 MiB SSH input remained linear-time in testing. `npm test` completed with 536/537 passing; the lone failure is in `test/fingerprint.js` and appears unrelated to this change on the current Node runtime.

findings.title: SSH output can inject a second authorized key through comments
findings.body:
A newline in a key comment produces a second SSH public-key record. For example, setting `key.comment` to `one\nssh-ed25519 <attacker key>` makes `key.toString('ssh')` return two lines; the second line parses successfully as an Ed25519 key. The shipped converter writes this format by default for public keys.

**Preconditions:** A workflow converts an attacker-supplied OpenSSH private key (or otherwise accepts an attacker-controlled comment) and installs the resulting SSH output in an `authorized_keys`-style file.

**Evidence:** The new writer appends `key.comment` without rejecting or escaping CR/LF (`lib/formats/ssh.js:110-113`), and `Key#toBuffer()` selects this writer by default (`lib/key.js:81-98`). The OpenSSH private-key reader assigns its length-prefixed, unvalidated comment to the key (`lib/formats/ssh-private.js:125-133`); `PrivateKey#toPublic()` preserves it (`lib/private-key.js:77-84`). `sshpk-conv` parses the input and writes `key.toBuffer(fmt)` before adding its newline (`bin/sshpk-conv:140-182`). Thus a crafted private-key comment reaches an additional output record without an application needing to mutate the returned key.

**Impact:** An attacker can add their own public key when this conversion output is used as an authorized-key file, gaining the ability to authenticate as that account until the record is removed. This crosses an authorization boundary and is recoverable by removing the key, so severity is **high** under the review policy.

**Fix:** Preserve the one-record-per-output invariant: reject comments containing `\r` or `\n` (or normalize both to spaces) before appending them in the SSH writer.

findings.title: SSH parser accepts contradictory ECDSA algorithm labels
findings.body:
The reader accepts an ECDSA public-key line whose outer algorithm label contradicts its wire payload, then silently rewrites the label on output. For example, changing only the first field of a valid `ecdsa-sha2-nistp256` line to `ecdsa-sha2-nistp521` returns a P-256 `Key`; `toString('ssh')` then emits `ecdsa-sha2-nistp256`. OpenSSH rejects the contradictory original line.

**Evidence:** The reader maps every `ecdsa-sha2-*` outer label to generic `ecdsa` (`lib/formats/ssh.js:33`) and compares only that generic type after parsing (`lib/formats/ssh.js:60`). The RFC4253 reader checks the inner payload label against its curve (`lib/formats/rfc4253.js:92-96`), so a valid P-256 payload passes this generic outer check. The SSH writer derives its label from the parsed payload curve (`lib/formats/ssh.js:103-108`; `lib/formats/rfc4253.js:49-50`), causing the silent change.

**Impact:** A caller that validates, stores, or converts submitted standard SSH public-key text accepts an invalid record and changes its declared algorithm. The returned key correctly exposes the P-256 curve, so no in-library signature-verification downgrade follows. The effect is confined to one supplied record and recoverable by rejecting or replacing it; severity is **low** under the review policy.

**Fix:** Before accepting the parsed key, require the outer token to equal `rfc4253.keyTypeToAlg(key)` (or, for ECDSA, require its suffix to equal the parsed curve).

summary:
Recorded two findings:

- **Medium:** Malformed SSH keys block the event loop in regex backtracking.
- **Low:** Uncommented SSH keys gain an `undefined` comment on round-trip.

The PR restores the SSH public-key parser, but its ambiguous regexes permit attacker-controlled ReDoS through the public `parseKey` API. It also corrupts valid uncommented keys during parse/serialize cycles. I installed dependencies and ran `npm test`; 536 of 537 tests passed, with one pre-existing compatibility failure in `test/fingerprint.js` under the current dependency/runtime resolution.

findings.title: Malformed SSH keys block the event loop in regex backtracking
findings.body:
A malformed SSH public-key string can make the synchronous public parser spend seconds in regex backtracking before it rejects the input, blocking the Node event loop for every request handled by that process.

**Preconditions:** The application passes an untrusted SSH public-key string to `parseKey`, either explicitly as format `ssh` or through auto-detection.

**Evidence:** `Key.parse` accepts caller data and dispatches it to the format reader (`lib/key.js:216-234`); `auto` selects the SSH reader for `ssh-` headers (`lib/formats/auto.js:20-27`). Before decoding, `read` matches input against both patterns (`lib/formats/ssh.js:27-31`). The overlapping repetitions in `SSHKEY_RE` at `lib/formats/ssh.js:17` and `SSHKEY_RE2` at `lib/formats/ssh.js:19` backtrack quadratically on malformed suffixes. For example, `ssh-rsa A` followed by 30,000 spaces and `\n\n!\n!` took about 2.7 seconds through `parseKey`; `ssh-rsa ` plus 30,000 `A` characters and `!\n!` took about 0.7 seconds. Both inputs ultimately fail parsing.

**Impact:** An untrusted request can temporarily deny service to all users sharing the Node process and can repeat the block. This is **medium** severity under the review policy: broad reach with recoverable impact.

**Fix:** Use the bounded, non-overlapping token and trailer patterns from the fixed version, or parse fields without ambiguous regex repetitions.

findings.title: Uncommented SSH keys gain an `undefined` comment on round-trip
findings.body:
Parsing a normal two-field SSH public-key line invents the literal comment `undefined`; serializing that key then changes the authorized-key record by appending ` undefined`.

**Evidence:** The comment capture is optional (`lib/formats/ssh.js:17`), so a valid no-comment key has no `m[3]` or `m[4]`. The no-comment path uses partial RFC4253 parsing (`lib/formats/ssh.js:56-57`), which records consumed bytes (`lib/formats/rfc4253.js:128-130`) and enters recovery (`lib/formats/ssh.js:65`). Concatenating `m[2] + m[3]` coerces the missing capture to `undefined` at `lib/formats/ssh.js:74`; the recovered trailer passes the alphanumeric check and is assigned as the comment (`lib/formats/ssh.js:88-92`). The existing valid `SSH_1133` fixture has no comment (`test/metadata.js:12-15`); parsing it produces `key.comment === 'undefined'`, and the writer appends that truthy value (`lib/formats/ssh.js:110-113`). It also prevents `Key.parse` from supplying its documented filename/default fallback because the erroneous comment is truthy (`lib/key.js:237-238`).

**Impact:** Any caller that reads and rewrites an uncommented SSH key emits a changed record and loses its intended filename/default comment. This is **low** severity under the review policy: contained, recoverable data corruption.

**Fix:** Treat an absent optional capture as an empty string before concatenating it during comment recovery.

summary: Reviewed `src/run.js` and its Git-command call paths. I recorded one high-severity finding for shell command injection through attacker-controlled Git options passed to `exec`. Lint passes; the test suite has 51 passing tests and 2 acceptance failures because `vimdiff` is unavailable in the environment.

findings.title: Attacker-controlled Git options execute shell commands
findings.body:
`run()` passes a string to `child_process.exec`, which invokes a shell. The public `startTag` and `endTag` options are interpolated into Git command strings without validation, so a consumer that forwards an attacker-controlled tag runs that attacker's shell command with the host process's privileges.

**Preconditions:** A consumer accepts a tag value from an untrusted source and calls the API against a clean Git worktree and a remote with the expected tags.

**Evidence:** `src/run.js:8-10` calls the shell-backed `exec` with its command string. `src/index.js:32-43` accepts `startTag`/`endTag`, then passes them to `checkOutTag` at `src/index.js:64,69`; `src/check-out-tag.js:6-7` constructs `git rev-parse ${tag}`. A tag value such as `v1; printf marker > /tmp/marker; #` makes that shell execute `printf` before the operation later fails. The same pattern also reaches `git diff` at `src/index.js:127` and `git clone` with `remoteUrl` at `src/index.js:225`.

**Impact:** This crosses the library consumer's input trust boundary and gives the input provider arbitrary code execution as the process user. Per the review policy, cross-boundary code execution has high severity and persists until the host is remediated.

**Fix:** Execute Git with an executable plus argument array through `spawn` or `execFile` with no shell, and write `git diff` output using Node rather than shell redirection. Pass tag, URL, and path values as individual arguments (and use `--` for paths); do not attempt shell escaping.

summary: Reviewed the added conversion entry point and traced both PhantomJS strategies. The change activates a local-file access bypass in the existing rendering pipeline; I recorded one high-severity finding. Overall, this PR is not safe to merge until the local-resource policy distinguishes trusted generated files from untrusted navigation targets.

findings.title: Untrusted HTML can render local files while local access is disabled
findings.body:
Untrusted HTML can redirect PhantomJS to an absolute local path such as `/etc/hostname`. `conversion()` writes that HTML, dispatches it to PhantomJS, and returns the rendered PDF to the caller even when `allowLocalFilesAccess` is omitted or false.

**Preconditions:** The application converts HTML supplied by a less-trusted caller, as this package is designed to do.

**Evidence:** The added converter accepts caller HTML and sends it to either Phantom strategy (`lib/conversion.js:37-42`, `lib/conversion.js:58-71`). JavaScript is enabled unless explicitly disabled (`lib/scripts/conversionScriptPart.js:8`), so input such as `<script>location='/etc/hostname'</script>` makes PhantomJS request a bare absolute filesystem path. The only local-file guard aborts URLs that literally begin `file:///` (`lib/scripts/conversionScriptPart.js:18-28`), so this request bypasses it when `allowLocalFilesAccess` is false. PhantomJS renders the resulting document (`lib/scripts/conversionScriptPart.js:176-177`), and both strategies return its output as a stream (`lib/serverStrategy.js:64-68`; `lib/dedicatedProcessStrategy.js:69-73`). This also violates the documented false-by-default local-file setting (`README.md:80`).

**Impact:** A caller who may submit HTML can obtain contents of files readable by the conversion process. This crosses the caller/service trust boundary and disclosure cannot be recalled, so severity is high under the review policy.

**Fix:** When local access is disabled, permit only `http:` and `https:` resource URLs; retain a separately trusted exception for the converter's own generated HTML file. Add a regression test for a script redirect to an absolute path without a URI scheme.

summary:
Reviewed the new command runner and its callers. I recorded three low-severity findings covering child-process startup errors, output-buffer limits in custom diffs, and UTF-8 path corruption across stream chunks.

`npm test` ran 51 tests successfully; two acceptance tests failed because `vimdiff` is unavailable in the environment, not because of this change. The worktree is clean.

findings.title: Git startup failures terminate the caller process
findings.body:
`runWithSpawn()` has no listener for spawn failures. If Git cannot start, Node emits an unhandled `error` event and terminates the process instead of rejecting the Promise, so the callers' `try`/`catch` cannot report the failure.

**Preconditions:** Git is unavailable, or a caller supplies an invalid `cwd`.

**Evidence:** `src/run.js:23-38` starts the child and registers only `stdout`, `stderr`, and `close` handlers; its sole rejection path is the nonzero `close` handler. `src/index.js:32-44` accepts `cwd`, then calls `isGitClean({ cwd })` inside a `try`/`catch` at `src/index.js:199-203`. That reaches `runWithSpawn('git', ..., options)` through `src/git-status.js:5-10`. With `cwd: '/definitely/not/a/directory'`, `spawn` emits `error: spawn git ENOENT`; without an error listener, Node exits before the Promise rejects.

**Impact:** A configuration error terminates the CLI or embedding Node process rather than returning its documented async error. This has contained, recoverable availability impact, so it is low severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** Attach an `error` listener that rejects exactly once, and guard the later `close` handler from resolving or rejecting again.

findings.title: Verbose custom-diff commands fail at exec's output limit
findings.body:
The shell runner buffers all command output using `exec()`'s default `maxBuffer`. A successful custom-diff command that writes more than the Node default (200 KiB on the project's minimum Node version, 1 MiB on current Node) is rejected with `ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDIO_MAXBUFFER` solely because of its log output.

**Evidence:** `src/run.js:8-12` promisifies `exec` without setting `maxBuffer`. The supported custom-diff path passes user commands to that runner with only `cwd` in `src/create-custom-remote.js:24-27,38-40`; it is exposed by `src/index.js:209-220` and CLI options at `bin/git-diff-apply.js:29-37`. A `startCommand` that writes 1,100,000 bytes to stdout fails on current Node with `ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDIO_MAXBUFFER` even when it exits zero. `src/git-remove-all.js:7-13` already uses the streaming runner specifically because `git ls-files` can produce large output, but that does not cover custom commands.

**Impact:** Ordinary verbose setup or build commands cannot create a custom diff, despite completing successfully. The failure is confined to that invocation and can be retried with quieter output, so it is low severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** Stream custom-command output, or expose and set a suitable `maxBuffer` for this path rather than relying on `exec`'s small default.

findings.title: Chunked Git output corrupts non-ASCII file paths
findings.body:
`runWithSpawn()` decodes every stdout buffer separately. A UTF-8 character split at a stream boundary becomes replacement characters; `gitRemoveAll()` then uses the corrupted name to remove and stage files.

**Preconditions:** A repository has enough tracked non-ASCII paths for `git ls-files` to split a UTF-8 sequence across output chunks, and `core.quotePath=false` so Git emits the names directly.

**Evidence:** `src/run.js:18,24-26` initializes `stdout` as a string and appends each Buffer, which decodes each chunk independently. `src/git-remove-all.js:11-15` splits that result into paths, then removes and stages each at `src/git-remove-all.js:50-52,61`. With 1,000 tracked paths containing repeated `é`, `git ls-files` emitted chunks of 65,536 bytes whose boundary split `é` as `c3 | a9`. The returned list contained U+FFFD, and `gitRemoveAll()` failed with `fatal: pathspec '...��...' did not match any files` after removing 189 worktree files but staging only 152 deletions.

**Impact:** Reset and custom-diff operations fail on valid repositories and leave a partial worktree change until the caller recovers it. The impact is contained and recoverable with Git reset, so it is low severity under the review policy.

**Fix:** Accumulate Buffers and decode once after close (or use a stateful decoder). For Git paths, request and parse NUL-delimited `git ls-files -z` output so names are not display-quoted or newline-delimited.

summary:
Reviewed the full `index.js` addition and its Markdown, PhantomJS, stream, and temporary-file paths. The PR correctly removes the unsafe default that enabled raw HTML rendering, but I recorded three issues affecting UTF-8 stream input, temporary-file cleanup in long-lived processes, and stale Remarkable option documentation.  

`npm test` passes: 37 tests passed.

findings.title: Chunked UTF-8 Markdown is corrupted during PDF conversion
findings.body:
Markdown received as normal `Buffer` chunks can split a UTF-8 character. The transform converts each chunk independently with `md += chunk`, so Node replaces the incomplete bytes before the next chunk arrives. The rendered HTML, and therefore the PDF, contain replacement characters instead of the original text. **Preconditions:** Input arrives in more than one Buffer chunk across a multibyte UTF-8 character. This is possible through the documented `fs.createReadStream(...).pipe(markdownpdf())` API and `.from(path, { highWaterMark })`. **Evidence:** `index.js:35-39` appends each Buffer by implicit string conversion; `index.js:77` renders that already-corrupted string. With a file containing `# A😀B\n` and `highWaterMark: 4`, the chunks are `23 20 41 f0`, `9f 98 80 42`, and `0a`. The conversion emits `

A����B

` and the generated PDF extracts as `A����B`. `.from(path, opts)` forwards its options to `fs.createReadStream`, and the README documents direct ReadStream input at `README.md:44-46`. **Impact:** One conversion produces permanently incorrect document content until the user regenerates it from the source. This is contained and recoverable, so severity is low under the review policy. **Fix:** Decode the input as one UTF-8 stream, such as by calling `inputStream.setEncoding('utf8')` before it is consumed or using `StringDecoder` in the transform, so incomplete sequences carry over to the next chunk.

findings.title: The Remarkable default documented for PDF conversion is no longer true
findings.body: The documented default for Remarkable no longer matches the code. Users who rely on the stated default will expect embedded HTML to be rendered, but the new default sends no `html` setting to Remarkable and the default preset escapes HTML instead. **Evidence:** `README.md:131-135` states the default is `{ html: true, breaks: true }`. The changed initialization only supplies `{ breaks: true }` at `index.js:28` and selects the `default` preset at `index.js:29`; Remarkable's default preset has `html: false`. Thus a default conversion of `x` renders the tag as text rather than bold HTML. **Impact:** Callers following the API documentation can silently receive PDFs with escaped markup. The output is limited to the conversion and can be regenerated after a configuration or documentation correction, so severity is low under the review policy. **Fix:** Change the documented default to `{ breaks: true }` and state that callers needing raw HTML must explicitly set `remarkable.html: true`.

findings.title: PDF conversions retain temporary files until process exit
findings.body:
Each conversion leaves its temporary HTML and PDF files on disk until the Node process exits. A long-lived process that performs conversions therefore consumes temp-directory space and inodes without bound; an endpoint that lets clients request PDFs can be exhausted by repeated ordinary requests.

**Preconditions:** The process remains running while it performs multiple conversions.

**Evidence:** `index.js:89-96` creates both files but discards the `tmp.file` cleanup callbacks, and `index.js:117-122` reads the PDF without removing either path after the read completes. `tmp.setGracefulCleanup()` at `index.js:12` only cleans the module's queued files at process exit. With `tmp@0.0.33`, three successful `.from.string(...).to.string(...)` conversions in one process left 12 files in `TMPDIR` (the wrapper creates one unused pair and the helper creates the conversion pair); all were removed only after process exit.

**Impact:** In a long-lived PDF service, normal requests can cause a broad availability failure once the shared temporary filesystem is exhausted. Restarting the process removes the files, so the failure is recoverable. This is medium under the review policy.

**Fix:** Keep the cleanup callbacks returned by `tmp.file` and invoke them after the PDF stream has finished, and on every error path. Avoid creating the unused wrapper instance as well, or ensure its files are cleaned immediately.

summary: Reviewed the full added `bl.js` implementation and its stream, buffer, copy, and search paths. I recorded three findings for API and stream behavior defects in the new module. `npm test` passes: 753 tests passed.

findings.title: BufferList.end drops Writable completion arguments
findings.body:
`BufferList` is a `Duplex`, but its `end` override drops Writable's `encoding` and completion-callback arguments. For example, `bl.end('61', 'hex', cb)` stores the UTF-8 bytes `36 31`, never calls `cb`, and returns `undefined`; a normal Writable stores byte `61`, invokes `cb` after finish, and returns itself. Code that uses the common `end(chunk, callback)` form can therefore wait forever for cleanup, while binary callers corrupt the final chunk.

**Evidence:** `BufferList.prototype.end` accepts only `chunk` and calls the parent with only that argument at `bl.js:109-110`. The inherited writable implementation accepts `end(chunk[, encoding][, callback])`; `BufferList` inherits from that Duplex at `bl.js:2,32-36`. The stored bytes come from `_write` at `bl.js:91-96`. Reproduced with the declared `readable-stream`: `new BufferList().end('61', 'hex', cb)` yields `3631`, leaves `cb` uncalled, and does not return the list.

**Impact:** This affects one caller's final write or completion handling and is recoverable by retrying with `write()`/`end()`, so it is low severity under the contained/recoverable policy.

**Fix:** Preserve Writable's full signature: accept `chunk, encoding, cb`, forward all three to `DuplexStream.prototype.end`, and return its result while retaining the collection callback behavior.

findings.title: Self-appending a BufferList blocks the process
findings.body:
Appending a nonempty list to itself never returns. A consumer can call the documented `b.append(b)` API with a normal `BufferList`, which synchronously consumes CPU and keeps adding the same buffers until the process is killed for memory use.

**Preconditions:** The list contains at least one buffer.

**Evidence:** The `BufferList` branch loops while `i < buf._bufs.length` at `bl.js:68-71`. When `buf === this`, each iteration calls `append` on an existing Buffer (`bl.js:71`), and `_appendBuffer` pushes it onto that same `_bufs` array at `bl.js:85-87`. The length therefore grows with `i`, so the loop condition remains true. Reproduced with `const b = new BufferList(Buffer.from('x')); b.append(b)`; it did not return before a one-second timeout.

**Impact:** A call on one process can block its event loop and exhaust its memory, but it requires code holding the list instance and a restart recovers the process. Under the contained/recoverable policy, with the trusted-caller discount, this is info severity.

**Fix:** Snapshot the source buffers before appending, or special-case `buf === this`, so iteration is bounded by the original source length.

findings.title: An empty BufferList ends output before later writes
findings.body:
Piping or adding a data listener to an empty, still-writable `BufferList` ends its readable side before later writes arrive. A normal Duplex source can be connected before its producer writes; here the destination finishes and silently misses every subsequent chunk even though `bl.write()` retains them in the list.

**Evidence:** `_read` calls `push(null)` whenever the current list length is zero at `bl.js:99-102`; `push(null)` is permanent readable EOF. Nothing checks whether the writable side has ended. `_write` still accepts and appends later chunks at `bl.js:91-96`. Reproduced by attaching a `data` listener to `new BufferList()`, writing `'later'` on `setImmediate`, and observing only `end` while `bl.toString()` is `'later'`. The README presents the object as a `DuplexStream` that can pipe out at `README.md:71-84`.

**Impact:** A caller that connects its pipeline before receiving data loses the data for that one operation; retrying with a new stream recovers it. This is low severity under the contained/recoverable policy.

**Fix:** Do not push `null` merely because the list is temporarily empty. Signal readable EOF only after the writable side ends, and arrange for later writes to satisfy pending reads.

summary:
Reviewed the added `bl.js` implementation and its stream, buffer-copy, indexing, and numeric-read paths. Recorded one high-severity finding: negative `consume()` values corrupt the logical length and let later slices expose uninitialized process memory.

The PR matches vulnerable `bl` 3.0.0 behavior; the available fixed variant adds the missing input normalization and copy-length safeguard. `npm test` passes all 753 tests, but the suite does not cover the negative-consumption disclosure path.

findings.title: Negative consumption can disclose uninitialized process memory
findings.body:
A caller that can supply a consumption count can make `slice()` return bytes that were never stored in the list. For example, after `new BufferList(Buffer.from('abcd')).consume(-2)`, the retained buffer is `cd` but `length` becomes 6; `slice(0, 5)` returns a five-byte buffer whose final three bytes come from `Buffer.allocUnsafe()`.

**Preconditions:** An application passes an attacker-controlled value to the public `consume()` API and returns or otherwise exposes a derived `slice()`/`toString()` result.

**Evidence:** The negative count takes the partial-consumption branch: `Buffer.slice(-2)` retains only the last two bytes while `this.length -= -2` raises the logical length (`bl.js:234-243`). `slice()` delegates to `copy()` (`bl.js:128-134`), which trusts the inflated length, allocates `Buffer.allocUnsafe(len)` (`bl.js:137-151`, `bl.js:180-181`), copies only the physical buffers, and returns the whole allocation without truncation (`bl.js:183-200`). Reproduced on Node 24.18.0: the tail of the returned five-byte buffer was `9ff101`, not list data; `--zero-fill-buffers` changed that tail to zeros. `toString()` and numeric readers expose the same sink through `slice()` (`bl.js:230-232`, `bl.js:368-375`).

**Impact:** This can disclose stale process-memory bytes to an untrusted caller. Per the review severity policy, the leak crosses a trust boundary and cannot be revoked after disclosure, so it is high severity.

**Fix:** Normalize `bytes` with `Math.trunc()` and leave the list unchanged for `NaN` and non-positive values. Also make the cross-buffer copy path return only the initialized prefix as a defense-in-depth check when logical and physical lengths differ.

summary: Reviewed the full 520-line tooltip source addition and its tooltip/popover, packaging, and build paths. The added source contains the CVE mitigation, but the shipped browser bundles remain stale; I recorded one high-severity finding. No other newly introduced issues were confirmed.

findings.title: Browser bundles retain the tooltip attribute XSS path
findings.body: The security fix is available only to consumers that load `js/tooltip.js`; the advertised browser bundles still parse attacker-controlled `data-container` and `data-viewport` values as HTML. For example, an application that bulk-initializes attacker-influenced `[data-toggle="tooltip"]` markup can show a tooltip with `data-container=""`. The stale bundle passes that value directly to jQuery's `appendTo`, which constructs the image and runs its handler in the application's origin. **Preconditions:** An attacker can control attributes on an element the application initializes as a tooltip. **Evidence:** Element data attributes are merged into tooltip options at `js/tooltip.js:86-96`. The new source safely treats `container` as a document selector at `js/tooltip.js:207`, but the unchanged production bundle still calls `$tip.appendTo(this.options.container)` at `dist/js/bootstrap.js:1476`; its viewport initialization also directly invokes `$()` at `dist/js/bootstrap.js:1323`. The minified bundle retains the same logic. Browser examples and documentation load `dist/js/bootstrap(.min).js` (`docs/_includes/footer.html:27-29`), and Bower publishes `dist/js/bootstrap.js` as its main artifact (`bower.json:17-20`). **Impact:** This is same-origin script execution for users of the normal browser distribution. It crosses the application's trust boundary and is recoverable by replacing the bundle, so it is **high** under the review policy. **Fix:** Regenerate and commit `dist/js/bootstrap.js` and `dist/js/bootstrap.min.js` from the new source (and verify both use document-scoped selector lookup for `container` and `viewport`).

summary: Reviewed the full added notification module and traced its platform and custom-command paths. I validated the shell execution behavior and callback handling with harmless notifier shims, and recorded four findings. The PR introduces a high-impact command-injection path plus several contained notification-delivery regressions.

findings.title: Untrusted notification content executes shell commands
findings.body:
An application that forwards untrusted event text to `growl()` lets that text run as shell code. On Linux with a harmless `notify-send` shim first on `PATH`, passing `$(touch /tmp/oz-growl-test/marker)delivered` as `msg` created the marker; the shim received only `delivered`.

**Preconditions:** The application passes attacker-controlled notification content or an affected option to this API.

**Evidence:** `quote` is `JSON.stringify` at `lib/growl.js:12`, so the Linux path adds a shell double-quoted message at `lib/growl.js:262-269`. Double quotes do not prevent command substitution. The module then joins all arguments into one string and gives it to `child_process.exec` at `lib/growl.js:289`, which invokes a shell. Other platform branches also combine message and option values into that same command string.

**Impact:** An untrusted notification value crosses into a shell and can execute arbitrary commands as the Node process user. Per the review severity policy, this crosses a trust boundary and the command can make permanent changes, so severity is high.

**Fix:** Do not construct a shell command. Invoke the selected executable with `child_process.spawn` or `execFile` and pass each value as a separate argument; retain the callback/error behavior.

findings.title: A custom notifier redirects later notifications
findings.body:
A custom notifier selected for one call becomes the notifier for every later call in the process. For example, with harmless platform and custom shims, an `exec` call followed by `growl('second')` invoked the custom shim twice (`custom:first`, `custom:second`); the platform notifier was never called. The repository’s own sequence does this: its custom calls at `test.js:22-29` precede a normal URL notification at `test.js:31`.

**Evidence:** `cmd` is module state (`lib/growl.js:13`) initialized once for the platform (`lib/growl.js:25-118`). Any `options.exec` overwrites it at `lib/growl.js:170-175`. A following call without `exec` does not restore the platform configuration and formats the message using the `Custom` branch at `lib/growl.js:276-285` before executing it at `lib/growl.js:289`. The documented `exec` option describes a command for that invocation, not a global backend change (`Readme.md:77-82`).

**Impact:** One notification can route later, unrelated notifications to the wrong executable, losing expected UI and options such as URLs. The result is contained to this process and recoverable by restart, so the review policy rates it low.

**Fix:** Keep the detected platform descriptor immutable and select a local custom descriptor only for the call that supplies `options.exec`.

findings.title: Priority options fail or crash notification delivery
findings.body:
Supplying documented priority options either drops the priority, makes an invalid command, or throws before a notification is sent. The test example uses `{ priority: 2 }` at `test.js:9`, but the Darwin and Windows ranges hold numbers while the implementation compares the string form, so `2` never matches. On Linux `notify-send`, a valid string priority produces `notify-send [object Object] low "message"` rather than `notify-send -u low "message"`. On Linux-Growl and custom backends, any truthy priority throws because the descriptor has no `priority` object.

**Evidence:** The numeric ranges are at `lib/growl.js:48-62` and `lib/growl.js:105-115`; Linux-Growl has no priority descriptor at `lib/growl.js:67-78`; Linux `notify-send` defines its flag as `priority.cmd` at `lib/growl.js:87-94`; and Custom has none at `lib/growl.js:170-175`. The common code stringifies the option, unconditionally dereferences `cmd.priority.range`, and pushes the descriptor object rather than `cmd.priority.cmd` at `lib/growl.js:212-217`.

**Impact:** A normal option can lose or prevent a notification, and unsupported-backend calls can synchronously interrupt the caller. Each failure is contained to the request and recoverable, so the review policy rates it low.

**Fix:** Guard missing priority support, compare values without changing their type (and allow zero if supported), and append `cmd.priority.cmd` with the supplied value.

findings.title: The documented two-argument callback is discarded
findings.body:
The documented `growl(message, callback)` form never invokes the callback. A harmless `notify-send` shim confirmed that `growl('message', function () { ... })` completes without running that function.

**Evidence:** The API example explicitly documents the two-argument form at `lib/growl.js:153-155`. However, `growl()` treats its second argument only as an options object and sets `fn` to a no-op when the third argument is absent (`lib/growl.js:164-168`). It then supplies that no-op to `exec` at `lib/growl.js:289`.

**Impact:** Callers using the documented API cannot observe notification success or errors. The failure is contained to one notification and recoverable, so the review policy rates it low.

**Fix:** When `typeof options === 'function'`, assign it to `fn` and replace `options` with an empty object before option processing.

summary: Reviewed the new `lib/growl.js` implementation and its public API paths across supported backends. The switch from shell execution to `spawn()` removes the previously reported command-injection path; I marked that existing finding fixed. I recorded two low-severity regressions in the interim implementation: documented custom notifier commands no longer execute, and notifier launch failures can terminate the consuming process instead of reaching its callback.

findings.title: Documented custom notifier commands cannot run
findings.body:
The documented custom-notifier commands no longer execute. For example, `growl('hello', { exec: 'tmux display-message' })` calls `spawn('tmux display-message', ['hello'])`, which fails with `ENOENT`; the README also promises shell redirection such as `echo "%s" > messages.log`, but this revision attempts to execute that complete string as a filename.

**Evidence:** The public API documents `exec` as a shell command and gives both forms as examples in `Readme.md:77-82`. The Custom path replaces `%s` within the full command string at `lib/growl.js:276-283`. The code then makes that unparsed string the executable and calls `spawn(cmd_to_exec, args)` at `lib/growl.js:286-288`. `spawn()` does not split command strings or interpret shell syntax.

**Impact:** Callers cannot use the documented custom notification integration, including commands with normal arguments. The failure affects one notification and is recoverable after correcting the library, so the review policy rates it low.

**Fix:** Parse the documented custom-command form into an executable and argument vector before calling `spawn`, while preserving message substitution as one argument. Do not restore shell execution for untrusted message text.

findings.title: Notifier launch failures terminate the caller process
findings.body:
After the switch to `spawn`, normal notifier completion and launch errors are never delivered to the supplied callback. A successful `growl('x', { exec: '/bin/true' }, cb)` leaves `cb` uncalled; a missing executable emits an unhandled `ENOENT` error and terminates the host process even when a callback was supplied.

**Evidence:** The documented callback form is used by the repository's custom-exec examples (`test.js:22-29`) and notification callback example (`Readme.md:55-57`). The function receives `fn` at `lib/growl.js:163-167`, but the only invocation is the unsupported-platform path at `lib/growl.js:177-178`. The result of `spawn(cmd_to_exec, args)` is discarded at `lib/growl.js:286-288`, so no `close` handler calls `fn` and no `error` handler consumes or forwards launch errors.

**Impact:** A missing notifier binary can crash any consuming Node process rather than reporting a recoverable delivery error; successful callers also cannot observe completion. This needs a missing executable or custom notifier setting, so the review policy rates it low.

**Fix:** Retain the child process, forward its `error` event to `fn`, and call `fn` on close with the documented result. Keep the no-op default callback so launch errors are always observed.

summary:
Recorded two findings:

- **Medium:** The package entry point imports a helper that is not shipped (`angular-http-server.js:12`), so both the CLI and module fail with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`.
- **Low:** `--https --open` launches the browser with `http://` although the server is listening with TLS (`angular-http-server.js:25-33`, `41-44`).

The PR adds the server entry point and moves file-path handling into a new helper import, but omits that helper and its tests from the package. I also verified the documented HTTPS/open alias mismatch.

findings.title: The package entry point imports a helper that is not shipped
findings.body:
Every normal package entry point terminates before the server starts. The new executable unconditionally imports a project-relative helper that this PR does not add, so installing the declared dependencies cannot supply it.

**Evidence:** `angular-http-server.js:12` calls `require('./lib/get-file-path-from-url')`, but `git ls-tree -r 068a848` contains no `lib/` path and `package.json:37-41` declares only third-party dependencies. Both the package `main` and the installed CLI point to this file (`package.json:7`, `package.json:34-36`). After a normal production dependency install, `node angular-http-server.js --path example` exits with `Error: Cannot find module './lib/get-file-path-from-url'` before startup.

**Impact:** All users of the CLI and package module are unable to use the server. This affects every installation but is recoverable by publishing the missing source file, so the impact is medium under the reach × persistence policy.

**Fix:** Add and package `lib/get-file-path-from-url.js` with this change (and its tests), or replace the import with an implementation included in the package.

findings.title: `--https --open` launches the browser with the wrong scheme
findings.body:
The documented `--https --open` combination starts a TLS listener but opens a plaintext HTTP URL, so the browser cannot load the server. `--ssl --open` works, making this an alias-specific regression.

**Evidence:** The README documents `--open` and both `--https` and `--ssl` (`README.md:27-36`). The server treats either HTTPS flag as TLS (`angular-http-server.js:25-33`), but `start()` chooses `https://` for `opn()` only when `argv.ssl` is set (`angular-http-server.js:41-44`). Thus `angular-http-server --https --open` opens `http://localhost:8080` although only an HTTPS server is listening there.

**Impact:** Users selecting the documented `--https` spelling must manually correct the URL or use the other alias. The failure is recoverable and confined to this optional flag combination, so it is low severity under the reach × persistence policy.

**Fix:** Compute one HTTPS boolean from `argv.ssl || argv.https` and use it for both listener selection and the URL passed to `opn()`.

Reviewed the added conversion entry point and its immediate PhantomJS strategy paths. I recorded three findings: local-file disclosure, temporary-ID path traversal, and shared factory configuration state. `npm test` passes (28 tests). No material changed surface remains unreviewed; I did not extend review into unrelated dependencies or external application wrappers.

findings.title: Untrusted URLs can render local files while local access is disabled
findings.body:
A caller who controls a conversion URL can receive a PDF of any file readable by the PhantomJS process even when `allowLocalFilesAccess` is left false. For example, `conversion({ url: 'file:///etc/passwd' }, cb)` retains the supplied URL and sends it to the default Phantom server.

**Evidence:** `convert` preserves a nonempty `opt.url` and dispatches it unchanged at `lib/conversion.js:63-71`; the server forwards it at `lib/serverStrategy.js:40-44`. The Phantom request hook returns early for any request prefixed by `body.url` before it checks and aborts `file:///` requests at `lib/scripts/conversionScriptPart.js:18-27`. Thus the primary `page.open(body.url)` at `lib/scripts/conversionScriptPart.js:85` opens the local file, and the rendered PDF is returned to the caller at `lib/serverStrategy.js:64-67`. The documented default says local files require `allowLocalFilesAccess: true` (`README.md:76-80`).

**Impact:** An untrusted URL crosses the conversion service boundary and discloses locally readable data. The resulting disclosure is permanent, so this is high severity under the review reach × persistence policy.

**Fix:** Apply the `file:///` restriction to the primary navigation as well as subresources. Do not exempt `body.url` from the local-file check unless `allowLocalFilesAccess` is true.

findings.title: Caller-controlled temporary IDs write outside the configured directory
findings.body:
An application that forwards conversion options from an untrusted request lets the caller write files outside the configured temporary directory. A `tmpId` such as `../public/owned-` is concatenated into each temporary filename; Node normalizes the `..` rather than keeping it under `tmpDir`.

**Preconditions:** The application lets an untrusted caller set `tmpId`.

**Evidence:** `convert` takes `opt.tmpId` without validation at `lib/conversion.js:36-56`. `writeHtmlFile` uses it in `path.resolve(path.join(options.tmpDir, ...))` and immediately writes attacker HTML at `lib/conversion.js:8-14`; this happens before strategy selection at `lib/conversion.js:58-73`. The same ID chooses the Phantom render output at `lib/conversion.js:63-64`, and both strategies return a stream from that path (`lib/serverStrategy.js:64-67`, `lib/dedicatedProcessStrategy.js:69-73`). For `tmpDir: '/srv/app/tmp'`, `tmpId: '../public/owned-'` makes the first write `/srv/app/public/owned-html.html`.

**Impact:** This crosses the request boundary and creates or truncates attacker-controlled HTML/PDF-named files wherever the conversion process has write permission, outside the administrator-selected temporary directory. The filename suffix and process permissions bound the effect, so this is medium severity under the review reach × persistence policy.

**Fix:** Ignore caller-provided temporary IDs, or validate that every resolved path remains inside a private per-conversion temporary directory.

findings.title: Factory instances overwrite each other's conversion configuration
findings.body:
Creating a second converter changes the configuration used by every converter, including conversions already waiting on file I/O. The factory returns one module-scoped `convert` function and overwrites one module-scoped `options` object on each call. **Evidence:** `options` is module-scoped at `lib/conversion.js:7`, every factory call replaces it at `lib/conversion.js:81-87`, and each call returns the same `convert` function at `lib/conversion.js:36,96`. Conversion writes files asynchronously at `lib/conversion.js:8-34`; after those callbacks it reads the current global configuration for its output and strategy at `lib/conversion.js:64-73`. Thus `a = factory({strategy: 'phantom-server'}); a('

A

', cb); factory({strategy: 'bad'});` makes A's callback report `Unsupported strategy bad` once its write completes. **Impact:** A normal process using two factory configurations can send documents through the wrong strategy, temporary directory, proxy, or timeout configuration, or fail a conversion. The effect is contained to that process and recoverable, so this is low severity under the review reach × persistence policy. **Fix:** Build and return a new closure per factory call, with its own immutable configuration, instead of reading module-global options from `convert`.

No findings.

The new helper restores the imported link-destination parser used by inline links and reference definitions (`lib/rules_inline/links.js:4`, `lib/rules_core/references.js:3`). Its control-character rejection at `lib/helpers/parse_link_destination.js:50-53` matches upstream’s security fix; generated CJS output rendered representative C0 and DEL-prefixed `javascript:` destinations as literal text rather than links.
