Reviewed PR #2’s new Markdown-to-PDF implementation.

Recorded:
- **High:** Untrusted Markdown can execute in PhantomJS and read converter-local files.
- **Low:** Conversion I/O errors can terminate the caller process instead of reaching the documented callback.

`npm test` passed: 37 tests. I also confirmed the temporary-file accumulation and split UTF-8 handling issues, but did not re-report them because matching open findings already exist for this repository.

findings.title: Untrusted Markdown can read converter-local files
findings.body:
Attacker-controlled Markdown is rendered as active HTML in the PhantomJS `file://` page. A `<script>` tag passes through Remarkable unchanged, executes during conversion, and can read files accessible to the converter process; its contents can then be placed in the generated PDF returned to the caller.

**Preconditions:** The application converts Markdown supplied by a less-trusted user or tenant.

**Evidence:** `index.js:28` enables raw HTML by default and `index.js:43-77` renders it without sanitizing it. The resulting fragment is written to the temporary input (`index.js:88-117`), then `phantom/render.js:18-22` inserts it into the document and calls `page.setContent` with a `file://` base URL. A Markdown script using synchronous XHR to read a process-readable local file executed and placed that file's marker in the produced PDF.

**Impact:** A remote Markdown author can disclose process-readable configuration, credentials, or other local files through their conversion result. Under the review policy this crosses a trust boundary and the secret disclosure is permanent, so severity is high.

**Fix:** Do not enable Remarkable's `html` option by default; use the default options with `breaks: true` only. Raw HTML should require an explicit trusted-input opt-in.

findings.title: Conversion I/O errors terminate the caller process
findings.body:
Ordinary input and temporary-file I/O failures are not forwarded to the converter output. Node emits an unhandled stream error and terminates the process instead of calling the documented `.to(..., cb)` callback.

**Evidence:** The pipeline at `index.js:125-130` has no error forwarding for the source, either preprocessor, the renderer, or the temporary HTML writer; `index.js:98-100` waits only for the writer's successful `finish`. The final PDF reader is also piped without an error handler at `index.js:117-122`. Reproducing `.from('/definitely/not/a/file.md').to.string(cb)` exits with an unhandled `ENOENT` and never calls `cb`; a valid preprocessor that calls `cb(new Error(...))` and an `ENOSPC` write to the temporary HTML path behave the same way.

**Impact:** A deleted/missing source or routine storage failure can terminate a process using the documented API rather than reporting a recoverable conversion error. This is a contained, recoverable availability failure, so severity is low under the review policy.

**Fix:** Forward errors from every source and pipeline stage, including the PDF read stream, to the returned output stream and ensure the helper callbacks receive them. Stop or clean up the remaining stages after an error.

summary:
Reviewed the added link-destination parser and traced its inline-link, image, and reference-definition callers. I recorded one confirmed high-severity finding: `fnd_8uxganu9zgkwtibt`.

A targeted build and rendering reproduction succeeded for affected control-character URLs. The full legacy test suite could not run under Node 24 because Mocha did not load the repository’s ES-module test files.

findings.title: Untrusted Markdown can bypass the JavaScript URL filter with control characters
findings.body: Untrusted Markdown can render a link whose `href` starts with a C0 control character followed by `javascript:`. Browsers strip that leading control character while resolving the URL, so clicking the rendered link executes the attacker’s script in the page that trusted the rendered Markdown. **Preconditions:** The application renders attacker-controlled Markdown for another user or privileged page. **Evidence:** The bare-destination loop stops only for space and `0x09`–`0x0d` at `lib/helpers/parse_link_destination.js:50-52`. It therefore accepts `\x01javascript:alert(1)`, stores it unchanged at `lib/helpers/parse_link_destination.js:74-79`, and passes it to `validateLink`. The validator only rejects an exact pre-colon protocol match (`lib/parser_inline.js:157-165`), so `\x01javascript` passes. Inline links consume that stored value at `lib/rules_inline/links.js:55-61`, and the renderer emits it as `href` without removing controls at `lib/rules.js:148-152`. A local build rendered `[x](\x01javascript:alert(1))` as `x`; the same helper also accepts this in reference definitions (`lib/rules_core/references.js:31-33`). **Impact:** A Markdown author crosses the content-trust boundary and gains script execution in a viewer’s origin after a normal click on rendered content. This is **high** under the reach × persistence policy: it crosses a trust boundary and remains active until the malicious Markdown is removed, a recoverable outcome. **Fix:** Reject every ASCII control character, including DEL, while scanning an unbracketed destination (for example, stop when `code < 0x20 || code === 0x7f`) before validation and rendering.

summary: Reviewed the new extension-header parser and its client/server negotiation paths. The CVE regex hardening works and the existing test suite passes, but the PR is not ready to merge due to three recorded low-severity parser and negotiation regressions.

findings.title: Multiple quoted parameters can produce an invalid handshake header
findings.body:
`NOTOKEN` has the `g` flag, so each `.test()` starts at the previous match's `lastIndex`. With two values that require quoting, the second test can skip its separator and emit an invalid unquoted value. For example, `serializeParams('x', {first: 'a b', second: 'c d'})` returns `x; first="a b"; second=c d`; `parseHeader()` then rejects that header with `SyntaxError`.

**Evidence:** `NOTOKEN` is global at `lib/parser.js:4`, and `serializeParams()` reuses it at `lib/parser.js:63-66` without resetting `lastIndex`. Client offers and server responses pass extension-supplied parameter objects through this method at `lib/websocket_extensions.js:46-51` and `lib/websocket_extensions.js:100-105`.

**Impact:** An extension that returns multiple quoted string parameters sends an invalid WebSocket extensions header and the handshake fails. This is low severity: it requires a non-default extension parameter shape and causes a recoverable connection failure.

**Fix:** Remove `g` from `NOTOKEN`, or reset `NOTOKEN.lastIndex` before every test.

findings.title: Backslashes in extension parameters are lost or make headers invalid
findings.body:
Literal backslashes in quoted parameter values are not escaped when serializing, and all backslashes are discarded when parsing. `serializeParams('x', {path: 'foo\\bar'})` produces `x; path="foo\bar"`, but parsing it yields `path: 'foobar'`. A value ending in `\` instead produces an unterminated quoted string that `parseHeader()` rejects.

**Evidence:** The quoted-string grammar permits escaped ASCII characters at `lib/parser.js:5`. Parsing removes every backslash with `replace(/\\/g, '')` at `lib/parser.js:31-34`, while serialization escapes only `"` at `lib/parser.js:63-64`. These values are sent in client offers at `lib/websocket_extensions.js:46-51`, parsed from peer offers at `lib/websocket_extensions.js:91-100`, and parsed in client responses at `lib/websocket_extensions.js:60-81`.

**Impact:** Extensions that use legal backslash-containing string parameters negotiate altered settings or fail the handshake. This is low severity because it is limited to extensions using that uncommon parameter content and is recoverable by retrying after a corrected configuration.

**Fix:** Escape `\\` before escaping quotes during serialization, and decode quoted-pairs one pair at a time so `\\\\` becomes one literal backslash rather than being removed.

findings.title: Absent prototype-named offers are negotiated as present
findings.body:
An absent offer for a registered extension named `constructor` is returned as the inherited `Object` constructor instead of `[]`. Thus a client can send `Sec-WebSocket-Extensions: unrelated` and still cause `generateResponse()` to call that extension's `createServerSession()` and return a `constructor` response, even though the client never offered it. The same normal-object index lets an incoming `__proto__` offer alter the private offer lookup prototype.

**Preconditions:** The server registers a custom extension whose token-valid name collides with an inherited property, such as `constructor`.

**Evidence:** `Offers` indexes names in `{}` at `lib/parser.js:76-78`, and `byName()` returns `this._byName[name]` without an own-property check at `lib/parser.js:95-96`. `Object.length` is `1`, so the absence check at `lib/websocket_extensions.js:97-100` does not skip an absent `constructor` offer. `Extensions.add()` accepts any string name at `lib/websocket_extensions.js:18-30`.

**Impact:** An unauthenticated handshake peer can make a specially named registered extension activate without negotiation, or cause an extension expecting an offer array to throw and reject the connection. This is low severity because it requires a non-default, trusted extension name and causes only a transient handshake failure or protocol error.

**Fix:** Use null-prototype maps for `_byName`, and have `byName()` return an entry only when it is an own property.

summary: Reviewed the full `request/util.js` addition and its XHR, Node, script, iframe, and registry consumers. The `__proto__` guard blocks the previously reachable recursive `Object.prototype` mutation path while preserving ordinary request options. No PR-specific regressions were found; syntax validation passed, while the configured Intern suite could not run because `intern-client` is not installed.

Reviewed `lib/pdfinfo.js` and traced its async/sync execution paths, argument construction, tests, and the pre-fix implementation. The change replaces shell-based `exec` calls with `execFile`, so filenames and option values are passed as argv rather than parsed by a shell; command-injection metacharacters remain literal arguments. I found no new, evidence-backed issues to report.

Reviewed PR #2 in full. The added parser restores extension-header parsing and serialization, but I recorded two issues: a high-severity regex denial of service and a low-severity header-whitespace interoperability failure. Existing parser findings from the related review were checked and not duplicated. `npm test` passes: 79 tests, 97 assertions.

findings.title: Malformed extension headers block the event loop in regex backtracking
findings.body:
A remote WebSocket peer can block the Node event loop with a short malformed `Sec-WebSocket-Extensions` header. For example, `x; y="` followed by 40 backslashes and no closing quote takes about 1.55 seconds in `Parser.parseHeader()` on Node 24; each two added backslashes roughly triples the work.

**Evidence:** `QUOTED` lets a backslash match either `\\[\x00-\x7f]` or the raw-text alternative at lib/parser.js:5. `parseHeader()` synchronously validates the complete untrusted header through the anchored `EXT_LIST.test()` at lib/parser.js:18 before it throws. With no closing quote, the regexp explores the exponentially many one- and two-character partitions of the backslash run. Server negotiation passes the client header directly to this parser at lib/websocket_extensions.js:91-95; client activation does the same for a server response at lib/websocket_extensions.js:60-62.

**Impact:** An unauthenticated network peer can repeatedly stall every request handled by the single Node event loop. This crosses a trust boundary and remains re-triggerable, so severity is high under the review policy.

**Fix:** Exclude backslashes from the raw quoted-text character class, leaving them valid only as part of a two-character escape (for example, add `\\` to that class's exclusions). Add a regression test with an unterminated backslash-heavy quoted parameter and a bounded parse time.

findings.title: Tab-separated extension parameters are rejected
findings.body:
A conforming peer that uses horizontal tab whitespace around an extension separator has its handshake rejected. For example, `Parser.parseHeader('foo;\tbar=1')` throws `SyntaxError`, even though HTTP's implied linear whitespace for the RFC 6455 extension grammar permits HTAB as well as space.

**Evidence:** The extension-list grammar only permits literal spaces around `;` and `,` at lib/parser.js:7-8, and `parseHeader()` rejects anything that does not match that grammar at lib/parser.js:18-19. Incoming client offers flow into this parser before server extension selection at lib/websocket_extensions.js:91-100; received server responses follow the same path at lib/websocket_extensions.js:60-65.

**Impact:** A standards-conforming peer can be unable to negotiate extensions. This is a recoverable interoperability failure, so severity is low under the review policy.

**Fix:** Accept HTTP linear whitespace (space or HTAB) wherever the separator grammar allows optional whitespace, and add tab-bearing request and response header tests.

summary:
Reviewed the new `SaxParser` implementation and its parser-to-editor serialization paths. I recorded one high-severity finding: malformed CDATA can escape the serialized comment wrapper and execute attacker-supplied JavaScript when untrusted content reaches the normal `editor.setContent` flow.

I also checked attribute validation, internal-element state, bogus-element handling, and downstream `DomParser` consumers. The stale internal-element state can skip schema defaults in a narrow custom-schema case, but I did not record it as a separate finding.

findings.title: Untrusted CDATA can escape its serialized comment and execute script
findings.body: An attacker can close the comment emitted for a CDATA node and inject live HTML into the editor. With `]]>`, the one-pass replacement removes ``; normal `setContent` serializes the result as `]]-->`. The first `-->` closes the comment, so the image is inserted through `innerHTML` and its `onerror` runs in the editor's origin. **Preconditions:** The application passes attacker-controlled HTML to the ordinary `editor.setContent` path. **Evidence:** `trimComments` only makes one pass at `src/core/main/ts/api/html/SaxParser.ts:59-61`, and the CDATA branch passes its output to the parser callback at `src/core/main/ts/api/html/SaxParser.ts:499-500`. The editor converts CDATA to a comment node at `src/core/main/ts/init/InitContentBody.ts:97-105`; the writer emits comment content without escaping at `src/core/main/ts/api/html/Writer.ts:138-140`. Default `setContent` parses and serializes non-raw input at `src/core/main/ts/content/SetContent.ts:81-90`, then assigns the resulting HTML to the editor body at `src/core/main/ts/content/SetContent.ts:45-47`. **Impact:** This is a high-severity cross-trust-boundary DOM XSS: content supplied by an untrusted actor runs script in the editor user's origin. It persists in the live DOM and can be re-read through raw-content paths. **Fix:** Strip comment delimiters until the string no longer changes (including delimiters exposed by an earlier replacement) before the CDATA value can be serialized into a comment.

summary: Reviewed the new `lib/pdfinfo.js` wrapper and its public async and sync execution paths. I recorded one high-severity finding: shell command construction permits arbitrary command execution through caller-controlled PDF arguments. I reproduced the issue through both public APIs; the repository test suite was not run because dependencies are not installed.

findings.title: Untrusted PDF arguments execute shell commands
findings.body:
The public filename and `add_options()` inputs are joined into a shell command and passed to `exec`/`execSync`. An application that supplies an untrusted upload name or option can therefore execute arbitrary commands with its Node process privileges.

**Evidence:** The constructor merely wraps `filename` in double quotes (`lib/pdfinfo.js:6`), so a filename such as `"; touch /tmp/pdfinfo-marker; #` forms `pdfinfo ""; touch /tmp/pdfinfo-marker; #"`. `getInfoSync()` and `getInfo()` pass the resulting joined string to shell-based `execSync` and `exec` (`lib/pdfinfo.js:26`, `lib/pdfinfo.js:36`). I reproduced marker creation through both public methods. `add_options()` also appends unescaped input to the same command (`lib/pdfinfo.js:8-18`).

**Impact:** This crosses the application trust boundary when a caller accepts a filename or options from a less-trusted user, and arbitrary commands can read or alter assets available to the process. Per the review severity policy, cross-boundary, permanent impact is high.

**Fix:** Do not construct a shell command. Pass `['pdfinfo', ...this.options.additional]` to `execFile`/`execFileSync` (or equivalent non-shell APIs), keeping each value as one argument. This fixes both filename and option injection.

summary:
**This run stopped early at the run's time limit, so its results are partial.**

Reviewed the complete added `request/util.js` surface and its XHR, script, iframe, and Node consumers. I recorded four findings: global prototype pollution from untrusted request options, plus three low-severity regressions in `frameDoc`, Node Stream bodies, and object-valued arrays.

I did not run the full Intern suite or live browser integration because dependencies were not installed and the run ended during review. The key browser and Node failure paths were traced through the relevant call sites.

findings.title: Untrusted request options pollute Object.prototype
findings.body:
A caller that passes parsed, attacker-controlled JSON as `options` to the public script request API can modify `Object.prototype` for the whole JavaScript realm. For example, `script.get('/x.js', JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"isAdmin":true}}'))` leaves `({}).isAdmin === true` before the script is attached.

**Preconditions:** Application code passes untrusted parsed JSON as request options.

**Evidence:** `script()` calls `util.deepCopy({}, options)` at `request/script.js:123-126`. `deepCopy` enumerates every key at `request/util.js:43-46`; for `__proto__` on `{}`, `target[name]` is `Object.prototype`. The object value then takes the existing-object recursion path at `request/util.js:48-58`, which writes the supplied properties to that prototype at `request/util.js:61`. This matches the upstream security fix: skip `name === '__proto__'` before copying.

**Impact:** This injects arbitrary inherited properties into every plain object in the browser realm. A remote actor who reaches an application path that forwards their JSON to request options can affect later authorization, configuration, and `for...in` logic across the application. Severity is high: the public API crosses the application's input trust boundary and the pollution persists for the realm lifetime.

**Fix:** Do not copy `__proto__` (and ideally reject other prototype-mutating keys) in `deepCopy` before reading or assigning the target property.

findings.title: Script requests cannot use the documented frameDoc option
findings.body:
The documented `frameDoc` option cannot be used. Passing an iframe `Document` through `script.get()` turns it into a plain object before the script transport attaches its element.

**Evidence:** `script()` clones caller options with `util.deepCopy({}, options)` at `request/script.js:123-126`. `frameDoc` is documented as a `Document` at `request/script.js:208-211`, but `shouldDeepCopy` excludes only FormData, Element, Blob, and ArrayBuffer (`request/util.js:34-40`). A Document is not an Element, so `deepCopy` creates `{}` for it at `request/util.js:48-58`. The truthy plain object reaches `attach`, where it replaces the fallback document and `createElement` is called on it (`request/script.js:29-31`). It is not a Document and the request fails.

**Impact:** Any supported script request targeted at a child iframe fails instead of attaching the script. This is a contained, recoverable request failure, so severity is low.

**Fix:** Preserve Document values when copying request options (more generally, do not recursively clone DOM nodes/documents).

findings.title: Node requests lose their documented Stream body during option copying
findings.body:
The documented Node `Stream` request body is cloned into a plain object before dispatch, so `node.post(url, { data: stream })` calls `pipe` on a non-Stream (or has no `pipe` method) rather than on the supplied readable stream.

**Evidence:** `node()` identifies the original value as a Stream but then replaces options with `util.deepCreate(defaultOptions, options)` at `request/node.js:22-25`. Stream objects are not excluded by `shouldDeepCopy` (`request/util.js:34-40`), and `deepCopy` creates a new `{}` for object properties whose default is not an object (`request/util.js:48-58`). The eventual send path invokes `options.data.pipe(req)` at `request/node.js:112-117`. The API documents `data: String|Object|Stream` at `request/node.js:142-145`.

**Impact:** A documented streaming request body fails or is sent from an invalid cloned object. The failure affects one caller request and is recoverable, so severity is low.

**Fix:** Preserve Stream instances while merging options, or restore the original stream after `deepCreate` before dispatch.

findings.title: Request option arrays corrupt null and other object-valued members
findings.body:
Object-valued array members are copied as generic objects, bypassing the type handling used for normal option properties. A normal query such as `{ multi: [null, "ok"] }` is changed to `{ multi: [{}, "ok"] }`, so it serializes as `multi=%5Bobject%20Object%5D&multi=ok` rather than `multi=null&multi=ok`.

**Evidence:** `deepCopyArray` sends every `typeof ... === 'object'` value, including `null`, to `deepCopy({}, value)` (`request/util.js:68-76`). `deepCopy` has special handling for Date and nested arrays only outside this array path (`request/util.js:48-58`). XHR merges public options through this helper (`request/xhr.js:199-205`) and `parseArgs` serializes object queries with `ioQuery.objectToQuery` (`request/util.js:175-188`). The encoder explicitly supports array values and emits each member (`io-query.js:19-29,37-43`).

**Impact:** Requests with supported array-valued query or object-data members can send incorrect values. This is a contained, recoverable request-data error, so severity is low.

**Fix:** Have `deepCopyArray` apply the same null, array, Date, and opaque-object rules as `deepCopy`, preserving values that must not be recursively cloned.

Reviewed the full `SaxParser.ts` addition and recorded five findings: one high-severity form-action script URL bypass and four low-severity parsing, validation, and performance defects. The CDATA loop correctly fixes the intended CVE behavior, but its fixed-point implementation has quadratic runtime. Browser tests were not run because dependencies are not installed; the worktree remains clean.

findings.title: CDATA delimiter cleanup blocks the editor for quadratic time
findings.body:
`trimComments` blocks synchronously for quadratic time on one accepted CDATA token. For `n`, parse `<![CDATA[` + `<`.repeat(n) + `-->` + `!--`.repeat(n) + `]]>`. The first replacement removes `-->`; each later pass removes exactly one newly adjacent `<!--`, so the loop makes `n + 1` full-string replacements over Θ(n)-sized strings. An investigator measured actual `SaxParser.parse` at about 5.7, 17.8, 59.1, and 218 ms for n=1,000, 2,000, 4,000, and 8,000, respectively.

**Evidence:** The token pattern accepts arbitrary CDATA payload until `]]>` at `src/core/main/ts/api/html/SaxParser.ts:275-282`; the CDATA branch calls `trimComments` synchronously at `src/core/main/ts/api/html/SaxParser.ts:503-504`. That helper repeats a global search and replacement until no delimiter remains at `src/core/main/ts/api/html/SaxParser.ts:59-64`. Normal content processing reaches this parser through `DomParser` and `SetContent` (`src/core/main/ts/api/html/DomParser.ts:425-435,633-635`; `src/core/main/ts/content/SetContent.ts:81-86`). The previous candidate used one replacement only; this PR adds the loop.

**Impact:** An actor who can supply HTML that TinyMCE parses, including pasted or application-provided content, can freeze one recipient's browser main thread. This is **low** severity: the impact is contained to the parsing editor and clears when the parse completes or the page is closed, although it can be retriggered.

**Fix:** Preserve fixed-point delimiter removal, but implement it with an overlap-aware linear-time scanner or worklist rather than rescanning and reallocating the full payload for every newly exposed delimiter.

findings.title: A constructor element crashes HTML parsing
findings.body:
An ordinary `<constructor>` tag aborts HTML parsing. `Schema` stores special-element end-tag regexps in a normal `{}` object, so `specialElements['constructor']` resolves to the inherited `Object` constructor rather than to a `RegExp`. The parser then calls its nonexistent `exec` method.

**Evidence:** Start-tag parsing accepts and lowercases `constructor` at `src/core/main/ts/api/html/SaxParser.ts:275-282,311-325`. `Schema` creates `specialElements` with `{}` and adds regexps only for configured own keys at `src/core/main/ts/api/html/Schema.ts:392,449-451`. `SaxParser` unconditionally treats every truthy lookup as an end-tag regexp and calls `.exec()` at `src/core/main/ts/api/html/SaxParser.ts:458-461`. Thus `SaxParser(...).parse('<constructor>')` reaches `Object.exec` and throws `TypeError: endRegExp.exec is not a function`. `DomParser` uses this parser for normal content parsing (`src/core/main/ts/api/html/DomParser.ts:425-435,633-635`).

**Impact:** Any supplied content containing this valid-looking custom-element name can stop parsing for the current editor/content operation. This is **low** severity because it affects one parsing operation and is recoverable by removing the tag or reloading.

**Fix:** Only enter the special-element branch for own map entries (for example, `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(specialElements, value)`), or construct the special-element map with a null prototype.

findings.title: Sanitization retains JavaScript form actions
findings.body:
The sanitizer retains `javascript:` form actions even though script URLs are disabled by default. A submitted retained form therefore executes its action in the editor document's browsing context. For example, normal content parsing preserves `<form action="javascript:alert(document.domain)"><input type="submit"></form>`; activating the submit control triggers the URL.

**Evidence:** The default schema permits `form[action]` and submit-capable inputs (`src/core/main/ts/api/html/Schema.ts:242-247`). Attribute names are normalized and accepted by schema validation at `src/core/main/ts/api/html/SaxParser.ts:202-238`, but the protocol filter's map includes `formaction` and omits `action` at `src/core/main/ts/api/html/SaxParser.ts:172-173,240-259`. The attribute is thus appended unchanged at `src/core/main/ts/api/html/SaxParser.ts:266-271`. `DomParser` installs it on the parsed node and passes normal content through this parser (`src/core/main/ts/api/html/DomParser.ts:425-435,474-514,633-635`); the writer serializes retained attributes without another protocol check (`src/core/main/ts/api/html/Writer.ts:58-71`). Existing tests specifically expect `javascript:` `formaction` to be removed (`src/core/test/ts/browser/html/SaxParserTest.ts:711-744`).

**Impact:** An attacker whose HTML is loaded into an editor can execute JavaScript when a victim submits the injected form, despite the default script-URL restriction. This crosses the content-author/editor-user trust boundary and the unsafe content may persist if saved, so the severity is **high**.

**Fix:** Add `action` to `filteredUrlAttrs` so form actions receive the same scheme validation as `formaction`.

findings.title: Internal marker state skips validation on the next empty tag
findings.body: An internal element leaves `isInternalElement` set for the next attribute-less tag, which skips that tag's schema-required, default, and forced attributes. With a schema such as `span[!data-mce-type],img[!src|alt=default|title:forced]`, parsing `` emits the otherwise-invalid ``; parsing `` alone rejects it for missing `src`. **Evidence:** Attribute-bearing tags set `isInternalElement` from `data-mce-type` at `src/core/main/ts/api/html/SaxParser.ts:357-363`, but the no-attribute branch only resets `attrList` at `src/core/main/ts/api/html/SaxParser.ts:369-372`. Required/default/forced attribute handling is skipped while the stale flag is true at `src/core/main/ts/api/html/SaxParser.ts:375-436`. `DomParser` passes validation on and uses the parser callbacks to append the emitted node (`src/core/main/ts/api/html/DomParser.ts:425-435,474-515,633-635`). **Impact:** An input ordering quirk bypasses schema enforcement for one following empty-attribute element. The retained element has no attacker-supplied attribute value, so this is a contained, recoverable validation error and **low** severity. **Fix:** Reset `isInternalElement` to `false` before each start tag's attribute handling, including the no-attribute branch.

findings.title: Bogus-subtree skipping consumes content after self-closed tags
findings.body: Skipping a `data-mce-bogus="all"` subtree can consume valid content after it when that subtree contains an explicitly self-closed non-void tag. For `keepafter`, the skip helper counts `` as another open element. The outer `` then only reduces the depth, so it also skips `keep` and emits only `after`. **Evidence:** The bogus marker moves the tokenizer to `findEndTagIndex` at `src/core/main/ts/api/html/SaxParser.ts:335-340`. That helper increments nesting for every non-short-ended start tag and does not recognize an explicit `/>` suffix at `src/core/main/ts/api/html/SaxParser.ts:88-113`. In contrast, ordinary parsing treats a non-short-ended tag ending in `/` as self-closing at `src/core/main/ts/api/html/SaxParser.ts:484-490`; `span` is not schema-short-ended (`src/core/main/ts/api/html/Schema.ts:434-435`). **Impact:** Content after an internal bogus subtree is silently lost for documents containing this valid HTML form. This is contained to one document and can be corrected by re-editing it, so it is **low** severity. **Fix:** Make `findEndTagIndex` ignore explicit self-closing start tags, matching the main parser's `/>` handling.

Recorded one high-severity finding: untrusted serialized strings can collide with predictable placeholders and become executable JavaScript expressions.

The added entry point restores `serialize-javascript` 3.0.0 behavior but omits the upstream CVE-2020-7660 fix present in the repository’s `origin/pr/fixed` branch. The test suite passes (`66 passing`). I also reviewed function-source HTML escaping and RegExp flag serialization; both have edge-case concerns, but I did not record them because their exploitation requires additional nonstandard caller-controlled JavaScript-object construction.

findings.title: Untrusted serialized strings can become executable placeholder expressions
findings.body:
An attacker who can supply a string in a value serialized alongside a supported non-JSON value can turn that string into executable JavaScript in the output. The marker UID is generated once with `Math.random()` and is present verbatim in serialization output; it can therefore be learned from one response from the process. The attacker then supplies `\\"@__R-<learned UID>-0__@\\"` (and arranges or waits for a regexp at index 0). JSON.stringify emits an escaped quote, but the replacement regexp still matches the marker within that JSON string and replaces it with `new RegExp(...)`, breaking out of the string when the documented eval/inline-script consumer processes it.

**Evidence:** `index.js:9-11` uses a process-wide, predictable marker and matches only the quoted marker, with no check for an escaping backslash. `index.js:81-82` writes regexp markers, and `index.js:176-181` escapes the JSON before `index.js:190-217` blindly replaces every marker occurrence. The fixed branch changes this exact code to use `randombytes` and captures a preceding backslash so escaped markers are left untouched.

**Impact:** This crosses the boundary from untrusted serialized state to code executed by consumers of this package's documented JavaScript output (`README.md:16-18`, `README.md:117-127`). It enables reflected or stored XSS in applications that embed the output, so severity is high under the review policy (trust-boundary code execution with recoverable persistence).

**Fix:** Generate the marker from cryptographic random bytes and change the replacement regexp/callback to retain a marker preceded by a backslash, as in the fixed upstream implementation.

The PR adds the vulnerable static-server fallback. It joins raw request paths to the web root without containment checks, allowing remote requests with literal `..` segments to list directories outside the configured root. I also checked the directory-listing error path and fallback index serving; both have race-dependent crash behavior but require a concurrent local filesystem change, so I did not report them.

findings.title: Unauthenticated requests can list directories outside the web root
findings.body:
An unauthenticated client can use a literal `..` request path to list directories outside the configured web root. For example, with web root `/tmp/webroot` and a sibling `/tmp/outside`, `GET /../outside/ HTTP/1.1` returns the contents of `/tmp/outside/` (clients that normalize paths need `curl --path-as-is` or a raw request).

**Evidence:** The fallback uses the raw parsed request pathname in `path.join(dir, pathname)` without rejecting parent components or verifying the result remains below `dir` (`simplehttpserver/simplehttpserver.js:57-61`). It then stats and reads that resulting directory and returns its listing (`simplehttpserver/simplehttpserver.js:61-79`, `simplehttpserver/simplehttpserver.js:101-142`). Express static falls through for this raw traversal, so it does not protect the fallback. This was reproduced with the declared Express 4.13/send 0.13 dependency line: a raw request for `/../outside/` returned a 200 directory listing containing a sentinel file outside the web root.

**Impact:** This crosses the server's web-root trust boundary and can disclose any process-readable directory or file reachable through the fallback. The default listener is all interfaces (`simplehttpserver/simplehttpserver.js:20-27`, `simplehttpserver/simplehttpserver.js:146`), so remote clients can exploit it when the service is reachable. Per the review policy's reach/persistence matrix, unauthorized data disclosure is high severity.

**Fix:** Reject dot-segment pathnames before filesystem access and resolve the target only if its relative path proves it remains under the absolute web root; apply that invariant to every fallback filesystem operation.
